While the Constitution does not formally classify the Directive Principles of State Policy, for a better understanding of their scope and intent, they are conventionally categorized based on their content and the underlying ideology. This classification helps in grasping the diverse objectives that the framers of the Constitution sought to achieve through these principles.

  • Socialistic Principles: These principles are aimed at providing social and economic justice and paving the way for a welfare state. They reflect the ideology of democratic socialism, which advocates for a mixed economy where the state plays a significant role in regulating the economy and ensuring equitable distribution of resources.
    • Article 38: The State shall strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting as effectively as it may a social order in which justice, social, economic and political, shall inform all the institutions of national life. It further directs the State to minimize inequalities in income, status, facilities, and opportunities, not only amongst individuals but also amongst groups of people residing in different areas or engaged in different vocations. This is the foundational article for the concept of a welfare state.
    • Article 39: This article contains several crucial directives aimed at securing specific socialistic goals:
      • (a) The State shall direct its policy towards securing that the citizens, men and women equally, have the right to an adequate means of livelihood. This emphasizes economic security for all.
      • (b) The ownership and control of the material resources of the community are so distributed as best to subserve the common good. This promotes equitable distribution rather than concentration of wealth.
      • (c) The operation of the economic system does not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment. This is a direct measure against monopolies and economic disparities.
      • (d) There is equal pay for equal work for both men and women. This is a significant step towards gender equality in the workplace.
      • (e) The health and strength of workers, men and women, and the tender age of children are not abused, and that citizens are not forced by economic necessity to enter avocations unsuited to their age or strength. This protects vulnerable sections of the workforce.
      • (f) Children are given opportunities and facilities to develop in a healthy manner and in conditions of freedom and dignity and that childhood and youth are protected against exploitation and against moral and material abandonment. (Added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976). This highlights the state's responsibility towards child welfare.
    • Article 39A: To promote equal justice and to provide free legal aid to the poor. (Added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976). This ensures that no citizen is denied justice merely due to economic or other disabilities.
    • Article 41: To secure for the people the right to work, to education, and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness, and disablement, within the limits of the State's economic capacity and development. This has led to schemes like MGNREGA and various social security programs.
    • Article 42: To make provision for just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief. This underpins labor laws and maternity benefit schemes.
    • Article 43: To secure a living wage, conditions of work ensuring a decent standard of life and full enjoyment of leisure and social and cultural opportunities for all workers. It also promotes cottage industries on an individual or co-operative basis in rural areas.
    • Article 43A: To take steps, by suitable legislation or in any other way, to secure the participation of workers in the management of undertakings, establishments, or other organizations engaged in any industry. (Added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976).
    • Article 47: To raise the level of nutrition and the standard of living of its people and the improvement of public health. This includes the prohibition of consumption of intoxicating drinks and drugs which are injurious to health (though this also has Gandhian undertones).
  • Gandhian Principles: These principles are based on the ideology of Mahatma Gandhi, reflecting his vision for a decentralized, self-sufficient India. They were incorporated to fulfill Gandhi's dreams for a truly independent nation.
    • Article 40: To organize village panchayats and endow them with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as units of self-government. This was a cornerstone of Gandhi's vision of 'Gram Swaraj' and was later realized through the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts.
    • Article 43: To promote cottage industries on an individual or co-operative basis in rural areas. This aims at rural economic self-sufficiency and employment generation.
    • Article 43B: To promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control, and professional management of co-operative societies. (Added by the 97th Amendment Act, 2011). This strengthens the cooperative movement, a key aspect of Gandhian economics.
    • Article 46: To promote with special care the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections of the people, and, in particular, of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, and to protect them from social injustice and all forms of exploitation. This reflects Gandhi's concern for the upliftment of the marginalized.
    • Article 47: To prohibit the consumption of intoxicating drinks and drugs which are injurious to health. This is a direct reflection of Gandhi's advocacy for temperance and public health.
    • Article 48: To prohibit the slaughter of cows and calves and other milch and draught cattle and to improve their breeds. This reflects the reverence for cattle in Indian culture, an aspect Gandhi deeply respected.
  • Liberal-Intellectual Principles: These principles are based on the ideology of liberalism, advocating for individual rights, modern administrative practices, and international peace. They aim to establish a modern, progressive, and globally responsible state.
    • Article 44: To secure for the citizens a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) throughout the territory of India. This aims to replace personal laws based on religious scriptures and customs with a common set of laws governing marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption for all citizens, promoting national integration.
    • Article 45: To provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years. (The original Article 45 mandated free and compulsory education for all children until they complete the age of fourteen years, but this was amended by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, which made education for 6-14 years a Fundamental Right under Article 21A).
    • Article 48: To organize agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines. This also includes the protection and improvement of the environment and safeguarding of forests and wildlife. (The environmental protection aspect was added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976).
    • Article 49: To protect monuments, places, and objects of artistic or historic interest declared to be of national importance. This reflects the state's duty to preserve cultural heritage.
    • Article 50: To separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State. This is crucial for ensuring the independence of the judiciary and upholding the rule of law.
    • Article 51: To promote international peace and security and maintain just and honourable relations between nations; to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organized peoples with one another; and to encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration. This article lays down the foundational principles of India's foreign policy.
⚡ PYQ Insight: (CDS 2019, 2021) "Which article directs the State to organize village panchayats?" Answer: Article 40 (Gandhian Principle).

Amendments to DPSP

Over the years, several amendments have been made to the Constitution, adding new Directive Principles or modifying existing ones, reflecting the evolving socio-economic needs and priorities of the nation. These amendments underscore the dynamic nature of the Constitution and the continuous effort to strengthen the welfare state objectives.

  • 42nd Amendment Act, 1976: This was a significant amendment, often referred to as a 'mini-Constitution,' which added four new DPSPs to the existing list:
    • Article 39(f): To secure opportunities for healthy development of children.
    • Article 39A: To promote equal justice and to provide free legal aid to the poor.
    • Article 43A: To secure the participation of workers in the management of industries.
    • Article 48A: To protect and improve the environment and to safeguard forests and wildlife.
  • 44th Amendment Act, 1978: This amendment added one DPSP:
    • Article 38(2): To minimize inequalities in income, status, facilities, and opportunities. This reinforced the commitment to social and economic justice.
  • 86th Amendment Act, 2002: This amendment changed the subject matter of Article 45:
    • It made elementary education (for children aged 6-14 years) a Fundamental Right under Article 21A. Consequently, Article 45 was amended to provide for early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years.
  • 97th Amendment Act, 2011: This amendment added a new DPSP relating to cooperative societies:
    • Article 43B: To promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control, and professional management of co-operative societies.

Criticism of DPSP

Despite their noble objectives, the DPSPs have faced criticism from various quarters since their inception. These criticisms primarily revolve around their non-justiciable nature and their perceived lack of clarity or coherence.

  • No Legal Force: The most significant criticism is their non-justiciable character. Critics argue that without legal enforceability, these principles are mere 'pious declarations,' 'moral homilies,' or 'constitutional platitudes' with no real teeth. K.T. Shah famously called them "a cheque on a bank, payable only when the bank's resources permit."
  • Illogically Arranged: Some critics argue that the DPSPs are not logically arranged and lack a consistent philosophy. They point out that principles from different ideologies (socialistic, Gandhian, liberal-intellectual) are mixed without a clear order, leading to potential confusion in their implementation.
  • Conservative: Critics like Ivor Jennings described the DPSPs as being based on the political philosophy of the 19th century, arguing that they are not suitable for the 21st century. They suggest that some principles are outdated or too conservative for a modern, progressive state.
  • Constitutional Conflict: The non-justiciable nature of DPSPs can lead to conflicts between the legislative and executive branches (which are guided by DPSPs) and the judiciary (which enforces Fundamental Rights). This tension has been a recurring theme in Indian constitutional history, particularly in cases involving the balance between individual rights and collective welfare.
  • Redundancy: Some argue that certain DPSPs are redundant or merely reiterate what is already implied in other parts of the Constitution or through general principles of governance.

Significance and Implementation of DPSP

Despite the criticisms, the Directive Principles of State Policy hold immense significance in the governance of India and have played a crucial role in shaping the nation's socio-economic landscape. They are not just moral ideals but have served as a constant reminder and guiding force for policymakers.

  • Guiding Principles for Legislation: DPSPs serve as a fundamental guide for the Union and State governments in enacting laws and formulating policies. They provide a framework for achieving the vision of a welfare state and social justice. Many laws, such as the Minimum Wages Act, Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, Maternity Benefit Act, and environmental protection acts, draw their inspiration directly from DPSPs.
  • Moral Authority and Public Opinion: Though not legally enforceable, DPSPs carry significant moral and political authority. Any government that disregards them risks losing public trust and electoral support. They serve as a yardstick for the public to measure the performance of the government.
  • Facilitating Stability and Welfare: By providing a broad framework for socio-economic development, DPSPs help in maintaining social stability and promoting the welfare of the people. They aim to reduce disparities and ensure inclusive growth.
  • Aid to Courts: While non-justiciable, courts often refer to DPSPs when interpreting Fundamental Rights or other constitutional provisions. They help courts determine the 'reasonableness' of restrictions on Fundamental Rights and understand the broader objectives of the Constitution.
  • Examples of Implementation:
    • Planning Commission/NITI Aayog: The establishment of the Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog) was a direct effort to implement the socio-economic goals enshrined in the DPSPs through five-year plans.
    • Land Reforms: Abolition of zamindari, ceiling on land holdings, and distribution of surplus land were aimed at implementing Article 39(b) and (c).
    • Labour Laws: Legislation like the Minimum Wages Act, Factories Act, Contract Labour Act, and Maternity Benefit Act are direct outcomes of Articles 39, 41, 42, and 43.
    • Panchayati Raj: The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts, which institutionalized local self-governance, are a direct fulfillment of Article 40.
    • Wildlife Protection: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, are legislative steps towards fulfilling Article 48A.
    • Legal Aid: The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, established a nationwide network for providing free and competent legal services to the weaker sections of society, in line with Article 39A.
    • MGNREGA: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005, is a significant step towards realizing the 'right to work' enshrined in Article 41.
    • Right to Education (RTE): While elementary education became a Fundamental Right, the spirit of universal education originated from Article 45.
    • Nationalisation of Banks: This was a step towards preventing the concentration of wealth and ensuring equitable distribution of resources, aligning with Article 39(b) and (c).

Relationship between Fundamental Rights and DPSP

The relationship between Fundamental Rights (FRs) and Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs) has been one of the most dynamic and debated aspects of Indian constitutional law. Both are crucial for the development of the individual and the nation, but their non-justiciable versus justiciable nature has often led to perceived conflicts, which the Supreme Court has addressed in several landmark judgments.

  • Initial Stance (Champakam Dorairajan Case, 1951): The Supreme Court initially held that in case of a conflict between FRs and DPSPs, Fundamental Rights would prevail. It stated that DPSPs, being non-justiciable, had to conform to and run as subsidiary to the Fundamental Rights. However, it also acknowledged that Parliament could amend FRs to implement DPSPs.
  • Parliament's Reaction (1st Amendment Act, 1951): To overcome the judgment in Champakam Dorairajan, Parliament enacted the 1st Amendment Act, 1951, adding Article 15(4) and 19(6) to enable the state to make special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes and for nationalization of certain trades.
  • Golaknath Case (1967): The Supreme Court reversed its earlier stance, holding that Fundamental Rights are 'transcendental' and 'immutable' and cannot be amended by Parliament, even for the implementation of DPSPs. This created a deadlock between Parliament and the Judiciary.
  • Parliament's Counter-Reaction (24th and 25th Amendment Acts):
    • 24th Amendment Act, 1971: Empowered Parliament to amend any part of the Constitution, including FRs, by passing a Constitutional Amendment Act.
    • 25th Amendment Act, 1971: Inserted a new Article 31C, which stated that no law giving effect to the DPSP contained in Article 39(b) and (c) could be challenged on the grounds that it violated Articles 14, 19, or 31. It also added a provision that such a law could not be questioned in court on the ground that it did not give effect to these principles.
  • Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973): This landmark judgment introduced the 'Basic Structure Doctrine.' The Supreme Court upheld the 24th Amendment, affirming Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution, including FRs. However, it also held that this power was not absolute and Parliament could not alter the 'basic structure' of the Constitution. Regarding Article 31C, the Court upheld its first part (protection for laws implementing 39(b) & (c) from Articles 14, 19, 31) but struck down the second part (which barred judicial review), stating that judicial review is a basic feature of the Constitution. This meant that while Parliament could prioritize certain DPSPs, the courts could still examine if the law genuinely aimed to implement those DPSPs.
  • 42nd Amendment Act, 1976: During the Emergency, Parliament further expanded Article 31C, extending its protection to *all* Directive Principles, not just Article 39(b) and (c). This effectively gave supremacy to all DPSPs over Fundamental Rights (Articles 14, 19, 31).
  • Minerva Mills Case (1980): The Supreme Court struck down the extended Article 31C (added by the 42nd Amendment), declaring it unconstitutional. The Court held that the harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is an essential feature of the basic structure of the Constitution. It reiterated that FRs are not ends in themselves but are the means to achieve the goals set out in the DPSPs. The Court stated that "the Indian Constitution is built on the bedrock of the balance between FRs and DPSPs."
  • Current Position: The current position, as established by the Minerva Mills case, is that Fundamental Rights are generally superior to DPSPs. However, this does not mean DPSPs are irrelevant. They are complementary and supplementary to each other. The courts strive to interpret FRs in light of DPSPs to achieve the goal of social justice. Parliament can still implement DPSPs, but it must do so without violating the basic structure of the Constitution. The principle of 'harmonious construction' is applied, meaning that courts attempt to interpret both sets of principles in a way that avoids conflict and allows both to operate effectively.
citizenship:
Citizenship in India

Constitutional Provisions

Citizenship in India is a fundamental aspect of the Indian polity, meticulously outlined in Part II of the Constitution, specifically spanning from Articles 5 to 11. This section lays down the foundational principles for who was considered a citizen at the commencement of the Constitution and empowers the Parliament to legislate on all subsequent matters related to citizenship. India, in a deliberate move to foster national unity and integrity, adopted the system of Single Citizenship. This means that every Indian citizen is a citizen of the Union of India and does not hold separate citizenship for the state they reside in, unlike federal systems such as the USA, which operates on a principle of dual citizenship (citizenship of the federal union and citizenship of the state).

The framers of the Indian Constitution, recognizing the immediate need to define citizenship at the nation's birth, primarily dealt with the citizenship of individuals at the specific moment of the Constitution's commencement, which was January 26, 1950. They consciously chose not to create a permanent and exhaustive law for citizenship, instead entrusting the crucial responsibility to the Parliament to legislate on all future matters concerning the acquisition, termination, and other related aspects of Indian citizenship. This foresight allowed for flexibility and adaptation of citizenship laws to evolving national circumstances and international dynamics.

  • Article 5: Citizenship at the Commencement of the Constitution: This article defined who became a citizen of India on January 26, 1950. It stipulated that any person who had their domicile in the territory of India and who was either born in India, or either of whose parents was born in India, or who had been ordinarily resident in India for not less than five years immediately preceding such commencement, would be a citizen of India. This provision primarily addressed the immediate post-partition scenario and the establishment of the new republic.
  • Article 6: Rights of Citizenship of Certain Persons Who Have Migrated to India from Pakistan: This article provided for the citizenship rights of individuals who migrated from Pakistan to India before July 19, 1948 (the date of introduction of the permit system) and those who migrated after this date but had registered themselves as citizens after residing in India for at least six months. It was a crucial provision to manage the massive population transfers following the partition.
  • Article 7: Rights of Citizenship of Certain Migrants to Pakistan: This article dealt with persons who migrated from India to Pakistan after March 1, 1947, but later returned to India under a permit for resettlement or permanent return. Such persons could register as citizens after six months of residence. This addressed the complex situation of individuals who initially moved to Pakistan but subsequently wished to return to India.
  • Article 8: Rights of Citizenship of Certain Persons of Indian Origin Residing Outside India: This article granted citizenship to persons of Indian origin residing outside India, provided they or any of their parents or grandparents were born in undivided India and they had registered as citizens through the diplomatic or consular representative of India in the country where they were residing. This provision aimed to maintain ties with the Indian diaspora.
  • Article 9: Persons Voluntarily Acquiring Citizenship of a Foreign State Not to be Citizens: This article explicitly states that if a person voluntarily acquires citizenship of a foreign state, they shall cease to be a citizen of India. This reinforces the principle of single citizenship and prevents dual nationality for Indian citizens.
  • Article 10: Continuance of the Rights of Citizenship: This article ensures that every person who is or is deemed to be a citizen of India under any of the preceding provisions shall continue to be such a citizen, subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament. It guarantees the continuity of citizenship unless explicitly altered by parliamentary law.
  • Article 11: Parliament to Regulate the Right of Citizenship by Law: This is the most pivotal article, empowering the Parliament of India to make any provision with respect to the acquisition and termination of citizenship and all other matters relating to citizenship. This article serves as the constitutional basis for the enactment of the Citizenship Act, 1955, and its subsequent amendments.
🔥 High-Yield Fact: Article 11 unequivocally empowers the Parliament (and not state legislatures, underscoring the unitary nature of citizenship law in India) to regulate the right of citizenship by law. This constitutional mandate led directly to the enactment of the comprehensive Citizenship Act, 1955. This Act is the primary legislation governing the acquisition and loss of Indian citizenship subsequent to the commencement of the Constitution, providing a detailed framework that has been amended multiple times to address contemporary challenges and policy objectives, including significant amendments in 1986, 2003, 2005, and most recently, in 2019.

Acquisition of Citizenship (Citizenship Act, 1955)

The Citizenship Act, 1955, as amended over the years, outlines five primary ways through which an individual can acquire Indian citizenship. These methods are designed to cover various scenarios, from birth within the territory to naturalization of foreigners, reflecting India's legal and demographic considerations.

  • By Birth (Jus Soli - Right of the Soil):
    • Original Provision (1950-1986): A person born in India on or after January 26, 1950, but before July 1, 1987, was a citizen of India by birth, irrespective of the nationality of their parents. This was a pure 'jus soli' principle, making citizenship dependent solely on the place of birth.
    • Amendment of 1986: To curb the influx of illegal immigrants, particularly from neighboring countries, the Act was amended. For persons born in India on or after July 1, 1987, citizenship by birth required that either of their parents must be an Indian citizen at the time of their birth. This introduced a 'modified jus soli' principle.
    • Amendment of 2003: Further tightening the provisions, for persons born in India on or after December 3, 2004, both parents must be citizens of India, or one parent must be a citizen of India and the other must not be an illegal migrant at the time of their birth. This amendment aimed to prevent children of illegal migrants from automatically acquiring Indian citizenship, emphasizing national security and demographic concerns.
    • Exclusions: Children of foreign diplomats and enemy aliens born in India are generally not considered citizens by birth.
  • By Descent (Jus Sanguinis - Right of Blood):
    • Original Provision (1950-1992): A person born outside India on or after January 26, 1950, but before December 10, 1992, was a citizen of India by descent if their father was an Indian citizen at the time of their birth. This provision was gender-biased, only recognizing paternal lineage.
    • Amendment of 1992: To remove gender discrimination, the Act was amended. For persons born outside India on or after December 10, 1992, citizenship by descent could be claimed if either of their parents was an Indian citizen at the time of their birth.
    • Amendment of 2003: Further modifications were introduced for persons born outside India on or after December 3, 2004. Such a person shall not be a citizen by descent unless their birth is registered at an Indian consulate within one year of the date of birth or with the permission of the Central Government after the expiry of the said period. Additionally, an undertaking must be given by the parents that the minor child does not hold a passport of another country. This measure was introduced to prevent dual nationality and ensure proper record-keeping for the diaspora.
    • Purpose: This method is crucial for children of Indian citizens working or residing abroad, ensuring their connection to their country of origin.
  • By Registration:

    This method allows certain categories of persons to acquire Indian citizenship upon application, provided they meet specific residency and other conditions. The process involves submitting an application to the prescribed authority and taking an oath of allegiance.

    • A person of Indian origin (PIO) who has been ordinarily resident in India for seven years immediately before making an application for registration. This category often includes individuals whose ancestors were Indian but who themselves were born abroad.
    • A person of Indian origin who is ordinarily resident in any country or place outside undivided India. This caters to the broader Indian diaspora.
    • A person who is married to an Indian citizen and has been ordinarily resident in India for seven years immediately before making an application for registration. This is a common route for foreign spouses of Indian citizens.
    • Minor children of persons who are citizens of India. This facilitates the citizenship of children whose parents are already Indian citizens but who may not qualify by birth or descent (e.g., adopted children).
    • Persons who are major and of full capacity and whose parents are registered as citizens of India under Section 5(1)(a) or 6(1) of the Act.
    • Persons who are major and of full capacity and who, or either of their parents, were earlier citizens of independent India, and have been ordinarily resident in India for twelve months immediately before making an application for registration.
    • Persons who are major and of full capacity and are registered as an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) Cardholder for five years, and have been ordinarily resident in India for twelve months immediately before making an application for registration. This provides a pathway for OCIs to eventually acquire full citizenship.
    • Key Requirement: All applicants under this category must take an oath of allegiance, affirming their faith in the Constitution of India.
  • By Naturalisation:

    This is a pathway for foreigners who are not of Indian origin to acquire Indian citizenship. It is a more stringent process, requiring a longer period of residence and other qualifications, reflecting the principle that citizenship is a privilege, not an automatic right, for those without direct ties to India.

    • The applicant must not be a citizen of any country where Indian citizens are prevented from becoming citizens by naturalisation. This is a reciprocity clause.
    • They must have renounced the citizenship of their own country. India's single citizenship principle is strictly enforced here.
    • They must have resided in India or been in government service for a total of twelve years, including a continuous period of one year immediately preceding the date of application, and for eleven years in the aggregate in the fourteen years preceding the one-year period. This long residency requirement ensures a deep integration into Indian society.
    • They must be of good character and have an adequate knowledge of a language specified in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution. This promotes cultural integration and communication.
    • They must intend to reside in India or to enter into service under the Government of India or an international organization of which India is a member.
    • Special Dispensation: The Government of India may waive some of these conditions in cases of exceptional merit, such as individuals who have rendered distinguished service to the cause of science, philosophy, art, literature, world peace, or human progress. This allows for flexibility to attract and retain talent beneficial to the nation.
    • Impact of CAA 2019: The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, introduced a significant change for specific minority communities (Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, and Christians) who migrated from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan due to religious persecution. For these individuals, the aggregate residency requirement for naturalisation was reduced from eleven years to five years. This amendment is highly debated and aims to provide a fast-track route to citizenship for these persecuted minorities.
  • By Incorporation of Territory:

    This method applies when a foreign territory becomes a part of India. The Government of India, by an order, specifies the persons who shall be citizens of India from a notified date. This is a consequence of territorial acquisition and ensures that the inhabitants of the newly incorporated territory automatically become citizens of India, integrating them into the national fabric.

    • Examples:
      • Puducherry (formerly Pondicherry): When it was integrated into India from French rule in 1962, the Government of India issued the Citizenship (Pondicherry) Order, 1962, to grant Indian citizenship to its residents.
      • Goa, Daman & Diu: After their liberation from Portuguese rule in 1961, the Citizenship (Goa, Daman & Diu) Order, 1962, provided for the citizenship of their inhabitants.
      • Sikkim: Upon its full integration into India as a state in 1975, its residents were granted Indian citizenship.
      • Dadra & Nagar Haveli: Integrated in 1961, similar orders were issued.
    • Mechanism: This is an executive action, where the Central Government issues a specific order under the Citizenship Act, 1955, detailing the terms and conditions for granting citizenship to the residents of the newly acquired territory.
⚠️ Trap Alert: Acquisition by "Marriage" is not a separate, distinct category under the Citizenship Act, 1955. Instead, if a foreigner marries an Indian citizen, they can apply for Indian citizenship through the method of Registration. The specific condition for this is that the person must have been ordinarily resident in India for seven years immediately before making the application. It is crucial for defence exam aspirants to understand this distinction, as "marriage" itself is not a direct route but a qualifying condition for the registration process. Confusing it with naturalisation or a standalone category is a common mistake.

Loss of Indian Citizenship

The Citizenship Act, 1955, also prescribes three ways in which an Indian citizen can lose their citizenship. These provisions are designed to uphold the principle of single citizenship and to address situations where an individual voluntarily chooses to abandon Indian citizenship or acts in a manner deemed detrimental to national interests.

  • By Renunciation:
    • This is a voluntary act where an Indian citizen, who is also a citizen of another country or intends to become one, declares their intention to renounce Indian citizenship.
    • The declaration is made in the prescribed manner, and upon its registration by the Central Government, the person ceases to be an Indian citizen.
    • However, if India is engaged in a war, the registration of such a declaration may be withheld by the Central Government. This is a national security safeguard.
    • When a person renounces Indian citizenship, every minor child of that person also ceases to be an Indian citizen. However, when such a child attains the age of eighteen, they may resume Indian citizenship by making a declaration of intent.
  • By Termination:
    • This occurs when an Indian citizen voluntarily acquires the citizenship of another country.
    • According to Article 9 of the Constitution and Section 9 of the Citizenship Act, 1955, Indian citizenship automatically terminates if a person voluntarily obtains citizenship of a foreign state.
    • This provision strictly enforces the principle of single citizenship in India. The moment an Indian citizen becomes a citizen of another country (without prior renunciation), their Indian citizenship is deemed terminated.
    • The Central Government, however, must be satisfied that the acquisition of foreign citizenship was voluntary.
  • By Deprivation:
    • This is a compulsory termination of Indian citizenship by the Central Government. It is a punitive measure and is generally applicable to citizens who have acquired citizenship by registration or naturalisation, though it can also apply to citizens by birth under certain circumstances.
    • The Central Government can deprive a citizen of their citizenship if:
      • The citizenship was obtained by fraud, false representation, or concealment of any material fact.
      • The citizen has shown disloyalty to the Constitution of India.
      • The citizen has unlawfully traded or communicated with an enemy during a war.
      • The citizen has, within five years of registration or naturalisation, been sentenced to imprisonment in any country for two years or more.
      • The citizen has been ordinarily resident out of India for seven years continuously, unless they are in service under the Government of India or an international organization of which India is a member, or have registered annually at an Indian consulate their intention to retain Indian citizenship.
    • This power of deprivation is exercised with caution and usually after an inquiry, as it involves taking away a fundamental right and identity.

Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) Cardholder Scheme

The concept of Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) was introduced by amending the Citizenship Act in 2005, primarily to address the demands of the Indian diaspora for some form of dual citizenship, without actually granting full dual nationality. It provides certain benefits and privileges to foreign citizens of Indian origin, allowing them to maintain a strong connection with India.

  • Who is eligible?
    • A foreign national, who was a citizen of India on or after 26th January 1950, or was eligible to become a citizen of India on 26th January 1950.
    • Belonged to a territory that became part of India after 15th August 1947.
    • Is a child or a grandchild or a great-grandchild of such a citizen.
    • A minor child of such persons.
    • Spouse of foreign origin of an Indian citizen or spouse of foreign origin of an OCI Cardholder, provided the marriage is registered and subsisted for a continuous period of not less than two years immediately preceding the presentation of the application.
    • Exclusions: Citizens of Pakistan and Bangladesh are explicitly not eligible for OCI status.
  • Benefits of an OCI Cardholder:
    • Multiple entry, multi-purpose lifelong visa for visiting India.
    • Exemption from registration with the Foreigners Regional Registration Officer (FRRO) or Foreigners Registration Officer (FRO) for any length of stay in India.
    • Parity with Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) in respect of all facilities available to them in economic, financial, and educational fields, except in matters relating to the acquisition of agricultural or plantation properties.
    • Parity with Indian nationals in the matter of entry fees to national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, national monuments, historical sites, and museums in India.
    • Can apply for Indian citizenship after 5 years of OCI registration and 12 months of continuous stay in India.
    • OCI cardholders can open special bank accounts in India, make investments, and undertake certain professional activities.
  • Disabilities of an OCI Cardholder:
    • Does not have the right to vote.
    • Does not have the right to be a member of the Legislative Assembly or Legislative Council or Parliament.
    • Does not hold any public office (e.g., President, Vice-President, Judge of Supreme Court or High Court).
    • Cannot acquire agricultural or plantation properties.
    • Cannot undertake certain research work without prior permission.
    • Cannot be employed in government service.
  • Merger of PIO and OCI Schemes: In 2015, the Persons of Indian Origin (PIO) Card scheme was merged with the OCI Card scheme. All existing PIO cardholders are deemed to be OCI cardholders. This streamlined the process and reduced confusion for the diaspora.

Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 (CAA)

The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, represents a significant and controversial amendment to the Citizenship Act, 1955. It was enacted with the stated objective of providing a pathway to Indian citizenship for specific religious minorities who have faced persecution in three neighboring countries.

  • Key Provisions:
    • It amends the Citizenship Act, 1955, to make Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian illegal migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan, who entered India on or before December 31, 2014, eligible for Indian citizenship.
    • It reduces the period of residency requirement for naturalisation for these specific groups from eleven years to five years.
    • The Act explicitly states that these migrants will not be treated as illegal migrants.
    • It exempts certain areas from its application, including tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and Tripura as included in the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution, and the area covered under the 'Inner Line' permit system notified under the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873. This exemption is primarily to protect the indigenous populations and their cultural identities in these regions.
  • Rationale and Controversy:
    • Government's Stated Rationale: The government argued that these minority communities faced religious persecution in their home countries (Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Pakistan are Islamic republics) and sought refuge in India. The CAA is intended to provide them with a dignified life and citizenship.
    • Criticisms: The Act faced widespread criticism for explicitly linking citizenship to religion, which opponents argued violates the secular principles enshrined in the Indian Constitution (Articles 14, 15, 21). Critics also pointed out the exclusion of Muslims from the list, arguing that persecuted Muslim minorities (e.g., Shias, Ahmadiyyas in Pakistan) were not included. Concerns were also raised about its potential impact on the National Register of Citizens (NRC) and the demographic balance in certain border states.
    • Legal Status: The Act has been challenged in the Supreme Court of India, with petitions arguing its unconstitutionality.
president:
The President of India

Executive Head of the State

The President of India holds the esteemed position as the constitutional head of the Indian State, embodying the sovereignty and unity of the nation. Referred to as the 'first citizen of India', the President is the paramount figure in the Indian political system, though primarily a nominal or titular executive in a parliamentary democracy. This means that while all executive actions are formally taken in the President's name, the real executive power rests with the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.

Furthermore, the President serves as the Supreme Commander of the Indian Armed Forces (Army, Navy, and Air Force), a critical role underscoring the civilian control over the military, a cornerstone of democratic governance. This authority is exercised in accordance with law, meaning decisions related to defence policy, deployment, and declarations of war or peace are made by the elected government, with the President's formal assent.

The office of the President is meticulously covered in Part V of the Constitution, specifically from Articles 52 to 78. These articles delineate the President's election, term, impeachment, powers, and functions, establishing the framework for this pivotal constitutional position.

  • Article 52: The President of India - States that there shall be a President of India. This article establishes the very existence of the office.
  • Article 53: Executive Power of the Union - Declares that the executive power of the Union shall be vested in the President and shall be exercised by him either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with this Constitution. It also explicitly states that the Supreme Command of the Defence Forces of the Union shall be vested in the President and the exercise thereof shall be regulated by law. This highlights the dual nature of the President's executive authority – both general administration and military command.
  • Nature of the Indian Presidency: Unlike the American President who is both the head of state and head of government, the Indian President is only the head of state. The Prime Minister is the head of government. This distinction is crucial for understanding India's parliamentary system, where the executive is accountable to the legislature.
  • Constitutional Significance: The President acts as a guardian of the Constitution, ensuring that the government functions within its prescribed limits. The President's role is to uphold, protect, and defend the Constitution and the law, as per the oath of office.

Election of the President (Article 54)

The President of India is elected indirectly, not directly by the people. This method was chosen by the framers of the Constitution to maintain the parliamentary character of the government and to avoid a potential conflict of authority between a directly elected President and a directly elected Prime Minister. The election is carried out by an Electoral College, a unique body specifically constituted for this purpose. The composition of this Electoral College ensures representation from both the Union and State levels, reflecting the federal structure of India.

The Electoral College consists of the following members:

  • Elected members of both the Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha): This includes all elected Members of Parliament (MPs) from both the Lower House (Lok Sabha) and the Upper House (Rajya Sabha). It is important to note that only elected members participate, ensuring that the President is chosen by representatives who have themselves been elected by the populace.
  • Elected members of the legislative assemblies of the states: This includes all elected Members of Legislative Assemblies (MLAs) from all the states of India. This provision ensures that the states also have a significant voice in the election of the President, reinforcing the federal principle.
  • Elected members of the legislative assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry: This inclusion was a significant amendment brought about by the 70th Amendment Act of 1992. Prior to this amendment, these Union Territories, despite having their own legislative assemblies, did not participate in the Presidential election. Their inclusion acknowledges their quasi-state status and provides them representation in this crucial national election. This amendment came into effect in 1995.

Manner of Election (Article 55)

The election of the President is conducted in accordance with the system of Proportional Representation by means of the Single Transferable Vote. This complex system is designed to ensure that the President is elected by a broad consensus and to give due weightage to the votes of both MPs and MLAs, despite the vast differences in the population of their constituencies. The voting is by secret ballot.

  • Value of Vote of an MLA: The value of the vote of each MLA is calculated based on the population of the state and the total number of elected MLAs in that state. The formula is:

    Value of vote of an MLA = (Total Population of the State / Total number of elected MLAs in the State) x 1/1000

    The term 'population' for this calculation means the population as ascertained at the last preceding census of which the relevant figures have been published. However, by the 84th Amendment Act of 2001, the population figures for the 1971 Census are to be used until the first census taken after the year 2026. This freeze was implemented to avoid penalizing states that have been successful in population control measures.

  • Value of Vote of an MP: The value of the vote of each MP (both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) is uniform across the country. It is calculated by dividing the total value of votes of all elected MLAs of all states by the total number of elected MPs of both Houses of Parliament.

    Value of vote of an MP = (Total value of votes of all elected MLAs of all States / Total number of elected MPs of Parliament)

  • Quota for Election: To be declared elected, a candidate must secure a fixed quota of votes. The quota is determined by the formula:

    Electoral Quota = (Total number of valid votes polled / (Number of candidates to be elected + 1)) + 1

    Since only one President is to be elected, the formula simplifies to: (Total number of valid votes polled / 2) + 1. This ensures that the winning candidate secures more than 50% of the votes polled, thus representing a clear majority.

  • Single Transferable Vote System: Voters mark their preferences (1, 2, 3, etc.) against the names of the candidates. If no candidate secures the quota in the first round of counting, the candidate with the lowest number of first preference votes is eliminated, and their second preference votes are transferred to the remaining candidates. This process continues until one candidate secures the required quota.
⚠️ Trap Alert: It is absolutely crucial to remember that Nominated members (of both Parliament and State Assemblies) and members of State Legislative Councils (Vidhan Parishad) DO NOT participate in the President's election. This is a frequently tested point in defence exams. The rationale behind excluding nominated members is that they are not directly elected by the people, and their participation might dilute the democratic legitimacy of the President's election. Similarly, Legislative Councils exist only in some states and are not uniformly present, hence their exclusion ensures uniformity in the electoral process.

Qualifications for Election as President (Article 58)

To be eligible for election as President, a person must fulfill the following conditions:

  • Must be a citizen of India.
  • Must have completed the age of 35 years.
  • Must be qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha. This means they must be registered as a voter in any parliamentary constituency.
  • Must not hold any office of profit under the Government of India or the Government of any State or under any local or other authority subject to the control of any of the said Governments. However, the President, Vice-President, Governor of any state, and a Minister of the Union or of any state are not deemed to hold any office of profit and are eligible to contest.

Oath or Affirmation (Article 60)

Before entering upon office, the President is required to make and subscribe to an oath or affirmation. This oath is administered by the Chief Justice of India or, in his absence, the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court available. In the oath, the President solemnly swears to faithfully execute the office, to preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution and the law, and to devote himself to the service and well-being of the people of India. This oath underscores the President's role as the guardian of the Constitution.

Term of Office (Article 56)

The President holds office for a term of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office. However, the President can:

  • Resign from office by writing under his hand addressed to the Vice-President. The Vice-President then communicates this resignation to the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
  • Be removed from office by impeachment for 'violation of the Constitution' (Article 61).
  • Continue to hold office, notwithstanding the expiration of his term, until his successor enters upon his office. This provision ensures continuity and avoids a vacuum in the highest office.

Impeachment of the President (Article 61)

The President can be removed from office before the expiry of his term only by the process of impeachment, for 'violation of the Constitution'. This is a quasi-judicial procedure and is a very stringent and difficult process, reflecting the high constitutional status of the President.

  • Grounds for Impeachment: The only ground specified is "violation of the Constitution." The Constitution, however, does not define what constitutes a 'violation of the Constitution', leaving it to be interpreted by Parliament.
  • Initiation of Charges: The impeachment charges can be initiated by either House of Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha).
  • Notice Requirement: The resolution to initiate impeachment proceedings must be signed by at least one-fourth of the total members of the House that is proposing the charges. A 14-day notice must be given to the President before such a resolution is moved.
  • Passing the Resolution: After the notice period, if the resolution is passed by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of that House, it is then sent to the other House.
  • Investigation by the Other House: The other House then investigates the charges. The President has the right to appear and be represented at such investigation.
  • Final Passing of Resolution: If, after the investigation, the second House also passes the resolution by a majority of not less than two-thirds of its total membership, then the President stands removed from office from the date on which the resolution is so passed.
  • Historical Context: No President of India has ever faced impeachment proceedings, highlighting the stability of the Indian political system and the respect accorded to the office.

Veto Powers (Article 111)

Article 111 of the Constitution deals with the President's power to assent to Bills passed by Parliament. This power is a crucial aspect of the legislative process, allowing the President to act as a check on parliamentary legislation and ensuring that bills are thoroughly considered before becoming law. When a Bill, after being passed by both Houses of Parliament, is presented to the President, he has three options:

  1. Absolute Veto: This power allows the President to withhold his assent to a Bill passed by Parliament. When the President exercises an absolute veto, the Bill ends and does not become an Act. This veto is generally used in two situations:
    • Private Member Bills: These are bills introduced by any member of Parliament who is not a minister. The President often withholds assent to such bills, effectively killing them.
    • Government Bills when the Cabinet Resigns: If a Bill is passed by Parliament but the Council of Ministers resigns before the President gives assent, the new Council of Ministers might advise the President to withhold assent to that Bill. A notable example is the PEPSU Appropriation Bill in 1954, where President Dr. Rajendra Prasad withheld assent after the ministry fell.
  2. Suspensive Veto: This power allows the President to return a Bill (other than a Money Bill or a Constitutional Amendment Bill) for reconsideration by Parliament. If Parliament passes the Bill again, with or without amendments, and presents it to the President, the President must give his assent. This means the President's suspensive veto can be overridden by a simple majority in Parliament.
    • Purpose: The suspensive veto is intended to give Parliament a second chance to reconsider a Bill, potentially addressing any concerns raised by the President. It acts as a delaying mechanism rather than an absolute rejection.
    • Exclusions: This veto cannot be used for Money Bills. A Money Bill can only be introduced in Parliament with the prior recommendation of the President. Therefore, when a Money Bill is presented to him for assent, the President can either give his assent or withhold his assent, but cannot return it for reconsideration. Similarly, Constitutional Amendment Bills also do not fall under the purview of suspensive veto; the President is bound to give assent to them (as per the 24th Amendment Act, 1971).
  3. Pocket Veto: This is a unique power where the President neither assents nor rejects the Bill, nor does he return it for reconsideration. Instead, he simply keeps the Bill pending for an indefinite period. The Constitution does not prescribe any time limit within which the President has to declare his decision on a Bill. This allows the President to effectively kill a Bill without outright rejecting it, by simply taking no action.
    • Example: The most famous instance of the pocket veto was by President Giani Zail Singh in 1986 for the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill. This Bill sought to grant the government sweeping powers to intercept mail and was widely criticized for infringing on civil liberties. President Zail Singh kept the Bill pending for several years without taking any action, effectively shelving it. This demonstrated the significant impact a President can have even by inaction.
    • Contrast with US President: While the US President also has a pocket veto, it can only be exercised when Congress adjourns without sending the bill back for reconsideration. The Indian President's pocket veto is more powerful as it can be exercised even when Parliament is in session, due to the absence of a time limit.
⚡ PYQ Insight: (NDA 2022) "Does the President of India possess the Qualified Veto?" Answer: NO. Qualified veto (which can be overridden by a higher majority) is possessed by the American President, not the Indian President. The Qualified Veto requires a higher majority in the legislature to override the President's veto, which is a stronger check on legislative power than the Indian President's Suspensive Veto.

Limitations on Veto Power

  • Constitutional Amendment Bills: The 24th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1971 made it obligatory for the President to give his assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill. He can neither withhold his assent nor return it for reconsideration. This ensures that the process of amending the Constitution is not unduly obstructed by the President.
  • State Bills Reserved by Governor: When a state bill is reserved by the Governor for the consideration of the President (Article 201), the President has similar options: assent, withhold assent, or direct the Governor to return the bill to the state legislature for reconsideration. However, if the state legislature passes the bill again and sends it back to the Governor, the President is not bound to give his assent, unlike in the case of a Bill passed by the Union Parliament. This provides a stronger central check on state legislation.

Powers and Functions of the President

The President of India is endowed with a wide array of powers and functions, categorized broadly into executive, legislative, financial, judicial, diplomatic, military, and emergency powers. While many of these powers are exercised on the 'aid and advice' of the Council of Ministers, their formal vesting in the President makes him the ultimate constitutional authority.

Executive Powers

All executive actions of the Government of India are formally taken in the name of the President (Article 77).

  • Appointment Powers: The President appoints the Prime Minister and other Ministers (on the advice of the PM). He also appoints the Attorney General of India, the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG), the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners, the Chairman and members of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC), Governors of states, the Chief Justice and judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, and Ambassadors and High Commissioners to other countries.
  • Administrative Powers: He can make rules for more convenient transaction of business of the Union government and for the allocation among Ministers of the said business. He also appoints commissions to investigate into the conditions of SCs, STs, and OBCs.
  • Inter-State Council: He can establish an Inter-State Council to promote Centre-state and inter-state cooperation.
  • Union Territories: He directly administers the Union Territories through administrators appointed by him.

Legislative Powers

The President is an integral part of Parliament, though not a member of either House.

  • Summoning and Proroguing Parliament: He can summon or prorogue the sessions of Parliament and dissolve the Lok Sabha.
  • Addressing Parliament: He addresses the Parliament at the commencement of the first session after each general election and the first session of each year, outlining the government's policies and programmes.
  • Sending Messages: He can send messages to either House of Parliament regarding a Bill pending in Parliament or any other matter.
  • Nomination: He nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha from persons having special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, and social service. (Prior to the 104th Amendment Act, 2019, he could also nominate 2 members of the Anglo-Indian community to the Lok Sabha if they were not adequately represented, but this provision has now been removed).
  • Ordinance-Making Power (Article 123): This is a very significant legislative power. When both Houses of Parliament are not in session and the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he can promulgate ordinances. These ordinances have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament but are temporary in nature. They must be approved by Parliament within six weeks of its reassembly, failing which they cease to operate.

Financial Powers

  • Money Bills: A Money Bill can be introduced in Parliament only with his prior recommendation.
  • Annual Financial Statement: He causes the Annual Financial Statement (Budget) to be laid before Parliament.
  • Demands for Grants: No demand for a grant can be made except on his recommendation.
  • Contingency Fund: He can make advances out of the Contingency Fund of India to meet unforeseen expenditures.
  • Finance Commission: He constitutes a Finance Commission every five years to recommend the distribution of revenues between the Centre and the states.

Judicial Powers

  • Appointment of Judges: He appoints the Chief Justice and judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts.
  • Pardoning Power (Article 72): He has the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions, and commutations of punishment or to suspend, remit, or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence. This power extends to:
    • Punishment or sentence by a court martial.
    • Punishment or sentence for an offence against a Union law.
    • Sentence of death.

    This power is independent of the judiciary and is an executive power. It is exercised on the advice of the Union Cabinet.

Diplomatic Powers

  • International Treaties: All international treaties and agreements are negotiated and concluded in the name of the President.
  • Representation: He sends and receives ambassadors and high commissioners.

Military Powers

  • Supreme Commander: He is the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of India.
  • Appointments: He appoints the chiefs of the Army, Navy, and Air Force.
  • War and Peace: He can declare war or conclude peace, subject to the approval of Parliament.

Emergency Powers (Part XVIII)

The President has extraordinary powers to deal with emergency situations, which are crucial for maintaining the sovereignty, unity, integrity, and security of the country.

  • National Emergency (Article 352): Can be declared on grounds of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion. It must be approved by Parliament within one month and can last for six months at a time, extendable indefinitely with parliamentary approval.
  • President's Rule (State Emergency) (Article 356): Can be imposed in a state if the President is satisfied that the government of the state cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution, either on the report of the Governor or otherwise. It must be approved by Parliament within two months and can last for six months, extendable up to a maximum of three years with parliamentary approval.
  • Financial Emergency (Article 360): Can be declared if the President is satisfied that a situation has arisen whereby the financial stability or credit of India or any part of its territory is threatened. It must be approved by Parliament within two months and continues indefinitely until revoked. (This emergency has never been imposed in India).

Relationship with Council of Ministers (Article 74 & 75)

The President acts on the 'aid and advice' of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister. This principle is enshrined in Article 74, which states that there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President, who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice.

  • 42nd Amendment Act, 1976: Made the advice of the Council of Ministers binding on the President.
  • 44th Amendment Act, 1978: Empowered the President to send back the advice for reconsideration once. However, if the Council of Ministers sends the same advice again, the President is bound to act on it. This amendment restored some discretion to the President, allowing for a 'suspensive veto' on executive advice, but ultimately upholding the supremacy of the elected government.
  • Article 75: Deals with the appointment of the Prime Minister and other Ministers, their collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha, and their individual responsibility to the President.

Succession to Presidency

In case of a vacancy in the President's office due to death, resignation, removal, or otherwise, the Vice-President acts as the President. If the Vice-President's office is also vacant, the Chief Justice of India, or in his absence, the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court available, acts as the President. This ensures that there is always someone to discharge the functions of the President, maintaining constitutional continuity.

  • Presidential (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969: This Act provides for the discharge of the functions of the President in certain contingencies. It was notably invoked in 1969 when President Zakir Husain passed away, and Vice-President V.V. Giri resigned to contest the presidential election. The then Chief Justice of India, M. Hidayatullah, acted as the President.
parliament:
The Parliament of India

Composition of Parliament

Under **Article 79** of the Indian Constitution, the Parliament of India is the supreme legislative body of the Republic of India. It is a bicameral legislature, meaning it consists of two houses, and operates under the Westminster parliamentary system. The Article explicitly states that the Parliament of the Union shall consist of three integral parts, each playing a distinct yet interconnected role in the legislative process and the governance of the nation. This structure ensures a system of checks and balances, representing both the people directly and the states of the Indian Union.

  1. **The President of India:** The President is not a member of either House of Parliament but is an indispensable part of its composition. The President's role is crucial for the enactment of laws and for summoning, proroguing, and dissolving Parliament. This reflects the constitutional head of state's involvement in the legislative process, embodying the sovereignty of the nation.
  2. **The Council of States (Rajya Sabha):** This is the Upper House of Parliament, often referred to as the 'House of Elders' or the 'Second Chamber'. It represents the states and union territories of the Indian Union. Its composition and powers are designed to provide a federal balance and a forum for deliberative review of legislation.
  3. **The House of the People (Lok Sabha):** This is the Lower House of Parliament, representing the people of India directly. It is the primary legislative body where members are directly elected by universal adult franchise. The Lok Sabha holds significant power, particularly in financial matters and in holding the executive accountable.
🔥 High-Yield Fact: The President is an integral part of Parliament even though he/she is not a member of either House. This constitutional design underscores the principle that no bill passed by both Houses can become law without the President's assent (as per **Article 111**). Furthermore, the President has the power to issue ordinances (**Article 123**) when Parliament is not in session, which have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, subject to subsequent approval by Parliament. The President also summons and prorogues the Houses and can dissolve the Lok Sabha, highlighting the executive's crucial link with the legislature.

Historical Context and Evolution of Parliament

The concept of a representative legislature in India evolved through various acts during British rule, starting from the Indian Councils Act of 1861, 1892, and 1909, leading to the Government of India Acts of 1919 and 1935. The Constituent Assembly, which drafted the Indian Constitution, adopted the parliamentary system, drawing inspiration from the British model, but adapting it to India's unique federal structure and diverse society. The bicameral system was chosen to ensure thorough deliberation on legislation and to provide representation for both the population and the states.

Rajya Sabha (Upper House)

The Rajya Sabha, or the Council of States, is designed to be a continuous body, providing stability and a platform for mature deliberation. Its structure reflects India's federal character, ensuring that the interests of the states are represented at the national level. The maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha is constitutionally fixed at **250 members**.

  • **Composition Breakdown:**
    • **238 members** represent the States and Union Territories. These members are elected indirectly by the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the respective States and by members of the electoral colleges for Union Territories, through the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote. This indirect election method ensures that the Rajya Sabha acts as a representative of the states rather than the direct populace.
    • **12 members** are nominated by the President of India. This provision, enshrined in **Article 80(3)**, allows for the inclusion of distinguished individuals who have special knowledge or practical experience in fields such as Art, Literature, Science, and Social Service. The rationale behind this nomination is to enrich the debates and legislative process with expertise that might not otherwise enter Parliament through electoral politics. Notable examples include scientists like Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, artists like Lata Mangeshkar, and sportspersons like Sachin Tendulkar.
  • **Permanent Body and Term of Members:** The Rajya Sabha is a **permanent body** and is not subject to dissolution, unlike the Lok Sabha. This ensures continuity in legislative functions and provides a stable forum for policy review. However, its members do not serve indefinitely. In accordance with **Article 83(1)**, one-third of its members retire every second year. This staggered retirement system ensures that there is always a significant number of experienced members, while also allowing for fresh perspectives and representation. Each member serves a term of **six years**.
  • **Qualifications for Membership (Article 84):**
    • Must be a citizen of India.
    • Must be at least 30 years of age.
    • Must possess such other qualifications as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament (e.g., Representation of the People Act, 1951, requires the person to be an elector for a parliamentary constituency in the state or union territory from which he/she is seeking election, though this requirement was removed in 2003).
  • **Presiding Officers:**
    • **Chairman:** The Vice-President of India is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (**Article 64** and **Article 89**). The Chairman presides over the sittings of the House, maintains decorum, and interprets the rules of procedure.
    • **Deputy Chairman:** The Rajya Sabha elects a Deputy Chairman from amongst its members. The Deputy Chairman performs the duties of the Chairman when the latter's office is vacant or when the Vice-President is acting as President or performing the duties of the President.
  • **Special Powers of Rajya Sabha:** While generally having co-equal powers with the Lok Sabha in ordinary legislation, the Rajya Sabha possesses certain exclusive powers that underscore its federal character:
    • **Article 249:** It can authorize Parliament to make laws on a subject enumerated in the State List (which is normally outside Parliament's purview) if it declares by a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest. Such a resolution remains in force for one year but can be extended.
    • **Article 312:** It can authorize Parliament to create new All-India Services common to both the Union and the States (e.g., Indian Administrative Service, Indian Police Service). This requires a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.
    • It has the sole power to initiate a resolution for the removal of the Vice-President (**Article 67(b)**).
  • **Quorum:** The quorum to constitute a meeting of the Rajya Sabha is one-tenth of the total number of members of the House (**Article 100(3)**), i.e., 25 members.

Lok Sabha (Lower House)

The Lok Sabha, or the House of the People, is the primary representative body of the Indian populace. Its members are directly elected by the citizens of India, making it the more powerful house in terms of financial legislation and executive accountability. The normal term of the Lok Sabha is five years, but it can be dissolved earlier by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister, or if the government loses the confidence of the House.

  • **Maximum Strength and Evolution:**
    • The maximum strength of the Lok Sabha is constitutionally capped at **550 members**. This limit was set after various delimitations and amendments.
    • Historically, the Lok Sabha's strength has evolved:
      • Originally, the Constitution provided for a maximum of 500 members.
      • The 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956, increased the maximum to 520.
      • The Goa, Daman and Diu Reorganisation Act, 1987, further increased it to 530 for states and 20 for Union Territories.
      • Prior to the 104th Amendment, the total strength was 545 (530 from states, 13 from UTs, and 2 nominated Anglo-Indians).
    • **Current Composition (Post-104th Amendment):**
      • **530 members** are chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the States.
      • **Up to 20 members** represent the Union Territories, chosen in such manner as Parliament may by law provide.
    • **Abolition of Anglo-Indian Nominated Seats:** The provision for the nomination of two members from the Anglo-Indian community by the President (under **Article 331**) was abolished by the **104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019**. This decision was based on the rationale that the community's population had significantly declined, and their representation through nomination was no longer considered necessary, as they were deemed to be adequately integrated into Indian society. This amendment came into effect on January 25, 2020.
  • **Direct Election and Universal Adult Franchise:** Members of the Lok Sabha are directly elected by the people on the basis of universal adult franchise. Every citizen of India who is 18 years of age or above, and not otherwise disqualified, has the right to vote. This direct mandate makes the Lok Sabha the most powerful chamber in terms of representing the will of the people.
  • **Qualifications for Membership (Article 84):**
    • Must be a citizen of India.
    • Must be at least 25 years of age.
    • Must possess such other qualifications as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament (e.g., Representation of the People Act, 1951, requires the person to be an elector for any parliamentary constituency).
  • **Term and Dissolution:** The normal term of the Lok Sabha is **five years** from the date appointed for its first meeting. However, it can be dissolved earlier by the President. This dissolution can occur if the ruling government loses its majority and no alternative government can be formed, or if the Prime Minister advises the President to dissolve the House and call for fresh elections. The term can also be extended beyond five years during a Proclamation of Emergency (**Article 352**) for a period not exceeding one year at a time, but not beyond six months after the Proclamation has ceased to operate (**Article 83(2)**).
  • **Presiding Officers:**
    • **Speaker:** The Speaker is the principal presiding officer of the Lok Sabha. He/she is elected by the members of the Lok Sabha from amongst themselves at its first meeting after the general elections. The Speaker maintains order and decorum in the House, interprets the rules of procedure, and is the final authority on parliamentary proceedings. The Speaker's decision on whether a bill is a Money Bill or not is final.
    • **Deputy Speaker:** The Deputy Speaker is also elected by the Lok Sabha from amongst its members. The Deputy Speaker performs the duties of the Speaker when the latter's office is vacant or when the Speaker is absent from a sitting of the House.
  • **Quorum:** The quorum to constitute a meeting of the Lok Sabha is one-tenth of the total number of members of the House (**Article 100(3)**), i.e., 55 members.
⚠️ Trap Alert: Money Bills (Article 110) are a critical area of distinction between the powers of the two Houses. They can ONLY be introduced in the Lok Sabha, not the Rajya Sabha. This supremacy of the Lok Sabha in financial matters is a cornerstone of parliamentary democracy, reflecting the principle of "no taxation without representation," as the Lok Sabha directly represents the taxpayers.
  • **Definition of Money Bill (Article 110):** A bill is deemed to be a Money Bill if it contains only provisions dealing with all or any of the following matters:
    • The imposition, abolition, remission, alteration, or regulation of any tax.
    • The regulation of the borrowing of money or the giving of any guarantee by the Government of India.
    • The custody of the Consolidated Fund or the Contingency Fund of India, the payment of money into or the withdrawal of money from any such Fund.
    • The appropriation of money out of the Consolidated Fund of India.
    • Declaring any expenditure to be expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India or increasing the amount of any such expenditure.
    • The receipt of money on account of the Consolidated Fund of India or the public account of India or the custody or issue of such money or the audit of the accounts of the Union or of a State.
    • Any matter incidental to any of the matters specified above.
  • **Speaker's Certification:** The final authority to decide whether a bill is a Money Bill or not rests with the Speaker of the Lok Sabha. The Speaker's decision on this matter is conclusive and cannot be challenged in any court of law or in either House of Parliament.
  • **Rajya Sabha's Restricted Powers:** Once a Money Bill is passed by the Lok Sabha, it is transmitted to the Rajya Sabha for its recommendations. The Rajya Sabha has very limited powers regarding Money Bills:
    • It cannot reject or amend a Money Bill.
    • It can only make recommendations, which the Lok Sabha may or may not accept.
    • It must return the Money Bill to the Lok Sabha within **14 days** from the date of its receipt. If the Rajya Sabha fails to return the bill within this period, it is deemed to have been passed by both Houses in the form in which it was passed by the Lok Sabha.
  • **Effect:** This constitutional provision ensures that the government, which is accountable to the Lok Sabha, has the ultimate say in financial matters, preventing any obstruction by the Upper House on budgetary and fiscal policies.

Functions and Powers of Parliament

The Parliament of India performs a multitude of functions essential for the governance of the country:

  • **Legislative Functions:** Parliament is the primary law-making body. It can make laws on subjects enumerated in the Union List and Concurrent List. In case of conflict on Concurrent List subjects, Union law prevails. Under specific circumstances (e.g., Article 249, Article 252, during an emergency), it can also legislate on State List subjects.
