Mechanics – Gravitation: Kepler’s Laws, Orbital & Escape Velocities, Satellites

1. Quick Kinematics Recap (Foundational for Orbital Problems)

Distance travelled – measured by the odometer.

Speed constant – classification of motion:

  • Uniform motion: equal distance in equal interval of time; velocity constant.
  • Non-uniform motion: unequal distance in equal interval of time; velocity can't be constant.

Avg. speed = total distance travelled / total time taken

Velocity = displacement / time

Acceleration (a) = change in velocity / time taken

Unit conversion: m/s → km/h multiply by 18/5; km/h → m/s multiply by 5/18.

Magnitude of velocity – vector quantity; speed – scalar quantity.

Deceleration = −a

Exam Tip: Always write the sign of acceleration when a body is slowing down; many marks are lost for missing the negative sign.

2. Newton’s Universal Law of Gravitation

Formula:
F = G · (m1 m2) / r²

Where:

  • F – gravitational force (N)
  • G – universal gravitational constant = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²
  • m1, m2 – masses of the two bodies (kg)
  • r – centre‑to‑centre distance (m)

Key Observations:

  • Force is always attractive.
  • Force varies inversely with the square of the distance – the inverse‑square law.
  • Gravitational force at the Earth's surface is 9.8 m/s² (standard acceleration due to gravity, g).

Mnemonic for the formula: “G is Great, m’s multiply, r squares the distance.”

3. Kepler’s Three Laws of Planetary Motion

Johannes Kepler (1571‑1630) formulated the three empirical laws that describe planetary orbits. They are the backbone of orbital mechanics and are directly used in NDA/CDS/AFCAT problems.

3.1 First Law – The Law of Ellipses

Statement: Every planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one of the two foci.

Ellipse Geometry:

ParameterSymbolExpression
Major axis (longest diameter)2aa = semi‑major axis
Minor axis (shortest diameter)2bb = semi‑minor axis
Eccentricityee = √(1 − b²/a²)
Perihelion distancerprp = a(1 − e)
Aphelion distancerara = a(1 + e)

Exam Tip: Remember that for a circular orbit e = 0, thus rp = ra = a.

3.2 Second Law – The Law of Equal Areas

Statement: A line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time.

Mathematically: dA/dt = constant = L/2m, where L is the angular momentum of the planet about the Sun.

Implication: When the planet is nearer to the Sun (perihelion) it moves faster; when farther (aphelion) it moves slower.

Mnemonic: “Equal Areas = Equal Times = Faster Near, Slower Far.”

3.3 Third Law – The Harmonic Law

Statement: The square of the orbital period (T) of a planet is proportional to the cube of the semi‑major axis (a) of its orbit.

Mathematical form (for any small body orbiting a massive central body):

T² = (4π²/GM) · a³

Or, in a convenient astronomical unit (AU) system for planets around the Sun:

T² (years) = a³ (AU)

Constants for the Sun:

  • Mass of Sun, M☉ = 1.989 × 10³⁰ kg
  • G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²

Exam Tip: When the problem gives T in minutes or seconds, convert to seconds before using the formula; similarly convert a to metres.

4. Orbital Velocity (Circular Orbits)

For a body of mass m moving in a circular orbit of radius r around a massive body of mass M, the required centripetal force is supplied entirely by gravity.

Derivation:

Set gravitational force equal to centripetal force:

G M m / r² = m v² / r  ⟹  v = √(G M / r)

Key Formula: vorb = √(GM/r)

Where:

  • vorb – orbital speed (m/s)
  • r – orbital radius (m)

Typical Values:

BodyRadius (m)Orbital Speed (km/s)
Low Earth Orbit (LEO) – 400 km above Earth6.78 × 10⁶7.8
Geostationary Orbit – 35,786 km4.22 × 10⁷3.07
Moon (circular orbit around Earth)3.84 × 10⁸1.02
Sun‑Mercury (average)5.79 × 10¹⁰47.9

Exam Tip: Remember to use the radius from the centre of the Earth (or Sun), not the altitude above the surface.

5. Escape Velocity

Escape velocity is the minimum speed needed for an object to break free from the gravitational attraction of a massive body without further propulsion.

Derivation (Energy Method):

Set kinetic energy equal to the magnitude of gravitational potential energy at the surface:

½ m ve² = G M m / r ⟹  ve = √(2GM / r)

Key Formula: ve = √(2GM/r)

Typical Escape Velocities:

BodyRadius (m)Mass (kg)Escape Velocity (km/s)
Earth6.371 × 10⁶5.972 × 10²⁴11.2
Moon1.737 × 10⁶7.35 × 10²²2.38
Mars3.389 × 10⁶6.42 × 10²³5.03
Jupiter6.991 × 10⁷1.898 × 10²⁷59.5

Important Note: Escape velocity is independent of the mass of the escaping object; only the planet’s mass and radius matter.

Mnemonic: “V = √(2GM/R) – 2 for “to get out” (double the orbital speed factor).

Exam Tip: Many questions ask for the ratio of escape velocity to orbital velocity. Since ve = √2 · vorb, the ratio is always √2 ≈ 1.414.

6. Satellite Motion – Period, Energy & Types

6.1 Orbital Period (Kepler’s 3rd Law in Practice)

For a circular orbit:

T = 2π √(r³/GM)

Where T is the period (s). This can be rearranged to find any missing variable.

Example Calculation – Geostationary Satellite:

  • Desired period = 24 h = 86 400 s
  • Set T = 86 400 s and solve for r:

r = [ (GMT²)/(4π²) ]^(1/3) = 4.22 × 10⁷ m

Altitude above Earth's surface = r − RE ≈ 35 786 km.

6.2 Energy of a Satellite

For a circular orbit:

  • Kinetic Energy (K) = ½ m v² = ½ GMm/r
  • Potential Energy (U) = −GMm/r
  • Total Mechanical Energy (E) = K + U = −½ GMm/r (negative, indicating a bound system)

Implication: The more distant the orbit (larger r), the less negative the total energy, i.e., the satellite is less tightly bound.

6.3 Types of Earth Satellites

CategoryAltitude (km)Typical PeriodApplications
Low Earth Orbit (LEO)160‑2 000≈ 90 minImaging, remote sensing, ISS
Medium Earth Orbit (MEO)2 000‑35 7862‑12 hNavigation (GPS, GLONASS)
Geostationary Orbit (GEO)≈ 35 78624 h (sidereal)Communication, weather monitoring
Highly Elliptical Orbit (HEO)Apogee > 35 786VariableCoverage of high latitudes (Molniya)

6.4 Perturbations Affecting Satellite Motion

Real satellites experience deviations from the ideal Keplerian orbit due to:

  • Earth’s oblateness (J₂ effect) – causes nodal regression.
  • Atmospheric drag (significant for LEO).
  • Solar radiation pressure.
  • Gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun.

Exam Tip: For most entrance‑exam questions, assume a perfect spherical Earth unless the question explicitly mentions J₂ or drag.

7. Gravitational Variation with Latitude

The magnitude of gravitational acceleration g is not uniform over the Earth’s surface.

Observations:

  • At the Pole the value of g is greater because the radius of Earth is smaller (≈ 6 371 km at equator vs. ≈ 6 357 km at pole) and the centrifugal effect of rotation is zero.
  • At the Equator g is slightly less due to larger radius and maximum centrifugal force.

Typical values:

  • Equator: 9.780 m/s²
  • Pole: 9.832 m/s²

Extracted point incorporated:

Gravitational force

  • Pole > Equator

7.1 Coriolis Force Variation

The Coriolis force, an apparent force due to Earth’s rotation, also varies with latitude.

Extracted point incorporated:

Coriolis force

  • Zero at Equator
  • High at Pole

Mathematically, the Coriolis acceleration is ac = 2 Ω v sin φ, where Ω = 7.292 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s (Earth’s angular speed) and φ is latitude.

Exam Tip: For projectile motion problems, remember that the Coriolis deflection is maximum at 45° latitude and zero at the equator.

8. Comprehensive Formula Sheet (All Must‑Know Equations)

  1. Universal Gravitation: F = G M m / r²
  2. Orbital Velocity: v = √(GM/r)
  3. Escape Velocity: ve = √(2GM/r)
  4. Orbital Period: T = 2π √(r³/GM)
  5. Kepler’s 3rd Law (General): T² = (4π²/GM) a³
  6. Specific Mechanical Energy: ε = −GM/(2a)
  7. Angular Momentum per unit mass: h = √(GMa(1−e²))
  8. Vis‑Viva Equation (speed at any point): v = √[GM(2/r − 1/a)]
  9. Gravitational Potential Energy: U = −GMm/r
  10. Kinetic Energy in Orbit: K = ½ GMm/r

Memorise the Vis‑Viva equation – it links speed, distance, and semi‑major axis in a single line.

9. Frequently Asked Numerical Problems (With Step‑by‑Step Solutions)

9.1 Problem 1 – Velocity of a Satellite at 500 km Altitude

Given: Altitude = 500 km, Earth radius = 6 371 km, MEarth = 5.972 × 10²⁴ kg

Solution:

  1. Find orbital radius: r = RE + h = (6 371 + 500) km = 6.871 × 10⁶ m.
  2. Apply v = √(GM/r): v = √[ (6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.972 × 10²⁴) / 6.871 × 10⁶ ] ≈ 7.6 km/s.

Answer: 7.6 km/s

9.2 Problem 2 – Escape Velocity from Mars

Data: MMars = 6.42 × 10²³ kg, RMars = 3.389 × 10⁶ m

Solution:

  1. ve = √(2GM/r) = √[2 × 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.42 × 10²³ / 3.389 × 10⁶] ≈ 5.0 km/s.

Answer: 5.0 km/s

9.3 Problem 3 – Period of a Moon‑like Satellite at 10⁸ m from Earth’s Centre

Given: r = 1.0 × 10⁸ m

Solution:

  1. Use T = 2π √(r³/GM).
  2. Plug values: T = 2π √[(1.0 × 10⁸)³ / (6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.972 × 10²⁴)] ≈ 1.1 × 10⁴ s ≈ 3.1 h.

Answer: ≈ 3.1 hours

10. Mnemonics & Quick Memory Aids

  • Kepler’s Laws: “K1 – O (Oval), K2 – A (Area), K3 – P (Period)”.
  • Orbital vs Escape: “Escape = √2 × Orbit”.
  • Vis‑Viva: “V for Velocity, V for (2/r − 1/a)”.
  • Energy Sign: “Bound = Negative, Unbound = Zero or Positive”.

11. Exam‑Focused Tips & Tricks

  1. Unit Consistency: Always convert distances to metres and masses to kilograms before plugging into formulas.
  2. Remember the 1 AU value: 1.496 × 10¹¹ m. Useful for planetary‑orbit problems.
  3. Quick Approximation: For Earth, vorb ≈ 7.9 km/s at the surface; ve ≈ 11.2 km/s. Use these as sanity checks.
  4. Sign of Energy: If the total mechanical energy (K + U) comes out negative, the orbit is bound (circular/elliptical). Zero → parabolic escape; positive → hyperbolic trajectory.
  5. Use the Vis‑Viva Equation when the problem gives one distance (e.g., perihelion) and asks for speed at another point.
  6. Latitude Effects: For questions on weight variation, recall the pole‑equator difference (≈ 0.5 %). For Coriolis, remember sin φ factor.
  7. Check the Question’s Frame: If the problem mentions “ignoring air resistance” or “spherical Earth”, stick to the ideal formulas. If it mentions “J₂” or “drag”, include the correction term.

12. Summary – What Must Be Memorised

  • Newton’s law of gravitation and the value of G.
  • All three Kepler’s laws (statements and mathematical forms).
  • Orbital velocity, escape velocity, and vis‑viva equations.
  • Orbital period formula and its derivation from Kepler’s 3rd law.
  • Typical numerical values for Earth, Moon, Mars, and the Sun (mass, radius, escape velocity).
  • Energy relations (K, U, total) for circular orbits.
  • Latitude dependence of g and the Coriolis force.
  • Key mnemonics and exam tips listed above.

With these notes you have a complete, self‑contained reference that covers every fact, formula, and nuance required for NDA, CDS, and AFCAT physics sections on gravitation and orbital mechanics.
ai-gen-physics-reflection-refraction-law:
Optics – Reflection & Refraction

1. Introduction

Optics is the branch of physics that deals with the behaviour of light and its interaction with matter. In the NDA, CDS and AFCAT syllabus, the most frequently tested sub‑topics are the laws of reflection and refraction, the formation of images by mirrors and lenses, and the phenomenon of total internal reflection (TIR). Mastery of these concepts requires a clear understanding of the governing equations, sign conventions, and the ability to apply them quickly to numerical problems.

2. Laws of Reflection

  1. Incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane.
  2. Angle of incidence (i) equals angle of reflection (r).
    i = r

The law is independent of the nature of the reflecting surface (smooth or rough). For a plane mirror, the image is laterally inverted, virtual, upright and of the same size as the object.

2.1 Mirror Formula (Plane Mirror)

Since the object distance (u) and image distance (v) are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign, the mirror equation reduces to:

ParameterValue for Plane Mirror
Object distance (u)–d (negative because object is in front of the mirror)
Image distance (v)+d (positive behind the mirror)
Magnification (m)–v/u = –(+d)/(–d) = +1

3. Laws of Refraction (Snell’s Law)

When a ray passes from one medium to another, its speed changes, causing the ray to bend. The quantitative relationship is given by Snell’s Law:

n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r

  • n₁, n₂ – refractive indices of the first and second medium respectively.
  • i, r – angles measured from the normal.

Refractive Index (n) is defined as the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum (c) to that in the medium (v):

n = c / v

Typical values (useful for quick calculations):

MediumRefractive Index (n)
Air (≈ vacuum)1.00
Water1.33
Glass (crown)1.52
Glass (flint)1.62
Diamond2.42

3.1 Critical Angle & Total Internal Reflection

When light travels from a denser medium (higher n) to a rarer medium (lower n), there exists an angle of incidence beyond which refraction ceases and the ray is reflected back into the denser medium. This is Total Internal Reflection (TIR).

sin c = n₂ / n₁  ( n₁ > n₂ )

c – critical angle. For angles i > c, the reflected ray obeys the law of reflection (i = r) and remains in the original medium.

Typical critical angles (highlighted for quick recall):

  • Water → Air: 48.6°
  • Glass (n = 1.52) → Air: 41.1°
  • Diamond → Air: 24.4°

Mnemonic: “Critical C for Clear Cut – C = 1 / n (approx) for air‑to‑glass, so larger n → smaller critical angle.”

4. Mirrors

Mirrors are reflective surfaces that form images by the law of reflection. Two main categories are plane mirrors and spherical mirrors (concave & convex).

4.1 Spherical Mirrors – Sign Conventions

QuantityPositive (+)Negative (–)
Object distance (u)Never (object always in front of mirror)–u (real object)
Image distance (v)Real image (formed on same side as object)–v (virtual image)
Radius of curvature (R)Center of curvature (C) in front of mirror (concave)–R (convex)
Focal length (f)f = R/2 (concave)f = –R/2 (convex)

4.2 Mirror Equation & Magnification

1/f = 1/u + 1/v

m = –v/u = h'/h (where h' = image height, h = object height)

4.3 Concave Mirror

  • Focal point (F) lies between the pole (P) and centre of curvature (C).
  • Real, inverted images are formed when the object is beyond the focal point (u < –f).
  • Virtual, upright, magnified images are formed when the object is between the pole and focal point (–f < u < 0).

Key Cases (concave)

Object PositionImage PositionNatureSize
∞ (parallel rays)F (real)InvertedSame size
at C (u = –R)at C (v = –R)Real, invertedSame size
at F (u = –f)at ∞Highly enlarged, virtual∞
between F and P (–f < u < 0)Behind P (virtual)UprightMagnified

4.4 Convex Mirror

  • Focal point is virtual, located behind the pole.
  • All images are virtual, upright, and reduced.
  • Never forms a real image.

v = (u · f) / (u + f) (remember f is negative)

4.5 Mirror Mnemonic

“C for Concave – Real & Inverted; V for Convex – Virtual & Upright.”

5. Lenses

Lenses are refracting surfaces that converge or diverge light. Two basic types:

  • Converging (Convex) Lens – thicker at the centre, positive focal length.
  • Diverging (Concave) Lens – thinner at the centre, negative focal length.

5.1 Sign Conventions for Lenses

QuantityPositive (+)Negative (–)
Object distance (u)Never (real object)–u
Image distance (v)Real image (formed on opposite side of object)–v (virtual image)
Focal length (f)Convex lensConcave lens
Radius of curvature (R)Centre of curvature on the side of incoming lightOpposite side

5.2 Lens Formula & Magnification

1/f = 1/v – 1/u

m = v/u = h'/h

Note the sign difference compared to mirrors (minus sign before 1/u).

5.3 Lens Maker’s Formula

1/f = (n – 1) (1/R₁ – 1/R₂)

Where:

  • n – refractive index of the lens material.
  • R₁ – radius of curvature of the first surface (positive if centre of curvature is on the same side as the incoming light).
  • R₂ – radius of curvature of the second surface (positive if centre is on the opposite side).

5.4 Types of Images Formed by Convex Lens

Object Position (u)Image Position (v)NatureSize
∞ (parallel rays)F (real)InvertedReduced
at 2Fat 2FReal, invertedSame size
between F and 2Fbetween F and 2FReal, invertedMagnified
at F∞Highly enlarged, virtual∞
between P and FBehind P (virtual)UprightMagnified

5.5 Diverging Lens (Concave)

  • All images are virtual, upright, and reduced.
  • Image forms on the same side as the object.

5.6 Power of a Lens

P (dioptres) = 1/f (metres)

Positive for converging lenses, negative for diverging lenses.

5.7 Combination of Lenses

When thin lenses are placed in contact, their powers add:

P_total = P₁ + P₂ + …

Resultant focal length: f_total = 1 / P_total

5.8 Lens Mnemonic

“Convex = Converge = Real & Inverted; Concave = Diverge = Virtual & Upright.”

6. Refraction at Spherical Surfaces

When a ray passes through a single spherical surface separating two media (n₁ → n₂), the relation is:

n₂ / v – n₁ / u = (n₂ – n₁) / R

Where R follows the same sign convention as for mirrors.

Special Cases:

  • Plane surface (R → ∞): n₂ / v = n₁ / u
  • Object at infinity (parallel rays): v = f = R / (n₂ – n₁)

7. Total Internal Reflection (TIR)

Key conditions for TIR:

  1. Light must travel from a medium of higher refractive index to a lower one (n₁ > n₂).
  2. Angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle c given by sin c = n₂ / n₁.

When TIR occurs, the reflected ray is completely reflected with no loss of intensity (ideal case). This principle is exploited in:

  • Optical fibres – light guided by successive TIR.
  • Prisms (e.g., Porro‑prism in binoculars) – to deviate the light path without loss.
  • Diamond brilliance – high n leads to low critical angle, causing many internal reflections
ai-gen-physics-dual-nature-of-matter-pho:
Dual Nature of Matter – Photoelectric Effect & de Broglie Wavelength

1. Why “Dual Nature”?

Classical physics treated light as a wave and matter as particles. Experiments at the turn of the 20th century showed that both light and massive particles exhibit wave‑like and particle‑like behaviour. This wave‑particle duality is the cornerstone of Modern Physics and is heavily tested in NDA, CDS and AFCAT examinations.

Key takeaway: Whenever a phenomenon involves either quantised energy exchange or interference/diffraction, think “dual nature”.

2. Photoelectric Effect

2.1 Historical Milestones

YearScientist(s)Contribution
1887 Heinrich Hertz Observed that ultraviolet light increased the spark gap discharge.
1902 J.J. Thomson First quantitative measurements of electron emission from metals.
1905 Albert Einstein Proposed photon concept & derived the photoelectric equation.
1915 Robert Millikan Experimental verification of Einstein’s equation (Nobel 1923).

2.2 Experimental Setup (Standard Millikan‑Hertz Apparatus)

  • Vacuum tube containing a clean metal plate (cathode) and an anode.
  • Monochromatic light of known frequency ν is incident on the cathode.
  • Variable retarding (stopping) potential Vs applied between cathode and anode.
  • Current I measured as a function of Vs.

2.3 Key Observations (Exam‑Friendly List)

  1. Emission occurs **only** if the incident light frequency exceeds a material‑specific threshold frequency ν₀.
  2. Kinetic energy of emitted electrons is **independent** of light intensity but **increases linearly** with frequency.
  3. The photocurrent is proportional to light intensity (more photons → more electrons).
  4. Increasing the retarding potential reduces the current; at a particular stopping potential Vs the current becomes zero.

2.4 Einstein’s Photoelectric Equation

Einstein (1905): Light consists of quanta (photons) each carrying energy E = hν.

hν = φ + Kmax

  • h – Planck’s constant = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s (or 4.135 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV·s).
  • ν – Frequency of incident radiation.
  • φ – Work function (minimum energy to liberate an electron) = hν₀.
  • Kmax – Maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons = eVs (e = elementary charge = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C).

2.5 Important Relations & Graphical Analysis

GraphKey Slope/InterceptPhysical Meaning
Stopping potential Vs vs. Frequency ν Slope = h/e ; Intercept = –φ/e Determines Planck’s constant and work function.
Photocurrent I vs. Light Intensity Linear (I ∝ Intensity) More photons → more electrons.

2.6 Typical Numerical Values (Memorise)

  • Work function of Sodium (Na) ≈ 2.28 eV (ν₀ ≈ 5.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz).
  • Work function of Platinum (Pt) ≈ 5.6 eV.
  • Threshold wavelength λ₀ = c/ν₀; for Na, λ₀ ≈ 540 nm.

2.7 Common Exam Questions & Quick Solving Tips

  1. Find stopping potential when light of wavelength λ = 400 nm shines on a metal with φ = 2.0 eV.
    Tip:* Convert λ → ν (ν = c/λ), then use hν = φ + eVs.
  2. Determine work function from a Vs–ν graph (slope = h/e, intercept = –φ/e).
    Tip:* Use the intercept directly; multiply by –e.
  3. Explain why increasing intensity does not increase Kmax**.
    Tip:* Emphasise photon‑energy is set by frequency, not by number of photons.

2.8 Mnemonic for Remembering Einstein’s Equation

“Happy Vacations Kick People” → hν = φ + Kmax

2.9 Applications (High‑Yield for Exams)

  • Photocells & solar panels – conversion of light to electric current.
  • Photo‑electron spectroscopy – determines surface composition via work function.
  • Night‑vision devices – rely on photo‑emission from cathodes.

3. de Broglie Hypothesis – Matter Waves

3.1 Historical Background

  • Louis de Broglie (1924) proposed that particles of matter have an associated wavelength λ = h/p.
  • His Ph.D. thesis earned the Nobel Prize (1929) after experimental confirmation.
  • Key experiments: Davisson–Germer (1927) electron diffraction, G.P. Thomson (1909) cathode‑ray diffraction (precursor).

3.2 Fundamental Formulae

λ = h / p
ai-gen-chemistry-chemical-bonding-ionic-:
Physical Chemistry – Chemical Bonding

Scope: Ionic, Covalent, Coordinate (Dative) and Metallic bonds – definitions, formation mechanisms, structural features, quantitative aspects, exceptions and exam‑friendly mnemonics.

1. Ionic Bond

1.1 Definition & Formation

An ionic bond is an electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by complete transfer of one or more electrons from a metal (electropositive) to a non‑metal (electronegative).

  • Metal → loses electrons → forms cation (e.g., Na → Na+)
  • Non‑metal → gains electrons → forms anion (e.g., Cl → Cl−)
  • Resulting lattice is held together by Coulombic forces.

1.2 Quantitative Parameters

Parameter Expression / Typical Value Relevance to Exams
Lattice Energy (U) U = k·(z+·z−)/r0 (Born‑Landé equation) Higher U ⇒ higher melting point, hardness, solubility in polar solvents.
Electronegativity Difference (Δχ) Δχ = χnon‑metal – χmetal Δχ ≥ 1.7 (≈ 1.9 in modern textbooks) predicts ionic character.
Ion‑size Ratio (rc/ra) 0.225 – 0.414 → tetrahedral; 0.414 – 0.732 → octahedral; 0.732 – 1.0 → cubic coordination. Helps predict crystal structure (e.g., NaCl, CsCl).

1.3 Common Ionic Structures

  • NaCl (Face‑Centered Cubic, 6:6 coordination)
  • CsCl (Body‑Centered Cubic, 8:8 coordination)
  • ZnS (Zinc blende, tetrahedral 4:4)

1.4 Physical Properties

  • High melting & boiling points (due to strong lattice energy).
  • Hard & brittle – slip of layers brings like charges together → fracture.
  • Good electrical conductivity in molten state or aqueous solution (mobile ions).
  • Soluble in polar protic solvents (water, methanol) – hydration energy > lattice energy.

1.5 Exceptions & Special Cases

  • Partial covalency in highly polarising cations (e.g., Al3+, Be2+) – leads to covalent character (Fajans’ rules).
  • Complex ionic salts such as NH₄Cl where the cation is a polyatomic ion.

1.6 Mnemonic for Lattice Energy Factors

“K‑Z‑R” – K (charge product), Z (charge magnitude), R (inter‑ionic distance). Remember: Keep Zipping Rapidly → higher U.

1.7 Quick Exam Tips

  1. Always compare Δχ with 1.7 to decide ionic vs covalent.
  2. For crystal structures, first calculate the ion‑size ratio; then match with the table of coordination numbers.
  3. When asked about solubility, compare lattice energy with hydration enthalpy – if ΔHhyd > U, the salt is soluble.

2. Covalent Bond

2.1 Definition & Types

A covalent bond is formed by the sharing of one or more pairs of electrons between two non‑metal atoms.

  • Non‑polar covalent – equal sharing (Δχ ≈ 0).
  • Polar covalent – unequal sharing (0 < Δχ < 1.7).
  • Multiple bonds – double (2 pairs) and triple (3 pairs) bonds.

2.2 Bond Length & Bond Energy

Bond Type Typical Bond Length (Å) Bond Energy (kJ mol⁻¹)
H–H0.74436
C–C (single)1.54347
C=C (double)1.34614
C≡C (triple)1.20839
O=O1.21498

2.3 Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) Theory

Predicts molecular geometry based on repulsion between electron pairs.

  • AXn – n bonding pairs, no lone pairs.
  • AXnEm – m lone pairs.
Electron DomainGeometryBond Angle (°)
2 (AX₂)Linear180
3 (AX₃)Trigonal planar120
4 (AX₄)Tetrahedral109.5
5 (AX₅)Trigonal bipyramidal90, 120
6 (AX₆)Octahedral90

2.4 Hybridisation

Mixing of atomic orbitals to form equivalent hybrid orbitals.

  • sp – linear, 180°, 2 hybrids (e.g., BeCl₂).
  • sp² – trigonal planar, 120°, 3 hybrids (e.g., BF₃).
  • sp³ – tetrahedral, 109.5°, 4 hybrids (e.g., CH₄).
  • sp³d – trigonal bipyramidal, 90°/120° (e.g., PCl₅).
  • sp³d² – octahedral, 90° (e.g., SF₆).

2.5 Polarity & Dipole Moment

Dipole moment (μ) = Q·d, where Q = charge separation, d = distance between centroids.

  • μ = 0 for non‑polar molecules (symmetrical charge distribution).
  • μ > 0 for polar molecules – magnitude gives degree of polarity (e.g., HCl μ ≈ 1.08 D).

2.6 Exceptions & Special Cases

  • Resonance – delocalised π‑electrons (e.g., O₃, NO₃⁻). Use resonance hybrids for bond order calculations.
  • Hypervalent molecules – central atom exceeds octet (e.g., SF₆). Explained by expanded octet or d‑orbital participation.
  • Electron‑deficient compounds – less than octet (e.g., BH₃). Often dimerise (B₂H₆).

2.7 Mnemonic for Hybridisation

“SPARK” – Single, Pair, Angle, Resonance, Keeping track of sp, sp², sp³.

2.8 Quick Exam Tips

  1. For any molecule, first write the Lewis structure → count electron domains → apply VSEPR.
  2. Use Δχ to decide if a bond is essentially ionic (>1.7) or covalent (<1.7).
  3. Remember that bond energy roughly doubles when bond order increases (single → double → triple).
  4. When asked about polarity, check both Δχ and molecular symmetry.

3. Coordinate (Dative) Bond

3.1 Definition

A coordinate bond (also called a dative covalent bond) is formed when both electrons in the shared pair originate from the same atom (the donor).

3.2 Common Donor‑Acceptor Pairs

  • Lewis bases (electron pair donors) – e.g., NH₃, H₂O, CO, CN⁻.
  • Lewis acids (electron pair acceptors) – e.g., BF₃, AlCl₃, metal ions (Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺).

3.3 Representative Examples

  • Ammonium ion (NH₄⁺) – N donates its lone pair to H⁺.
  • Carbonyl complexes – CO donates a lone pair to a metal centre (M←CO).
  • Complex ions – [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ – multiple coordinate bonds.

3.4 Bond Strength & Length

Coordinate bonds are generally comparable in strength to normal covalent bonds but often slightly longer because the donor atom retains partial negative character.

3.5 Role in Coordination Chemistry

Coordination number (CN) = number of donor atoms attached to the central metal. Geometry is dictated by CN and ligand field considerations (e.g., octahedral for CN = 6).

3.6 Mnemonic for Ligand Types

“H‑B‑C‑N‑O‑S” – Hydride, Borate, Cyanide, Nitrogen bases, Oxide, Sulphur bases – remember common donor atoms.

3.7 Quick Exam Tips

  1. Identify the donor atom by locating a lone pair in the Lewis structure.
  2. In complex ions, count the number of donor atoms → infer geometry (tetrahedral, square planar, octahedral).
  3. Remember that the charge on the complex equals the sum of metal oxidation state and ligand charges.

4. Metallic Bond

4.1 Definition & Electron Sea Model

A metallic bond is a non‑directional attraction between positively charged metal cations and a delocalised “sea” of valence electrons.

  • Electrons are free to move throughout the lattice → electrical conductivity.
  • Delocalisation provides cohesion, giving metals high melting points and ductility.

4.2 Quantitative Aspects

PropertyTypical ValueExplanation
Electrical Conductivity10⁶ – 10⁸ S m⁻¹Free electrons carry charge.
Thermal Conductivity100 – 400 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹Electron movement transfers kinetic energy.
Young’s Modulus50 – 200 GPaStrong metallic bonding.
Density (e.g., Fe)7.87 g cm⁻³Close packing of atoms.

4.3 Crystal Structures of Metals

  • Body‑Centered Cubic (BCC) – Fe, Cr, W. Coordination number = 8.
  • Face‑Centered Cubic (FCC) – Cu, Al, Au. Coordination number = 12.
  • Hexagonal Close‑Packed (HCP) – Mg, Ti, Zn. Coordination number = 12.

4.4 Physical Properties Explained

  • Malleability & Ductility – Slip of atomic planes is accommodated by the electron sea without breaking bonds.
  • Luster
ai-gen-chemistry-metals-non-metals-prope:
Metals & Non‑Metals – Properties, Reactivity Series & Extraction

1. Overview

The inorganic chemistry of metals and non‑metals forms a core part of the NDA, CDS & AFCAT syllabi. Understanding their physical and chemical behaviour, the reactivity series of metals and the various extraction techniques is essential for scoring high marks.

2. Classification of Elements

Category Typical Examples General Position in Periodic Table
Metals Fe, Cu, Al, Zn, Pb, Ag, Au, Na, K, Mg, Ca Left‑hand side & centre (s‑block, d‑block, f‑block)
Non‑metals H, C, N, O, P, S, Cl, Br, I Right‑hand side (p‑block)
Metalloids (Semi‑metals) B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te Stair‑step line between metals & non‑metals

3. Physical Properties – Metals vs Non‑Metals

Property Metals Non‑metals
State at STP Usually solid (except Hg, liquid) Solid, liquid (Br) or gas (H, N, O, F, Cl)
Appearance Shiny, metallic luster Dull, non‑metallic
Electrical Conductivity Good conductors (metals) – electron sea model Poor conductors (except graphite)
Thermal Conductivity High (e.g., Cu, Al) Low (except carbon in graphite)
Malleability & Ductility Highly malleable & ductile Brittle, break on hammering
Density Generally high (e.g., Pb, Au) Low (e.g., O₂, N₂) to moderate (e.g., S)
Melting/Boiling Points High (except alkali metals) Varied – generally low for gases, moderate for solids

4. Chemical Properties – Metals

  • Reaction with Oxygen – Form metal oxides (basic in nature).
    General equation: M + O₂ → MO
  • Reaction with Water –
    • Alkali metals (Li, Na, K) react vigorously, producing metal hydroxides and H₂.
    • Alkaline earth metals (Ca, Mg) react slowly; Sr & Ba react vigorously.
    • Transition metals (Fe, Cu) show little/no reaction with cold water.
  • Reaction with Acids – Produce hydrogen gas and corresponding salt.
    M + 2HCl → MCl₂ + H₂↑
  • Displacement (Single‑Replacement) Reactions – More reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution.
  • Amphoteric Oxides – Some metal oxides (Al₂O₃, ZnO) react both with acids and bases.
  • Corrosion – Oxidation in moist air; Fe → Fe₂O₃·nH₂O (rust). Protective coatings (zinc galvanisation) are used.

5. Chemical Properties – Non‑Metals

  • Reaction with Oxygen – Form covalent oxides (acidic or neutral).
    Example: 2S + 3O₂ → SO₃ (acidic oxide).
  • Reaction with Metals – Form salts (ionic).
    Example: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.
  • Acid‑Base Behaviour –
    • Acidic non‑metals (Cl, S, P) form acids on reacting with water.
    • Amphoteric non‑metals (B, Si) show both acidic & basic character.
  • Allotropes – Different structural forms (e.g., C: diamond, graphite, fullerenes).
  • Oxidation States – Wide range (e.g., N: –3 to +5).

6. Reactivity Series of Metals

The reactivity series arranges metals in descending order of their tendency to lose electrons (oxidise). It is a vital tool for predicting displacement reactions, extraction methods and corrosion behaviour.

Rank Metal (Symbol) Typical Reactions Notes / Exceptions
1 Li (Lithium) Reacts violently with water; forms Li₂O. Extracted by electro‑lysis of molten LiCl.
2 K (Potassium) Explosive reaction with water; K₂O formed. Electro‑lysis of KCl (highly reactive).
3 Ca (Calcium) Reacts with cold water, giving Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. Obtained by electro‑lysis of molten CaCl₂.
4 Na (Sodium) Violent reaction with water; Na₂O formed. Electro‑lysis of molten NaCl (Downs cell).
5 Mg (Magnesium) Reacts with hot water; MgO + H₂. Extracted by electro‑lysis of molten MgCl₂.
6 Al (Aluminium) Does not react with water/air due to protective Al₂O₃ layer. Extracted by Hall‑Héroult electrolytic process.
7 Zn (Zinc) Reacts with dilute acids, not with water. Obtained by reduction of ZnO with carbon.
8 Fe (Iron) Reacts with acids; forms Fe₂O₃ on oxidation. Extracted in blast furnace (reduction with coke).
9 Sn (Tin) Displaces Pb from its salts. Reduced from SnO₂ with carbon.
10 Pb (Lead) Displaces hydrogen from acids slowly. Reduced from PbO with carbon.
11 (H) (Hydrogen – non‑metal) Displaces metals above it (e.g., Zn, Fe) from acids. Used as a reference point.
12 Cu (Copper) Does not displace H₂ from acids; forms blue CuSO₄ with H₂SO₄ (oxidising). Extracted by reduction of Cu₂O with carbon or by electrolytic refining.
13 Ag (Silver) Very low reactivity; does not react with acids. Extracted by electrolytic refining of AgNO₃ solution.
14 Au (Gold) Inert; does not react with most reagents. Extracted by cyanidation (Au(CN)₂⁻) and electrolytic deposition.

Mnemonic to remember the series (up to Cu):

“Please Stop Calling Me A Zebra, Not A Cow, So Please Don’t Let My Cat Eat A Goat.”
Corresponds to: Li, K, Ca, Na, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb, (H), Cu, Ag, Au

7. Extraction of Metals – General Principles

Extraction involves converting a metal from its natural ore to a usable metallic form. The method depends on the metal’s position in the reactivity series and the nature of its ore.

7.1 Steps Common to Most Extraction Processes

  1. Concentration (Beneficiation) – Removal of gangue by crushing, grinding, washing, magnetic separation, froth flotation, etc.
  2. Reduction – Chemical reduction of the concentrated ore to metal.
  3. Purification – Removal of impurities by electrolytic refining, zone refining, or distillation.

7.2 Classification of Extraction Techniques

  • Thermal Reduction – Use of carbon (coke) or carbon monoxide at high temperatures.
  • Electrolytic Reduction – Electro‑lysis of molten salts or aqueous solutions.
  • Hydrometallurgical Methods – Leaching, solvent extraction, precipitation.
  • Biometallurgy – Use of microorganisms for leaching (e.g., bio‑leaching of copper).

8. Extraction of Specific Metals – Detailed Pathways

8.1 Iron (Fe)

Iron is the most widely extracted metal; its ores include hematite (Fe₂O₃) and magnetite (Fe₃O₄).

  1. Concentration – Beneficiation by magnetic separation (magnetite) and washing.
  2. Reduction in Blast Furnace (invented 1850s)
    Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂
    Coke (carbon) provides both heat and reducing CO.
  3. Purification –
    • Puddling (historical) – Oxidative removal of carbon.
    • Basic Oxygen Process (BOP) – Modern method using O₂ to oxidise impurities.

8.2 Aluminium (Al)

Aluminium is extracted from bauxite (Al₂O₃·2H₂O). The process is energy‑intensive.

  1. Bayer Process (1888) – Conversion of bauxite to pure Al₂O₃ by digestion with NaOH, precipitation, and calcination.
  2. Hall‑Héroult Electrolysis (1886) – Electro‑lysis of molten Al₂O₃ dissolved in cryolite (Na₃AlF₆).
    2Al₂O₃(l) → 4Al(l) + 3O₂(g)
  3. Energy consumption ≈ 13–15 kWh/kg – a key exam fact.

8.3 Copper (Cu)

Primary ores: chalcopyrite (CuFeS₂), bornite (Cu₅FeS₄).

  1. Concentration – Froth flotation to produce copper concentrate (~30 % Cu).
  2. Roasting – Convert sulfides to oxides:
    2Cu
ai-gen-chemistry-environmental-chemistry:
Environmental Chemistry – Air, Water & Soil Pollution; Greenhouse Effect & Ozone

1. Quick Overview

Environmental chemistry deals with the **chemical processes** that occur in the environment and the **impact of human activities** on air, water and soil. For defence exams (NDA, CDS, AFCAT) the focus is on:

  • Major pollutants & their sources
  • Standard limits (WHO, CPCB, US EPA)
  • Mechanisms of pollution & control technologies
  • Greenhouse gases (GHGs) and their global warming potential (GWP)
  • Ozone layer chemistry, depletion and recovery

2. Air Pollution

2.1 Definition

Air pollution = presence of harmful or excessive quantities of substances (gases, particulates, vapours) in the atmosphere.

2.2 Classification of Pollutants

Type Key Species Primary Sources Environmental/Health Impact
Primary (Primary) Pollutants SO2, NOx, CO, PM10, PM2.5, VOCs, NH3 Fossil‑fuel combustion, metal smelting, vehicular exhaust, biomass burning Acid rain, respiratory diseases, visibility reduction, photochemical smog
Secondary Pollutants Ozone (O3), nitrate & sulphate aerosols, peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN) Atmospheric reactions of primary pollutants (photolysis, oxidation) Ground‑level ozone – lung inflammation; aerosols – climate forcing

2.3 Major Air Pollutants – Details

  • Sulphur Dioxide (SO2)
    • Source: Coal & oil combustion, metal smelting.
    • Reaction: SO2 + H2O → H2SO3 (acid rain).
    • Standard: 75 µg·m⁻³ (24‑hr, WHO).
  • Nitrogen Oxides (NO, NO2)
    • Source: High‑temperature combustion, lightning.
    • Form NO2 + H2O → HNO3 (acid rain).
    • Standard: 40 µg·m⁻³ (annual, WHO).
  • Carbon Monoxide (CO)
    • Source: Incomplete combustion of carbonaceous fuels.
    • Mechanism: Binds to haemoglobin → reduces O₂ transport.
    • Standard: 9 ppm (8‑hr, WHO).
  • Particulate Matter (PM)
    • PM10 – particles ≤10 µm; PM2.5 – ≤2.5 µm.
    • Sources: Dust, combustion, industrial processes.
    • Health: Deep‑lung penetration, cardiovascular diseases.
    • Standard: 25 µg·m⁻³ (PM2.5, 24‑hr, WHO).
  • Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs)
    • Examples: Benzene, Toluene, Xylene, Formaldehyde.
    • Role: Precursors for photochemical ozone.
    • Standard (Benzene): 5 µg·m⁻³ (annual, WHO).

2.4 Photochemical Smog – Mechanism (Mnemonic: “NO‑NO₂‑O₃‑VOCs”)

  1. NO emitted from vehicles.
  2. Sunlight photolyzes NO₂ → NO + O·.
  3. Free O· reacts with O₂ → O₃ (ground‑level).
  4. VOCs react with NO to regenerate NO₂, sustaining the cycle.

2.5 Control Technologies (Exam Tip: Remember “C‑A‑B‑S”)

  • C – Combustion optimisation (low‑NOx burners).
  • A – Absorption/Adsorption (scrubbers for SO₂, activated carbon for VOCs).
  • B – Biological treatment (bio‑filters for odours).
  • S – Scrubbing & Separation (electrostatic precipitators for PM).

3. Water Pollution

3.1 Definition

Water pollution = introduction of contaminants into water bodies (rivers, lakes, oceans, groundwater) that degrade water quality and endanger ecosystems and human health.

3.2 Types of Water Pollution

Category Typical Contaminants Major Sources Key Effects
Organic (Biochemical Oxygen Demand – BOD) Domestic sewage, agricultural runoff, food processing waste. Municipal discharge, livestock farms. O₂ depletion → fish kills.
Inorganic (Chemical Oxygen Demand – COD) Heavy metals (Pb, Cd, Hg), nitrates, phosphates, cyanides. Industrial effluents, mining. Acidification, toxicity.
Microbiological Pathogenic bacteria, viruses, protozoa. Untreated sewage, animal waste. Water‑borne diseases (cholera, dysentery).
Thermal Elevated temperature water. Power‑plant cooling discharge. Reduced dissolved O₂, altered species composition.

3.3 Important Water Quality Parameters (Mnemonic: “D‑C‑T‑P‑M”)

  • D – pH (acid‑base balance).
  • C – Conductivity (total dissolved solids).
  • T – Temperature (affects solubility of gases).
  • P – Phosphate & Nitrate (eutrophication potential).
  • M – Microbial count (coliforms, E. coli).

3.4 Major Water Pollutants – Quick Facts

  • Lead (Pb)
    • Source: Battery plants, paints, gasoline (historical).
    • Effect: Neurological damage, especially in children.
    • WHO limit for drinking water: 10 µg·L⁻¹.
  • Arsenic (As)
    • Source: Natural groundwater, mining.
    • Effect: Skin lesions, cancers.
    • WHO limit: 10 µg·L⁻¹.
  • Nitrates (NO₃⁻)
    • Source: Fertiliser runoff, septic tanks.
    • Effect: Methemoglobinemia (“blue baby”).
    • WHO limit: 45 mg·L⁻¹.
  • Phosphates (PO₄³⁻)
    • Source: Detergents, agricultural runoff.
    • Effect: Eutrophication → algal blooms → hypoxia.
    • Typical safe level: 0.1 mg·L⁻¹.

3.5 Water Treatment Overview (Mnemonic: “C‑F‑R‑D”)

  1. C – Coagulation & Flocculation (Alum, ferric chloride).
  2. F – Filtration (sand, membrane).
  3. R – Disinfection (chlorine, UV, ozone).
  4. D – Desalination (if required) (reverse osmosis, multi‑stage flash).

4. Soil Pollution

4.1 Definition

Soil pollution = accumulation of hazardous chemicals in the soil that alter its physical, chemical or biological properties.

4.2 Sources & Common Contaminants

Source Contaminant(s) Typical Concentration Limits (India) Environmental Impact
Industrial waste dumps Heavy metals (Pb, Cd, Cr, Hg) Pb: 300 mg·kg⁻¹ (agricultural soil) Phytotoxicity, bio‑accumulation in food chain.
Pesticide & herbicide application DDT, Endosulfan, Glyphosate DDT: 0.1 mg·kg⁻¹ Soil fauna decline, groundwater leaching.
Oil spills & petroleum hydrocarbons PAHs, BTEX (Benzene, Toluene, Ethylbenzene, Xylene) PAHs: 0.2 mg·kg⁻¹ Reduced microbial activity, carcinogenic risk.
Landfill leachate Ammonia, heavy metals, organic acids NH₃‑N: 50 mg·L⁻¹ (permissible) Soil acidification, nitrate leaching.

4.3 Soil Pollution Mechanisms

  • Adsorption – metals bind to clay & organic matter; pH controls mobility.
  • Leaching – soluble contaminants move with percolating water to groundwater.
  • Volatilisation – organics (e.g., pesticides) can evaporate, entering the atmosphere.
  • Bio‑accumulation – uptake by plants → entry into food chain.

4.4 Remediation Techniques (Mnemonic: “P‑B‑R‑V”)

  1. P – Phytoremediation (hyper‑accumulator plants for metals).
  2. B – Bioremediation (microbial degradation of organics).
  3. R – Soil Washing / Remediation (chemical extraction, surfactants).
  4. V – Vitrification / Immobilisation (thermal treatment to lock contaminants).

5. Greenhouse Effect & Global Warming

5.1 What is the Greenhouse Effect?

The **greenhouse effect** is the trapping of outgoing infrared (IR) radiation by atmospheric gases, raising Earth’s surface temperature to ~15 °C (vs. 0 °C without greenhouse gases).

Cell Division: Mitosis vs. Meiosis & Significance

Cell division is a fundamental biological process by which a parent cell divides into two or more daughter cells. It is essential for growth, repair, reproduction, and the maintenance of life. There are two primary types of cell division: Mitosis and Meiosis. Understanding their mechanisms and significance is crucial for competitive exams like NDA, CDS, and AFCAT.

I. The Cell Cycle: The Life of a Cell

The cell cycle is the ordered sequence of events that a cell passes through from the time it is formed until it divides into two daughter cells. It consists of two main phases: Interphase and the M-phase (Mitotic/Meiotic phase).

A. Interphase (The Non-Dividing Phase)

Interphase is the longest phase of the cell cycle, during which the cell grows, replicates its DNA, and prepares for division. It is further divided into three sub-phases:

  • G1 Phase (First Gap/Growth Phase):
    • The cell grows in size and synthesizes proteins and organelles (e.g., mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum) necessary for DNA replication and cell division.
    • Metabolically active.
    • The cell decides whether to divide or enter a quiescent state (G0).
    • DNA content is 2C (diploid, two copies of each gene), and chromosome number is 2n.
  • S Phase (Synthesis Phase):
    • DNA replication occurs, resulting in the duplication of the genetic material.
    • Each chromosome now consists of two identical sister chromatids, joined at the centromere.
    • The amount of DNA doubles from 2C to 4C, but the chromosome number remains the same (2n), as the sister chromatids are still considered a single chromosome until they separate.
    • Histone proteins are synthesized to package the newly replicated DNA.
    • In animal cells, the centriole also duplicates.
  • G2 Phase (Second Gap/Growth Phase):
    • The cell continues to grow and synthesizes proteins (e.g., tubulin for spindle fibers) required for cell division.
    • Checks for DNA damage and ensures complete replication.
    • Prepares the cell for entry into the M-phase.
    • DNA content is 4C, and chromosome number is 2n.
  • G0 Phase (Quiescent Stage):
    • Some cells exit the cell cycle after G1 and enter a metabolically active but non-dividing state.
    • Examples include mature nerve cells, heart muscle cells, and some immune cells. These cells typically do not divide again.

B. M-Phase (Mitotic/Meiotic Phase)

This is the phase of actual cell division, involving both karyokinesis (nuclear division) and cytokinesis (cytoplasmic division).

  • Karyokinesis: Division of the nucleus, involving the separation of chromosomes.
  • Cytokinesis: Division of the cytoplasm, leading to the formation of two distinct daughter cells.

C. Cell Cycle Checkpoints

The cell cycle is tightly regulated by internal and external signals at specific checkpoints to ensure proper progression and prevent errors. Key checkpoints include:

  • G1 Checkpoint (Restriction Point): Crucial for deciding whether the cell will divide, delay division, or enter G0. Checks for cell size, nutrients, growth factors, and DNA damage.
  • G2 Checkpoint: Ensures DNA replication is complete and any DNA damage is repaired before entering mitosis.
  • M Checkpoint (Spindle Assembly Checkpoint): Occurs during metaphase and ensures all sister chromatids are correctly attached to the spindle microtubules before anaphase.

These checkpoints are regulated by proteins like cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs).

II. Mitosis (Equational Division)

Mitosis is a type of cell division that results in two daughter cells each having the same number and kind of chromosomes as the parent nucleus, typical of ordinary tissue growth. It is also known as equational division because the chromosome number in the daughter cells remains the same as in the parent cell.

A. Purpose and Occurrence

  • Purpose: Growth, repair, replacement of old/damaged cells, asexual reproduction in some organisms, regeneration.
  • Occurrence: Occurs in somatic cells (body cells) of multicellular organisms and in unicellular organisms for reproduction.

B. Phases of Mitosis (Karyokinesis)

Mitosis is a continuous process, but for descriptive purposes, it is divided into four distinct phases:

Mnemonic: PMAT (Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase)

  1. Prophase:
    • Chromatin condensation: The diffuse chromatin fibers condense and coil, becoming visible as distinct, compact chromosomes under a light microscope. Each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
    • Nuclear envelope disintegration: The nuclear membrane starts to break down into small vesicles.
    • Nucleolus disappears: The nucleolus, involved in ribosome synthesis, vanishes.
    • Centrosome migration: In animal cells, the duplicated centrosomes (each containing two centrioles) move to opposite poles of the cell.
    • Spindle formation: Microtubules begin to polymerize from the centrosomes, forming the mitotic spindle (spindle fibers). In animal cells, radial arrays of microtubules called asters form around the centrosomes.
  2. Metaphase:
    • Chromosome alignment: The condensed chromosomes align themselves along the equatorial plane of the cell, forming the metaphase plate (or equatorial plate). This alignment is crucial for equal distribution of genetic material.
    • Spindle fiber attachment: Spindle microtubules (specifically kinetochore microtubules) attach to the kinetochores – protein structures located at the centromere of each sister chromatid. Each sister chromatid is attached to spindle fibers from opposite poles.
    • Chromosomes are most condensed and distinct during this phase, making it ideal for kary

Biology – Revision Notes
Chapter: Tissues & Anatomy

1. Introduction to Histology

Histology is the microscopic study of tissues. It bridges the gap between gross anatomy and cellular biology, allowing us to understand how groups of cells cooperate to perform specialized functions. The discipline evolved in the 19th century with the invention of the compound microscope (1830‑1840) and the development of staining techniques by Camillo Golgi and Robert Koch.

Key Steps in Tissue Study

  • Fixation – preserves tissue architecture (e.g., 10 % formalin).
  • Embedding – usually in paraffin wax; for hard tissues, use resin.
  • Sectioning – microtome cuts 3‑10 µm sections; cryostat for frozen sections.
  • Staining – differentiates cell components (H&E, PAS, Toluidine blue, etc.).
  • Mounting & Observation – coverslip with mounting medium; examined under light, fluorescence or electron microscope.

2. Plant Tissues

Plant tissues are broadly classified into meristematic (actively dividing) and permanent (non‑dividing) tissues. Permanent tissues are further divided into simple (one cell type) and complex (more than one cell type).

2.1 Meristematic Tissues

Type Location Characteristics Function
Apical Meristem Tips of roots & shoots Small, densely cytoplasmic cells; thin primary walls Primary growth – length increase
Lateral Meristem Vascular cambium & cork cambium Divides periclinally & anticlinally Secondary growth – girth increase
Intercalary Meristem Nodes of grasses, internodes of monocots Located between mature tissues Allows rapid regrowth after grazing

2.2 Permanent Simple Tissues

2.2.1 Parenchyma

  • Thin primary walls; living cells.
  • Functions: photosynthesis, storage, secretion, and wound healing.
  • Types: Chlorenchyma (contains chloroplasts), Aeration parenchyma (air spaces – spongy mesophyll), Storage parenchyma (starch, oils, proteins).

2.2.2 Collenchyma

  • Unevenly thickened primary walls (pectic cortical fibers).
  • Living cells; provide flexible support in growing organs.
  • Common in petioles, young stems, and leaf margins.

2.2.3 Sclerenchyma

Dead at maturity; heavily lignified secondary walls.

Form Shape Location Function
Sclereids (Stone cells) Variable – spherical, branched, or elongated Fruits (e.g., pear), seed coats, leaf veins Mechanical protection
Fibers Long, slender, tapering Vascular bundles, phloem, cortex Tensile strength; source of linen, jute

2.3 Permanent Complex Tissues

2.3.1 Xylem (Water Conducting Tissue)

  • Components: Tracheids, Vessel elements, Xylem fibers, Xylem parenchyma.
  • Key features: lignified, dead at maturity, have perforations (vessels) or pits (tracheids).
  • Primary vs. Secondary Xylem: Primary formed by apical meristem; Secondary by vascular cambium (produces growth rings – annual rings).

2.3.2 Phloem (Food Conducting Tissue)

  • Components: Sieve‑tube elements, Companion cells, Phloem fibers, Phloem parenchyma.
  • Sieve plates have pores for translocation of sugars.
  • Living cells (except fibers); rely on companion cells for metabolic support.
  • Secondary phloem is produced outward by the cork cambium.

2.4 Mnemonic for Plant Tissue Types

“M‑P‑C‑S” – Meristematic, Parenchyma, Collenchyma, Sclerenchyma – helps recall the four simple permanent tissues in order of increasing wall thickness.

3. Animal Tissues

Animal tissues are classified into four basic types based on structure and function: epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous. Each type can be further sub‑divided.

3.1 Epithelial Tissue

Forms protective linings, glands, and surfaces. Key properties: cellularity, polarity, avascularity, regeneration.

Classification Number of Cell Layers Shape of Cells Typical Location
Simple Squamous 1 Flat, scale‑like Alveoli, glomeruli, endothelium
Simple Cuboidal 1 Cube‑shaped Kidney tubules, thyroid follicles
Simple Columnar 1 Tall, column‑shaped Digestive tract, gall bladder
Stratified Squamous >1 Flat (surface cells) Skin epidermis, oral cavity
Pseudostratified Columnar Appears multilayered Columnar nuclei at different levels Respiratory tract (ciliated)
Transitional 1–2 Round to squamous Urinary bladder

Specialised Epithelia – Glands

  • Exocrine glands – secrete onto surfaces (e.g., sweat, salivary).
  • Endocrine glands – ductless, release hormones into blood (e.g., thyroid, adrenal).
  • Glandular epithelium may be unicellular (goblet cells) or multicellular (acinar).

3.2 Connective Tissue

Most abundant tissue type; functions include support, binding, transport, and protection.

3.2.1 Cellular Connective Tissue

  • Loose (areolar) connective tissue – abundant fibers (collagen, elastic, reticular) & ground substance; acts as a packing material.
  • Adipose tissue – stores triglycerides; two types: white (energy reserve) and brown (thermogenesis).
  • Reticular tissue – forms stroma of lymphoid organs (spleen, lymph nodes).

3.2.2 Dense Connective Tissue

  • Dense regular – parallel collagen bundles; tendons & ligaments.
  • Dense irregular – random collagen; dermis, organ capsules.
  • Elastic connective tissue – abundant elastic fibers; walls of large arteries, lung parenchyma.

3.2.3 Specialized Connective Tissue

  • Cartilage – chondrocytes in lacunae; three types:
    1. Hyaline – most common; tracheal rings, articular surfaces.
    2. Fibrocartilage – intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis.
    3. Elastic cartilage – external ear, epiglottis.
  • Bone (osseous tissue) – osteocytes in lacunae, mineralized matrix (hydroxyapatite Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2); compact vs. spongy.
  • Blood – fluid connective tissue; plasma (liquid matrix) + formed elements (RBCs, WBCs, platelets).

3.3 Muscle Tissue

Contractile tissue responsible for movement. Classified by striations and nuclei number.

Type Striation Nuclei Control Location
Skeletal Present Multinucleated Voluntary (somatic) Attached to bones
Cardiac Present One central nucleus Involuntary (autonomic) Heart wall
Smooth Absent One central nucleus Involuntary Walls of hollow organs (gut, vessels)

Key Molecular Basis of Contraction

  • Actin (thin) + Myosin (thick) filaments slide – Sliding Filament Theory.
  • ATP hydrolysis provides energy; Ca2+ binds troponin (skeletal/smooth) or calmodulin (smooth) to expose myosin‑binding sites.
  • In cardiac muscle, intercalated discs contain desmosomes and gap junctions for synchronized contraction.

3.4 Nervous Tissue

Specialised for rapid signal transmission.

  • Neurons – functional units; consist of soma, dendrites, axon, and terminal boutons.
  • Neuroglia (glial cells) – support, myelination, immune defence.
    • Astrocytes, oligodendrocytes (CNS), Schwann cells (PNS), microglia, ependymal cells.

Myelin sheath increases conduction velocity (saltatory conduction). Nodes of Ranvier expose voltage‑gated Na+ channels.

4. Comparative Overview – Plant vs. Animal Tissues

Aspect Plant Tissues Animal Tissues
Cell Wall Cellulose‑based, rigid, provides turgor support. Absent; extracellular matrix (ECM) varies (collagen, elastin, proteoglycans).
Growth Zones Meristems (apical, lateral, intercalary). Growth via cell proliferation in epithelia & stem cells (e.g., basal layer of skin).
Transport System Xylem (water) & Phloem (photosynthates). Circulatory system – blood vessels (closed system).
Regeneration High – many
ai-gen-biology-digestive-system-organs-e:
Digestive System – Organs, Enzymes, Absorption & Nutrition

1. Quick Overview

The digestive system converts ingested food into absorbable nutrients and eliminates waste. It works as a coordinated unit of mechanical and chemical processes, regulated by neural and hormonal signals. For defence‑service exams, remember the three‑step flow:

  1. Ingestion & Mechanical Breakdown
  2. Chemical Digestion (Enzymes & pH)
  3. Absorption & Transport

2. Organs of the Digestive Tract

All organs are arranged in a continuous tube from mouth to anus, with three major accessory glands.

2.1. Primary (Alimentary) Canal

Organ Length / Size Key Functions Major Secretions / Enzymes
Mouth (Oral Cavity) ~5 cm (tongue‑to‑pharynx)
  • Ingestion, mastication, bolus formation
  • Initial carbohydrate digestion (α‑amylase)
  • Lubrication (saliva)
 Salivary α‑amylase, lingual lipase, mucins
Pharynx & Esophagus ≈12 cm (pharynx + esophagus)
  • Swallowing (voluntary → involuntary)
  • Peristaltic transport to stomach
 None (mechanical only)
Stomach ≈25 cm (average adult)
  • Temporary storage & mixing (churning)
  • Protein denaturation (HCl, pH ≈ 1.5‑3)
  • Activation of pepsinogen → pepsin
 Pepsin, gastric lipase, intrinsic factor, HCl
Small Intestine ≈6 m total; duodenum ≈ 25 cm, jejunum ≈ 2.5 m, ileum ≈ 3.5 m)
  • Major site of chemical digestion
  • Absorption of carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins & minerals
  • Hormonal regulation (CCK, secretin, GIP)
 Pancreatic amylase, trypsin, chymotrypsin, lipase, brush‑border enzymes (lactase, maltase, sucrase, peptidases)
Large Intestine (Colon) ≈1.5 m
  • Water & electrolyte re‑absorption
  • Fermentation of undigested residues by gut flora
  • Formation & storage of feces
 No digestive enzymes (microbial enzymes only)
Rectum & Anus ≈12 cm (rectum) Defecation control (internal & external sphincters) None

2.2. Accessory (Exocrine) Organs

  • Liver – Produces bile (≈ 0.5 L/day), stores glycogen, detoxifies, synthesises plasma proteins.
  • Gallbladder – Concentrates bile (up to 20‑fold) and releases it in response to CCK.
  • Pancreas (exocrine) – Secretes pancreatic juice containing enzymes (amylase, proteases, lipase) and bicarbonate (≈ 100 mEq/L) to neutralise gastric acid.

3. Digestive Enzymes – Who, Where & What?

Enzymes are classified by substrate (carbohydrate, protein, lipid) and by origin (salivary, gastric, pancreatic, brush‑border). Remember the mnemonic:

“S‑P‑B‑C” – Saliva, Pancreas, Brush‑border, Stomach – the four major enzyme sources.

3.1. Carbohydrate‑Digesting Enzymes

Enzyme Source Optimal pH Substrate → Product
Salivary α‑amylase (ptyalin) Salivary glands 6.7‑7.0 Starch → Maltose, maltotriose, α‑limit dextrins
Pancreatic α‑amylase Pancreas 7.1‑8.0 Starch → Maltose, maltotriose, limit dextrins
Maltase Brush‑border (small intestine) 6.0‑6.5 Maltose → 2 Glucose
Sucrase Brush‑border 6.0‑6.5 Sucrose → Glucose + Fructose
Lactase Brush‑border 6.0‑6.5 Lactose → Glucose + Galactose

3.2. Protein‑Digesting Enzymes

Enzyme Source Optimal pH Substrate → Product
Pepsin Stomach (pepsinogen → pepsin, activated by HCl) 1.5‑3.0 Proteins → Peptide fragments (mostly ≤ 10 aa)
Trypsin Pancreas (trypsinogen → trypsin, activated by enteropeptidase) 7.5‑8.5 Peptides → Smaller peptides + amino acids
Chymotrypsin Pancreas (chymotrypsinogen → chymotrypsin) 7.5‑8.5 Peptides → Smaller peptides
Carboxypeptidase Pancreas 7.0‑8.0 Peptide C‑terminal → Free amino acid
Brush‑border peptidases (aminopeptidase, dipeptidase) Enterocytes 6.0‑7.0 Peptides → Amino acids

3.3. Lipid‑Digesting Enzymes

Enzyme Source Optimal pH Substrate → Product
Lingual lipase Tongue (minor) ~7.0 Triglycerides → Free fatty acids + monoglycerides (≈ 10 % of total)
Gastric lipase Stomach (chief cells) 3‑4 Triglycerides → Diglycerides + free fatty acids
Pancreatic lipase (with colipase) Pancreas 7.5‑8.0 Triglycerides → 2 Free fatty acids + 2‑monoglyceride
Phospholipase A₂ Pancreas 7.0‑8.0 Phospholipids → Lysophospholipid + fatty acid
Lipase‑dependent bile salts (micelle formation) Liver (bile) + pancreas Neutral (≈ 7.0) Facilitates solubilisation of lipids for enzyme access

3.4. Enzyme Regulation – Key Points for Exams

  • Secretin – Stimulated by acidic chyme in duodenum; ↑ pancreatic HCO₃⁻ secretion.
  • Cholecystokinin (CCK) – Triggered by fats & amino acids; ↑ pancreatic enzyme release & gallbladder contraction.
  • Gastrin – Released by G‑cells (stomach); ↑ HCl & pepsinogen secretion.
  • Enterogastric reflex – Inhibits gastric emptying when duodenum is acidic or overly distended.

4. Digestion & Absorption – Step‑by‑Step

4.1. Mouth → Stomach (Mechanical + Initial Chemical)

  • Mastication reduces particle size → increases surface area.
  • Saliva (≈ 0.5 L/day) provides lubrication and α‑amylase activity.
  • Swallowing initiates peristalsis; the epiglottis prevents aspiration.

4.2. Stomach – Protein & Limited Lipid Digestion

  • Gastric glands secrete HCl (pH ≈ 1.5‑3) → denatures proteins, activates pepsinogen.
  • Pepsin cleaves peptide bonds preferentially at aromatic residues (Phe, Trp, Tyr).
  • Gastric lipase works best at low pH, contributing ~ 10 % of total lipid hydrolysis.
  • Intrinsic factor (IF) binds vitamin B₁₂ for later ileal absorption.

4.3. Duodenum – The Chemical Hub

Four major secretions converge:

  1. Bile (from liver & gallbladder) – Emulsifies fats into micelles.
  2. Pancreatic juice – Enzymes + HCO₃⁻ (neutralises gastric acid).
  3. Brush‑border enzymes – Final carbohydrate & peptide breakdown.
  4. Enteric hormones – Regulate secretions and motility.

4.4. Small Intestine – Absorption Zones

Use the mnemonic “D‑J‑I” – Duodenum (Digest), Jejunum (Absorb nutrients), Ileum (Absorb B₁₂ & bile salts).

Human Physiology – Circulatory System

Quick Exam Overview

Key Points to Remember for NDA/CDS/AFCAT:

  • Heart is a muscular pump weighing 250‑300 g in males and 200‑250 g in females.
  • Normal resting heart rate = 60‑100 bpm; cardiac output (CO) = Stroke Volume (SV) × Heart Rate (HR).
  • Blood volume ≈ 5 L (≈ 7 % of body weight).
  • Major vessels: Aorta, Pulmonary artery & vein, Superior & Inferior vena cava.
  • Four cardiac phases: Atrial systole, Isovolumetric contraction, Ventricular ejection, Isovolumetric relaxation.
  • Heart sounds: S1 – “lub” (AV valves), S2 – “dub” (semilunar valves).

1. Anatomy of the Heart

1.1 External Features

Structure Location / Description Clinical Relevance
Apex Pointed tip, directed inferiorly, anteriorly & to the left (5th intercostal space, mid‑clavicular line). Point of maximal impulse (PMI) – palpated in thoracic exam.
Base Broad superior part, faces right shoulder; contains the three major veins (SVC, IVC, pulmonary veins). Orientation for echocardiography.
Interventricular Septum Divides left & right ventricles; contains the bundle of His. Ventricular septal defect (VSD) – most common congenital heart lesion.
Coronary Sulcus Groove separating atria from ventricles; houses coronary arteries. Site of coronary artery atherosclerosis.

1.2 Internal Chambers & Valves

Mnemonic for valve order (from right to left, atrium to ventricle): TRAP – Tricuspid, Right (pulmonary) semilunar, Aortic, (Left) Mitral (bicuspid).

Chamber Wall Thickness Typical Pressure (mm Hg) Key Function
Right Atrium (RA) Thin 0‑5 Receives de‑oxygenated blood from SVC, IVC & coronary sinus.
Right Ventricle (RV) Moderate 15‑30 (systolic) Pumps blood to pulmonary artery (low‑resistance circuit).
Left Atrium (LA) Thin 5‑12 Receives oxygen‑rich blood from four pulmonary veins.
Left Ventricle (LV) 1.0‑1.2 cm (thickest) 120‑140 (systolic) Generates systemic arterial pressure.

1.3 Conduction System

  • Sino‑atrial (SA) node – “natural pacemaker”; intrinsic rate 70‑80 bpm.
  • Atrioventricular (AV) node – delay of 0.1 s to allow ventricular filling.
  • Bundle of His → Right & Left Bundle Branches → Purkinje fibers – rapid ventricular depolarisation.

2. Blood Vessels – Structure & Function

2.1 General Classification

All vessels consist of three layers (from inside out):

  1. Tunica intima – endothelium + sub‑endothelial connective tissue.
  2. Tunica media – smooth muscle (regulates diameter).
  3. Tunica externa (adventitia) – connective tissue, nerves, vasa vasorum.

2.2 Arteries

  • High pressure, thick tunica media.
  • Elastic arteries (e.g., aorta, pulmonary trunk) contain abundant elastic fibers – maintain blood flow during diastole (Windkessel effect).
  • Muscular arteries (e.g., femoral, brachial) regulate regional blood flow via vasoconstriction/dilation.

2.3 Veins

  • Low pressure, thin walls, large lumen.
  • Contain valves (especially in limbs) to prevent backflow.
  • Major systemic veins: Superior & Inferior vena cava; pulmonary veins (carry oxygenated blood).

2.4 Capillaries

Site of exchange – single‑layer endothelium with a basement membrane.

Type Structure Function
Continuous Uninterrupted endothelial lining; tight junctions. Most tissues – brain (BBB), skin, muscle.
Fenestrated Trans‑endothelial pores (≈ 60 nm). Kidney glomeruli, endocrine glands – high filtration.
Discontinuous (Sinusoidal) Large gaps, discontinuous basement membrane. Liver, spleen, bone marrow – exchange of cells & large proteins.

3. Blood – Composition & Functions

3.1 Quantitative Overview

  • Total volume: 5 L (≈ 7 % of body weight).
  • Plasma: 55 % of blood volume; cells: 45 % (hematocrit).

3.2 Plasma – Major Solutes

Component Concentration (g/L) Physiological Role
Albumin 35‑50 g/L Maintains oncotic pressure, carrier for hormones & drugs.
Globulins 20‑35 g/L Immunoglobulins, transport proteins, complement.
Fibrinogen 2‑4 g/L Key clotting factor; converted to fibrin.
Electrolytes Na⁺ 135‑145 mmol/L, K⁺ 3.5‑5.0 mmol/L, Cl⁻ 95‑105 mmol/L Maintain osmotic balance, nerve impulse transmission.

3.3 Cellular Elements

Cell Type Normal Count (×10⁶/µL) Primary Function
Erythrocytes (RBCs) 4.5‑5.5 (male) / 4.0‑5.0 (female) Oxygen transport via haemoglobin (Hb ≈ 15 g/dL).
Leukocytes (WBCs) 4‑11 ×10³/µL Immunity – neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils.
Platelets (Thrombocytes) 150‑400 ×10³/µL Primary role in haemostasis & clot formation.

3.4 Haemoglobin & Oxygen Transport

  • Structure: tetrameric protein (2 α + 2 β chains) each with a heme group.
  • O₂‑binding curve: Sigmoidal due to cooperative binding.
  • Key constants:
    • P₅₀ (partial pressure at 50 % saturation) ≈ 26.6 mm Hg at pH 7.4, 37 °C.
    • Bohr effect: ↓pH or ↑CO₂ → right shift (decreased affinity).

4. Cardiac Cycle – Detailed Chronology

The cardiac cycle repeats with each heartbeat and consists of two major phases: systole (contraction) and diastole (relaxation). Total duration at rest ≈ 0.8 s (≈ 75 beats/min).

4.1 Phase‑by‑Phase Description

Phase Time (seconds) Valve Status Key Events
Atrial Systole 0.10‑0.12 s AV valves open, semilunar valves closed ↑ atrial pressure → ~30 % of ventricular filling (atrial kick).
Isovolumetric Contraction 0.05 s All valves closed Ventricular pressure rises sharply; no volume change.
Ventricular Ejection 0.30‑0.35 s Semilunar valves open, AV valves closed Blood expelled into aorta & pulmonary trunk; peak systolic pressure reached.
Isovolumetric Relaxation 0.08 s All valves closed Ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure; ventricles relax.
Rapid Ventricular Filling 0.10‑0.12 s AV valves open, semilunar valves closed ≈ 70 % of ventricular filling occurs.
Diastasis (Slow Filling) Variable (up to 0.30 s at rest) AV valves open Equilibrium phase; filling slows as
ai-gen-biology-nervous-system-neuron-cns:
Human Physiology – Nervous System

1. Quick Overview

The nervous system is the body’s rapid‑communication network. It integrates sensory input, processes information and generates motor output. It is broadly divided into:

  • Central Nervous System (CNS) – brain & spinal cord.
  • Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) – all nerves & ganglia outside the CNS.

All functions are carried out by specialised cells called neurons and supporting glial cells.

2. Neuron – The Functional Unit

2.1 General Structure

Component Structure Primary Function
Soma (Cell Body) Contains nucleus, Nissl bodies, mitochondria Metabolic centre; integrates incoming signals
Dendrites Short, highly branched processes Receive afferent (sensory) impulses
Axon Long, single fibre; may be myelinated Conducts efferent (motor) impulses away from soma
Axon Hillock Conical region at axon origin Site of action‑potential initiation (high density of Na⁺ channels)
Myelin Sheath Layers of Schwann cells (PNS) or oligodendrocytes (CNS) Insulates axon; speeds conduction via saltatory propagation
Nodes of Ranvier Gaps in myelin (~1 µm long) Regenerate action potential; essential for rapid conduction
Synaptic Terminal (Bouton) Swollen axonal end containing synaptic vesicles Release neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft

2.2 Types of Neurons (by Function)

  • Sensory (Afferent) Neurons – carry information from receptors to CNS.
  • Motor (Efferent) Neurons – transmit commands from CNS to effectors (muscles/glands).
  • Interneurons – connect sensory & motor neurons within CNS; constitute >99% of CNS cells.

2.3 Types of Neurons (by Structure)

Structural Type Example Key Feature
Multipolar Motor neuron, pyramidal cell One axon, many dendrites – most common in CNS
Bipolar Retinal photoreceptor, olfactory receptor One axon, one dendrite – specialised sensory pathways
Unipolar (Pseudounipolar) Somatic sensory neuron Single process that bifurcates into peripheral & central branches

2.4 Action Potential – The Electrical Impulse

Resting membrane potential (RMP) ≈ ‑70 mV (inside negative). The classic 4‑phase sequence:

  1. Depolarisation – rapid Na⁺ influx (Na⁺ channels open) → membrane potential rises to ~+30 mV.
  2. Peak – Na⁺ channels inactivate; voltage‑gated K⁺ channels open.
  3. Repolarisation – K⁺ efflux restores negativity.
  4. After‑hyperpolarisation (undershoot) – K⁺ channels close slowly; membrane briefly more negative than RMP.

Key formulas (useful for exam calculations):

  • Conduction velocity (myelinated) ≈ 120 m/s (≈ 2 m per ms).
  • Conduction velocity (unmyelinated) ≈ 0.5–2 m/s.
  • Length constant (λ) = √(Rm / Ri) – determines how far a passive potential spreads.
  • Time constant (τ) = Rm × Cm – time required for membrane to charge to 63% of final value.

2.5 Synaptic Transmission

At the chemical synapse:

  1. Action potential arrives at the bouton.
  2. Voltage‑gated Ca²⁺ channels open → Ca²⁺ influx.
  3. Synaptic vesicles fuse (exocytosis) releasing neurotransmitter (e.g., ACh, dopamine).
  4. Neurotransmitter binds to postsynaptic receptors → either excitatory (Na⁺ influx) or inhibitory (Cl⁻ influx, K⁺ efflux).
  5. Neurotransmitter cleared by enzymatic degradation or re‑uptake.

Mnemonic for the steps: “A‑C‑V‑R‑C” – Action potential, Ca²⁺ entry, Vesicle fusion, Receptor binding, Clearance.

3. Central Nervous System (CNS)

3.1 Major Divisions

Region Sub‑structures Primary Functions (exam focus)
Brain
  • Cerebrum (cerebral cortex, basal nuclei, limbic system)
  • Diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus)
  • Brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata)
  • Cerebellum
  • Higher cognition, voluntary motor control, sensory integration (cerebrum)
  • Relay & modulation of sensory info (thalamus); homeostasis, endocrine control (hypothalamus)
  • Cardiovascular & respiratory centres (medulla); reflexes, arousal (midbrain)
  • Balance, posture, coordination (cerebellum)
Spinal Cord Cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral segments; dorsal & ventral horns Transmission conduit; houses reflex arcs; motor output via ventral horns; sensory input via dorsal horns.

3.2 Protective Coverings

  • Meninges – three layers:
    1. Dura mater – tough outermost; contains venous sinuses.
    2. Arachnoid mater – web‑like; subarachnoid space holds CSF.
    3. Pia mater – delicate inner layer adhering to brain surface.
  • Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) – produced by choroid plexus; cushions CNS, maintains ionic balance.
  • Blood‑Brain Barrier (BBB) – endothelial tight junctions + astrocytic end‑feet; restricts passage of large/charged molecules.

3.3 Key Historical Milestones (useful for “History” questions)

  • 1849 – Ramon y Cajal proposes neuron doctrine (neurons are discrete units).
  • 1906 – Hodgkin & Huxley formulate quantitative model of action potential (won Nobel 1963).
  • 1952 – Discovery of the synaptic vesicle cycle by Bernard Katz.

4. Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)

4.1 Functional Classification

Division Components Primary Role
Somatic Nervous System (SNS) Motor nerves to skeletal muscles; sensory afferents from skin, joints, proprioceptors. Voluntary movement & conscious sensation.
Autonomic Nervous System (ANS) Sympathetic & Parasympathetic trunks, visceral afferents, pre‑ & post‑ganglionic fibres. Involuntary control of heart, glands, smooth muscle.

4.2 Autonomic Sub‑Divisions – “SAME DAVE” Mnemonic

Sympathetic – Adrenal medulla, Muscarinic, Epinephrine (post‑ganglionic).

Parasympathetic – Direct (pre‑ganglionic) to organ, Acetylcholine (both pre‑ & post‑ganglionic), Vagus nerve (cranial X), Eyes (III), Dorsal motor nucleus (brainstem).

4.3 Cranial & Spinal Nerves

There are 12 cranial nerves (I‑XII) and 31 spinal nerve pairs. Remember the classic mnemonic for cranial nerves:

“On Old Command, The Four Interest Views In Xylophone Values, In Xylophones, Xylophones, In Very Interesting Xylophone Values.” (O = Olfactory, O = Optic, C = Oculomotor, …, X = Vagus, etc.)

5. Reflex Arc – The Fastest Response Pathway

5.1 General Architecture

A reflex arc is a simple neural circuit that bypasses the brain for speed. The classic five‑component model:

  1. Receptor – detects stimulus (e.g., muscle spindle).
  2. Afferent (Sensory) Neuron – carries impulse to CNS.
  3. Integration Centre – one or more interneurons in spinal cord gray matter.
  4. Efferent (Motor) Neuron – transmits command to effector.
  5. Effector – muscle or gland that produces response.

5.2 Types of Reflexes

Reflex Type Example Pathway Characteristics
Monosynaptic Patellar (knee‑jerk) reflex Single synapse between Ia afferent & alpha‑motor neuron; fastest (~30 ms).
Polysynaptic Withdrawal reflex (painful stimulus) Involves one or more interneurons; allows integration of multiple inputs.
Autonomic Reflex Pupillary light reflex Uses parasympathetic pathways; effector is sphincter pupillae.
Conditioned Reflex Pavlovian salivation Learned association; cortical involvement.
