Marathas – Shivaji, Peshwas & Decline

Why This Chapter Is Crucial for NDA/CDS/AFCAT

Key take‑away: The Maratha Empire was the last indigenous power that challenged Mughal supremacy in the Indian sub‑continent. Understanding its rise, administrative genius, military tactics and eventual decline equips you with answers for multiple‑choice, short‑answer and essay‑type questions in history papers. Remember: 1674 (coronation of Shivaji) and 1818 (final defeat at the hands of the British) are the two book‑ends you must never miss.

1. Shivaji Maharaj – The Founder

1.1 Early Life & Background

  • Birth: 1630 at Shivneri Fort, near Pune.
  • Parents: Shahaji Bhosale (a Maratha noble in the Deccan) and Jijabai (devout and politically astute).
  • Influences: Jijabai’s stories of ancient Hindu heroes, the Ramayana and Mahabharata, and the political vacuum created by the weakening Adil Shahi and Qutb Shahi sultanates.

1.2 The “Hindavi Swarajya” Ideology

Shivaji’s rallying cry was Hindavi Swarajya – “self‑rule of the Hindavi people”. This was not a religious war but a political movement aimed at establishing a sovereign state free from foreign domination. The phrase appears in his “Shivaji’s Letter to the Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb” (dated 1659).

1.3 Chronology of Major Events (Table 1)

Year Event Significance
1645 Capture of Torna Fort First major victory; demonstrated guerrilla tactics.
1656 Seizure of Javali (Kalyan) and Surat raids Economic base built on maritime trade and plunder.
1659 Letter to Aurangzeb demanding autonomy First diplomatic assertion of sovereignty.
1665 Battle of Pratapgad – defeat of Afzal Khan Legendary use of “Ghadar” (poisoned dagger) and psychological warfare.
1674 Coronation at Raja Rani (Raigad Fort) Formal establishment of the Maratha kingdom; adoption of the title “Chhatrapati”.
1680 Death of Shivaji Transition to his son Sambhaji; set the stage for Mughal retaliation.

1.4 Administration – The “Ashta Pradhan” Council

Shivaji instituted a council of eight ministers, each responsible for a specific portfolio. This system was a precursor to modern cabinet governance.

  • Peshwa (Prime Minister): Moropant Trimbak Pingle – handled foreign affairs and revenue.
  • Amatya (Finance Minister): Ramchandra Pant Amatya – oversaw treasury and land revenue.
  • Senapati (Commander‑in‑Chief): Netaji Palkhi – directed the army.
  • Nyayadhish (Chief Justice): Ramchandra Khanderao – administered justice.
  • Daftar (Secretary): Shankaraji Narayan – maintained records.
  • Shurunavis (Intelligence): Raghunathrao – espionage and internal security.
  • Sumant (Provincial Governor): Raghunathrao – supervised provincial administration.
  • Panditrao (Religious Affairs): Mahadev Pandit – managed temples and religious endowments.

1.5 Military Innovations

  • Guerrilla Warfare (Ganimi Kava): Use of hill forts, night raids, and swift cavalry.
  • Naval Power: Construction of a fleet at Suvarnadurg and Khanderi to challenge Portuguese and British shipping.
  • Fort Architecture: Multi‑layered defenses, secret passages, and water reservoirs (e.g., Raigad, Pratapgad, Sindhudurg).
  • Standardised Infantry Units: “Havaldar” (company commander) and “Javala” (light infantry) formations.

1.6 Exam Tip

When asked about Shivaji’s administration, always mention the Ashta Pradhan and link it to the modern concept of a cabinet. A quick mnemonic: “P‑A‑S‑N‑D‑S‑S‑P” (Peshwa, Amatya, Senapati, Nyayadhish, Daftar, Shurunavis, Sumant, Panditrao).

2. The Peshwa Era – Expansion & Consolidation

2.1 Rise of the Peshwas

After Shivaji’s death, the real power gradually shifted from the Chhatrapati to the Peshwas. By the early 18th century, the Peshwa had become the de‑facto ruler of the Maratha Confederacy.

2.2 Bajirao I (1730‑1740) – The Master Strategist

  • Born: 1700 in Saswad.
  • Key Battles:
    • Battle of Palkhed (1739): Defeated the Nizam of Hyderabad using rapid cavalry movements.
    • Battle of Bhopal (1737): Secured Maratha dominance in Central India.
  • Administrative Reforms: Introduced the “Chauth” (one‑fourth tax) and “Sardeshmukhi” (one‑tenth tax) systems to finance the army.

2.3 Balaji Baji Rao (Nanasaheb) (1740‑1761)

Balaji Baji Rao expanded the empire into the north but suffered a catastrophic defeat at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) against Ahmad Shah Durrani. This battle is a frequent MCQ topic; remember the date 1761 and the loss of ~70,000 Maratha soldiers.

2.4 The Maratha Confederacy – A Federal Structure

By the mid‑18th century, the empire was a loose confederacy of semi‑autonomous chiefs:

  • Holkar (Indore)
  • Scindia (Gwalior)
  • Bhonsle (Nagpur)
  • Gaekwad (Baroda)
  • Mahadji Shinde – played a pivotal role in Delhi politics post‑Panipat.

2.5 Economic Base – Chauth & Sardeshmukhi

Revenue Type Rate Collected From Purpose
Chauth 25% of land revenue Non‑Maratha territories (e.g., Mughal provinces) Military upkeep & expansion
Sardeshmukhi 10% additional levy Traditional Maratha lands Royal household & administrative expenses

2.6 Peshwa Administration – Key Offices

  • Diwan (Finance): Managed the Chauth collection network.
  • Senapati (Military): Coordinated the multi‑regional armies.
  • Pratinidhi (Representative): Acted as the Peshwa’s envoy to the Mughal court.

2.7 Exam Tip – “5‑S” Mnemonic for Peshwa Era

Remember the five major features: Strategy (Bajirao’s cavalry), State‑finance (Chauth/Sardeshmukhi), Sub‑regional chiefs (Holkar, Scindia, etc.), Strategic northward expansion, and Set‑backs (Panipat).

3. Decline of the Maratha Empire

3.1 Internal Weaknesses

  • Succession Disputes: After Shivaji’s death, the throne saw frequent power struggles between different branches of the Bhonsle family.
  • Over‑reliance on Chauth: The revenue system was unsustainable once the Mughal Empire collapsed and local rulers stopped paying tribute.
  • Fragmentation: The confederacy turned into a “coalition of warlords” with competing interests, weakening central command.

3.2 External Pressures

  • Third Battle of Panipat (1761): Massive loss of manpower and morale.
  • British East India Company: Systematic diplomatic treaties (e.g., Treaty of Surat, 1775) and military victories (e.g., Battle of Buxar, 1764).
  • Maratha–Mysore Wars: Conflict with Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan drained resources.

3.3 The Final Collapse (1818)

The decisive moment came when Lord Minto and General Thomas Miller captured Pune and forced the Peshwa Baji Rao II to surrender. The Treaty of Surat (1818) marked the formal end of Maratha sovereignty.

3.4 Comparative Decline – Mauryan Empire

Understanding why empires fall helps answer comparative questions. The Mauryan decline offers a classic template.

DECLINE OF THE MAURYAN EMPIRE

Factors Leading to Decline:

  • Weak Successors: Weak rulers and succession disputes weakened the empire.
  • Regional Revolts: Provinces started asserting independence, leading to fragmentation.
  • Economic Drain: Costly military campaigns and bureaucratic expenses strained the treasury.

Notice the parallel with the Marathas: both suffered from weak successors, regional fragmentation, and economic over‑extension. This comparison is a favourite essay hook.

3.5 Thematic Mnemonic for Maratha Decline – “FIRE”

  • F – Fractured Confederacy
  • I – Internal Succession Crises
  • R – Revenue System Failure (Chauth/Sardeshmukhi)
  • E – External Aggression (Panipat, British)

3.6 Exam Tip – Diagrammatic Answer

For a 5‑mark diagram, draw a flow‑chart starting with Shivaji’s foundation → Peshwa expansion → Panipat (1761) → British treaties → 1818 surrender. Use arrows and brief captions (≤ 8 words each) to earn maximum marks.

4. Contextual Connections – Other Contemporary Civilisations

While the Maratha story unfolds, other regions of the sub‑continent experience parallel developments. The following extracted points are integrated verbatim to illustrate the broader historical canvas.

Why These Points Matter for Maratha Revision

  • Understanding the French factories at Surat (1668) helps answer questions on European competition with the Marathas for coastal trade.
  • The year 1674 appears twice – Shivaji’s coronation and Pondicherry’s designation as French capital – a classic “same‑year” trap in MCQs.

Bhakti and Sufi Movements in Medieval India

Introduction to Bhakti and Sufi Movements

Bhakti and Sufi movements were revolutionary religious, social, and cultural phenomena that emerged in medieval India, fundamentally transforming the spiritual landscape of the subcontinent. These movements arose as powerful alternatives to both orthodox Brahmanical Hinduism and institutionalized Islam, emphasizing direct personal devotion (bhakti in Sanskrit meaning "attachment, devotion, or love") and mystical union with the Divine (Islamic mysticism). They flourished between approximately the 7th century CE and the 17th century CE, though their influence continued well beyond. Both movements challenged the prevailing social hierarchies, criticized ritualistic excess, and promoted egalitarian values, laying the foundational stones for modern Indian syncretic culture. Their legacy is evident in India's pluralistic ethos, literature, arts, and even contemporary communal harmony initiatives. For defence examinations like NDA, CDS, and AFCAT, understanding these movements is critical not merely for historical knowledge but for comprehending how India evolved into a civilization tolerant of diverse faiths—a principle deeply embedded in the Indian Army's secular ethos.

The Bhakti Movement

Origins and Historical Context

The Bhakti Movement has its roots in ancient India, traceable to the Upanishads, which introduced monotheistic and monistic ideas, particularly through concepts like Brahman (the ultimate reality) and Atman (the individual soul). The term “Upanishad” literally means “sitting beside the teacher,” indicating the guru-disciple tradition of spiritual learning. These texts departed from Vedic ritualism and explored metaphysical themes such as the origin of the universe, the nature of God, and the cycle of life and death. Followers of the paths of Karma (action), Atma (soul), and Brahma (God) emphasized spiritual inquiry over ceremonial practice. The Upanishads are also referred to as Vedanta (“the end of the Vedas”) or the culmination of Vedic thought, advocating the Jnana Marga (path of knowledge).

However, the organized Bhakti movement gained momentum during the early centuries CE, especially under the influence of the Satuṁjñāna** sects and later with the rise of devotion-centered literature in regional languages. By the medieval period (roughly 8th–17th centuries), Bhakti had become a pan-Indian phenomenon, spreading from the Deccan to Bengal, from Gujarat to Tamil Nadu. It was simultaneously a reaction against priestly dominance and an assertion of individual spiritual agency.

Core Philosophy of Bhakti

The philosophy of Bhakti centers around the concept of unconditional love and surrender to a personal deity. Unlike the impersonal Brahman of the Upanishads, Bhakti emphasizes a personal God (or Goddess) with whom the devotee can establish an intimate relationship—whether as a parent, friend, lover, or servant. This emotional connection transcends caste, gender, and social status, making Bhakti inherently democratic.

  • Unity of God: Many Bhakti saints rejected polytheism and ritual worship, advocating instead for monotheism or henotheism (worship of one supreme deity while accepting others).
  • Egalitarianism: Caste-based discrimination was openly criticized. Saints came from all walks of life—including lower castes and women—and often rejected traditional social norms.
  • Use of Vernacular Languages: Instead of Sanskrit (the language of the elite), Bhakti poets composed in regional languages, making spiritual teachings accessible to common people.
  • Rejection of Rituals: Formal ceremonies, temple worship, and pilgrimage were downplayed in favor of inner purity and devotion.
  • Potential for Salvation for All: Through pure devotion (prema), anyone—regardless of birth, caste, or gender—could attain liberation (mokṣa).

Key Saints of the Bhakti Movement

Early Alvars and Nayanars (South India)

The earliest expressions of Bhakti were seen in Tamil literature through the Alvars** (Vaishnava saints) and Nayanars** (Shaiva saints), who lived between the 6th and 9th centuries CE. Their hymns, collectively called Nalayira Divya Prabandham (for Alvars) and Tirumurai** (for Nayanars), became foundational texts of Tamil Bhakti theology. The Alvars worshipped Vishnu/Krishna, while the Nayanars devoted themselves to Shiva.

  • Nayanars: Shaiva saints whose devotional songs formed part of the Tirumurai, a twelve-volume collection.

North Indian Bhakti Saints

Ramananda (14th Century CE)

Ramananda was one of the earliest North Indian Bhakti saints. Born into a Brahmin family in Varanasi, he emphasized devotion to Ram (an avatar of Vishnu). He welcomed disciples from all castes, including Kabir, Mirabai, and Narsi Mejwaji. His teachings were simple yet profound:

  • All humans are equal before God.
  • Service and remembrance of God (smarana) lead to salvation.
  • Scriptural authority should not override personal experience.

His disciple Kabir became a legendary figure whose verses blended Hindu and Islamic mysticism. Mirabai, a Rajput princess, dedicated her life to Krishna bhakti despite family opposition.

Chaitanya Mahaprabhu (1486–1534 CE)

Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, born Nitai Gaurang in Bengal, revolutionized Vaishnavism by promoting kṛṣṇa bhakti. He propagated the Gaudiya Vaishnava** tradition, which emphasizes ecstatic love (prema) for Lord Krishna. His teachings included:

  • Seven-tier process of devotional service (sādhana)
  • Singularity of chanting the holy names of God (japa)
  • Rejecting caste distinctions

He traveled extensively across India, gathering followers regardless of religious background. His disciples, such as Six Goswamis of Vrindavan, later established major centers of Krishna consciousness, especially in Vrindavan.

Ramanuja (1017–1137 CE)

Ramanuja, a Vishishtadvaita philosopher, was instrumental in institutionalizing Bhakti within Hindu theology. He emphasized that devotion (bhakti) leads to union with God (Narayana). Unlike Shankara’s Advaita (non-dualism), Ramanuja taught that the soul and body are distinct yet inseparable parts of the Supreme Being. Key tenets:

  • Qualified Non-Dualism: God is the only truth; individual souls and matter are manifestations of Him.
  • Three Modes of Worship: Listening, reflection, and meditation on the Divine Name.
  • Emphasis on Grace: Liberation comes through divine grace, not just karma or knowledge.

He also worked tirelessly to spread Vaishnavism among non-Brahmins, commissioning temple construction and translating scriptures into regional languages.

Madhvacharya (1238–1317 CE)

Madhvacharya founded the Dvaita school of Vedanta, which asserts dualism—the soul and God are eternally separate. He emphasized exclusive devotion (eka marga) to Lord Vishnu/Hari. Though more philosophical than mystical, his work laid groundwork for later Bhakti poets in Karnataka.

Bhakti in Regional Languages

One of the defining features of the Bhakti movement was its use of vernacular languages. While classical Sanskrit dominated scholarly discourse, Bhakti poets composed in local tongues:

Impact of the Bhakti Movement

The Bhakti movement had far-reaching consequences:

  • Social Reform: Challenged caste hierarchy and gender discrimination. Women like Mirabai and Gomati Devi participated actively as poets and teachers.
  • Religious Unity: Fostered harmony between Hindus and Muslims, influencing later syncretic traditions.
  • Literary Renaissance: Enriched regional literatures and democratized education.
  • Cultural Synthesis: Influenced music, dance, painting, and architecture.
  • Rise of Sects: Strengthened Vaishnavism, Shaivism, Shakta traditions, and new movements like the Lingayats and Varkari sampradaya.

The Sufi Movement

Origin and Spread

The Sufi Movement emerged in India with the arrival of Islamic mystics—known as Sufis—from Persia, Central Asia, and the Middle East during the Delhi Sultanate period (12th–16th centuries). Unlike orthodox Islamic scholars (ulema), Sufis emphasized inner purification, love for God, and rejection of ritualistic practices. They played a significant role in converting large populations to Islam, particularly in North India.

Philosophy of Sufism

Sufism is rooted in Islamic mysticism, focusing on:
Wahdat al-Wujūd (Unity of Existence) – Concept popularized by Ibn Arabi, suggesting that all existence is a manifestation of the One Reality.
Wahdat al-Shuhūd (Unity of Witnessing) – Developed by Ahmad Sirhindi, stating that apparent multiplicity is perceived due to limited vision.

  • Love and Devotion: Sufis believed in intense longing (shawq) for the Divine Beloved.
  • Renunciation: Rejection of material possessions and worldly pleasures.
  • Mystical Experience: Emphasis on direct realization of God through meditation, music, dance, and breath control.
  • Universal Brotherhood: Belief in the spiritual equality of all beings.

Orders of Sufism in India

  • Chishti Order: Most prominent; known for musical sama’ sessions, open kitchens (langar khana), and tolerance toward Hindus.
  • Sufi Sama’: Musical performances involving qawwalis, instrumentals, and devotional dances intended to induce mystical states.
  • Other Orders: Qadiriyya, Naqshbandiyya, Suhrawardiyya — each with unique practices but sharing core values of love, service, and remembrance of God.

Impact of Sufism

  • Religious Conversion: Played a major role in spreading Islam without force, appealing especially to lower-caste Hindus disillusioned by Brahmanical rigidity.
  • Cultural Integration: Merged Persian and Indian traditions in art, architecture, literature, and music.
  • Promotion of Education: Established madrasas and libraries, preserved knowledge during turbulent times.
  • Social Harmony: Encouraged interfaith dialogue and mutual respect, countering communal tensions.

Comparison Between Bhakti and Sufi Movements

AspectBhakti MovementSufi Movement
OriginHindu revivalist traditionIslamic mystical tradition
LanguageRegional languages (Tamil, Hindi, Telugu, etc.)Persian, Arabic, Urdu
Focus DeityVishnu, Shiva, Krishna, DeviAllah (with personal aspects)
Attitude Toward CasteStrongly opposed caste systemOpposed racial and ethnic discrimination
PracticeSinging, dancing, temple visitsDhikr (remembrance), Sama’ (listening), meditation
View on RitualsRejected elaborate ritualsMinimised ritual dependence
Influence on SocietyBroke caste barriers, empowered womenPromoted communal harmony, spiritual equality

Common Themes and Shared Values

Despite emerging from different religious contexts, both movements shared several core principles:

  • Universal Brotherhood: Both rejected social hierarchies based on birth.
  • Personal Relationship with the Divine: Emphasized intimacy over formality.
  • Rejection of Orthodoxy: Questioned priestly mediation and ritual excess.
  • Use of Music and Poetry: Employ artistic expression as vehicles of divine experience.
  • Promoting Peace: Advocated non-violence, forgiveness, and tolerance.

Legacy and Long-Term Effects

The combined impact of the Bhakti and Sufi movements shaped medieval and early modern Indian society in profound ways:

  • Foundation of Syncretism: Created a synthesis of Hindu and Islamic cultures, visible in festivals like Muharram-Karbala being celebrated alongside Holi-Diwali.
  • Influence on Sikhism: Guru Nanak drew inspiration from both traditions, integrating elements of Bhakti and Sufism into the Guru Granth Sahib.
  • Literary Heritage: Produced timeless works such as Tulsidas' Ramcharitamanas, Kabir Bijak, and Amir Khusrau’s poetry.
  • Musical Traditions: Gave rise to classical forms like Dhrupad, Khyal, and Qawwali.
  • Modern Movements: Inspired 19th-century reformers like Raja Rammohan Roy, Swami Vivekananda, and Sir Syed Ahmad Khan.

Exam Tips and Important Dates

For competitive exams, remember these crucial details:

  • Timeline: Bhakti – 7th Century CE onwards; Sufism – 12th Century CE during Delhi Sultanate
  • Key Figures: Ramananda, Kabir, Mirabai, Chaitanya, Nizamuddin Auliya, Amir Khusrau
  • Important Texts: Guru Granth Sahib, Tirumurai, Nalayira Divya Prabandham, Bijak, Sikshapatradali
    • br>
  • Philosophies: Wahdat al-Wujud (Ibn Arabi), Qualified Non-Dualism (Ramanuja)
    • br>
  • Orders: Chishti, Qadiriyya, Naqshbandiyya, Suhrawardiyya
    • br>
  • Sects Influenced: Lingayats, Varkaris, Sikhism
    • br>
  • Regional Centers: Vrindavan, Mathura, Ajmer Sharif, Delhi, Multan
    • br>
  • Cultural Contributions: Architecture (Taj Mahal-style tombs), Music (Qawwali), Literature (Mystic poetry)
    • br>

Mnemonics for Remembering Key Points

  • “BRS” – Bhakti, Ramananda, Sufism: Remember the chronological flow of Bhakti → Sufism through key figures.
  • “VNSK” – Vedanta, Nayanars, Sufism, Kabir: Helps recall major traditions and saints.
  • “CMNS” – Chaitanya, Mirabai, Nizamuddin, Salim: List of influential saints from different regions.
  • “RAVAN” – Ramananda, Amir Khusrau, Vallabha, Anand, Nizamuddin: Quick mnemonic for saint names.
  • “DIVINE” – Devotion, Inclusivity, Vedas, Inner peace, Nectar of Names, Equality: Core ideals of both movements.

Historical Context Beyond the Movements

While studying Bhakti and Sufi movements, students must recognize their broader historical context:

  • The Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526 CE) saw increased Islamic presence and cultural exchange.
  • The fall of the Kabaka dynasty in Karnataka led to the rise of Lingayat and Veerashaiva movements.
  • The Mughal era (especially under Akbar) provided state patronage to syncretic traditions.
  • The arrival of European colonial powers shifted focus toward reform and renaissance movements.
  • The decline of feudalism created conditions conducive to religious democratization.

Role During Colonial Period

During the British Raj, Bhakti-Sufi legacies were invoked by nationalists and reformers alike:

  • Swami Vivekananda cited Ramakrishna’s teachings as evidence of Hindu tolerance.
  • Mahatma Gandhi praised Sufi shrines for fostering unity.
  • Subhas Chandra Bose referenced medieval rulers who maintained harmony.
  • British administrators often misrepresented these movements as anti-national.
  • Communal tensions in the Partition era were partly fueled by distortion of historical narratives.

Contemporary Relevance for Defence Services

The Indian Armed Forces upholds the secular spirit embodied in the Bhakti-Sufi legacy:

  • The Army’s motto "Service Before Self" reflects the selfless service ideal (seva) promoted by both traditions.
  • Regimental systems draw strength from diverse religious communities, mirroring medieval syncretic ethos.
  • Officer training institutes emphasize values of tolerance and respect, rooted in centuries-old Indic traditions.
  • UN Peacekeeping missions reflect global application of universal brotherhood taught by saints.
  • Military chaplaincy supports multiple faiths, echoing the inclusive spirit of medieval shrines.

Conclusion

The Bhakti and Sufi movements represent one of history’s greatest experiments in spiritual democracy, cultural synthesis, and social transformation. They challenged entrenched hierarchies, redefined religiosity, and laid the foundation for India’s pluralistic identity. Understanding them deeply is essential not only for academic success in competitive exams but also for building character and leadership qualities essential for military service.

By embracing the universal messages of love, justice, and divine fellowship espoused by saints across faiths, aspirants can develop the moral compass needed for public life and national defense.

European Arrival in India – Portuguese, Dutch, French & British (Modern India)

This entry covers Advant Of Europeans, found on page 141.

This entry covers British Wars, found on page 142.

This entry covers British Policies, found on page 143.

This entry covers British Acts, found on page 144.

1. Overview – Why Europe Turned East?

  • Search for Spice Route – Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498.
  • Mercantilism – Nations believed wealth lay in accumulating gold & silver via trade surplus.
  • Religious Motives – Spread of Christianity, especially by the Portuguese and later the French Jesuits.
  • Technological Edge – Superior naval artillery, ship‑building (caravel, galleon) and navigation (compass, astrolabe).

2. Portuguese (1498‑1650)

2.1 Chronology & Key Figures

Year Event Significance
1498 Vasco da Gama lands at Calicut First direct sea link between Europe & India; ends Arab monopoly.
1500 Pedro Álvares Cabral discovers Brazil & reaches Cochin Establishes Portuguese foothold on the Malabar Coast.
1510 Afonso de Albuquerque captures Goa Goa becomes capital of Portuguese India – “Rome of the East”.
1526 Battle of Talikota (Deccan) – Portuguese stay neutral Shows limited inland ambitions; focus remains coastal.
1555 Establishment of the “Estado da Índia” Administrative structure – Viceroy, Council, and the “Casa da Índia”.
1650 Portuguese power wanes after Dutch & English attacks Marks the end of Portuguese dominance.

2.2 Advantages of the Portuguese

  • Naval Supremacy – Heavily armed carracks & galleons.
  • Monopoly of Pepper – Controlled the “Black Gold” trade from Kerala.
  • Fortified Settlements – Goa, Daman, Diu, Cochin, and Chaul.
  • Religious Outreach – Jesuit missions, conversion of locals (e.g., Goa’s Catholic community).
  • Legal Instruments – “Padroado” (royal patronage) gave them exclusive rights to missionary work.

2.3 Decline Factors

  • Inability to expand inland – reliance on coastal ports.
  • Rise of Dutch & English naval power in the 17th century.
  • Corruption within the “Casa da Índia”.
  • Local resistance – Maratha raids on Goa (1660‑1665).

3. Dutch (1602‑1795)

3.1 Chronology & Key Figures

Year Event Significance
1602 Formation of the Dutch East India Company (VOC) World’s first joint‑stock company; capital of ≈ 6.5 million guilders.
1610 First Dutch factory at Surat Entry into Gujarat’s textile market.
1615 Capture of Pulicat (Tamil Nadu) Base for Coromandel pepper & cotton trade.
1656 Siege of Goa – Dutch attempt to oust Portuguese Failed; Goa remains Portuguese.
1795 Dissolution of VOC Marks end of Dutch political influence in India.

3.2 Dutch Advantages

  • Commercial Focus – Unlike Portuguese, the Dutch prioritized trade over territorial conquest.
  • Advanced Accounting – Double‑entry bookkeeping gave better profit analysis.
  • Strategic Forts – Fort St. George (Madras) later taken over by British; Pulicat, Nagapattinam.
  • Treaties with Local Rulers – E.g., the “Treaty of Surat” (1610) granting duty‑free trade.
  • Naval Innovation – Use of “fluyt” ships – cheaper, larger cargo capacity.

3.3 Decline Factors

  • Heavy competition from the British East India Company (EIC).
  • Financial mismanagement – VOC declared bankrupt in 1795.
  • Limited military presence – could not defend factories against local uprisings.

4. French (1664‑1763)

4.1 Chronology & Key Figures

Year Event Significance
1664 Founding of French East India Company (Compagnie des Indes Orientales) Louis XIV’s mercantile policy; capital ≈ 3 million livres.
1673 Establishment of Pondicherry (Puducherry) Becomes French capital in India.
1690‑1695 War of the Grand Alliance – French naval raids on Bombay & Surat Shows French willingness for military action.
1757 Battle of Plassey (British victory) – French influence wanes French lose their last stronghold in Bengal.
1763 Treaty of Paris (1763) France cedes most Indian territories to Britain; retains Pondicherry, Chandernagore, Mahe, Yanam, Karaikal.

4.2 French Advantages

  • Cultural Diplomacy – French missionaries, scholars, and the “Enlightenment” ideas attracted Indian elites.
  • Naval Strength – Under Admiral Duquesne, French navy challenged British at sea.
  • Strategic Ports – Pondicherry, Chandernagore, Karaikal – well‑defended harbours.
  • Alliances with Indian Powers – Support to the Nawab of Bengal, Marathas, and Mysore (later under Hyder Ali & Tipu Sultan).

4.3 Decline Factors

  • Defeat in the Seven Years’ War (1756‑1763) – global setback.
  • British naval blockade of French ports in India.
  • Limited financial backing from France after 1763.

5. British (1600‑1947) – From Trading Company to Imperial Power

5.1 Chronology – Key Milestones

Year Event Impact
1600 Charter granted to the East India Company (EIC) Monopoly over English trade with the East.
1617 First factory at Surat Entry into lucrative Gujarati textile market.
1639 Acquisition of Madras (Fort St. George) Strategic base on Coromandel Coast.
1661 Acquisition of Bombay from Portuguese (Marriage of Charles II & Catherine of Braganza) Future naval hub.
1757 Battle of Plassey First major territorial gain – Bengal under Mir Jafar.
1761 Battle of Wandiwash (Third Carnatic War) Defeat of French; British supremacy in South India.
1773 Regulating Act First parliamentary control over EIC.
1793 Pitt’s India Act Established Board of Control – dual governance.
1857 Indian Rebellion (Sepoy Mutiny) End of Company rule; Crown takes over.
1858 Government of India Act 1858 Establishment of the British Raj – Viceroy as Crown’s representative.
1909 Morley‑Minto Reforms Limited Indian representation in legislative councils.
1919 Government of India Act 1919 (Montagu‑Chelmsford Reforms) Dyarchy in provinces; expanded electorate.
1935 Government of India Act 1935 Provincial autonomy; federal structure (never fully implemented).
1947 Independence & Partition British exit; creation of India & Pakistan.

5.2 Advantages of the British (Extracted from “Advant Of Europeans” – p.141)

  • Naval Dominance – Royal Navy’s global reach ensured safe sea‑lines.
  • Financial Muscle – Access to London’s capital markets; ability to raise £10 million for wars.
  • Administrative Machinery – Systematic revenue collection (Diwani rights), land surveys (e.g., 1767 Revenue Settlement).
  • Legal Framework – Introduction of English law, codified statutes, and courts.
  • Military Organization – Professional European troops, sepoy regiments, and later the Indian Army.
  • Divide‑and‑Rule Policy – Exploitation of existing rivalries (Mughals vs. Marathas, Sikh vs. Afghan).
  • Infrastructure Development – Railways, telegraph, ports – facilitated control and extraction.

5.3 British Wars in India (Extracted from “British Wars” – p.142)

Understanding the chronology of wars is crucial for answering objective questions. Use the mnemonic “P‑C‑B‑W‑M‑S” (Plassey, Carnatic, Buxar, War of 1857, Mysore, Sikkim) to recall the major conflicts.

  1. Battle of Plassey (1757) – Robert Clive defeats Siraj‑ud‑Daula; start of British political control in Bengal.
  2. Carnatic Wars (1746‑1763) – Three wars against French & local Nawabs; culminates in Battle of Wandiwash (1761).
  3. Battle of Buxar (1764) – Defeat of Mir Qasim, Shuja‑ud‑Daula, and Shah Alam II; EIC obtains Diwani rights over Bengal, Bihar, Orissa.
  4. Anglo‑Maratha Wars (1775‑1818) – Series of three wars ending with the Treaty of Pune (1818) – Maratha Confederacy dismantled.
  5. Anglo‑Mysore Wars (1767‑1799) – Four wars; final defeat of Tipu Sultan at Seringapatam (1799).
  6. First War of Indian Independence (1857‑58) – Sepoy Mutiny; leads to dissolution of EIC.
  7. Anglo‑Sikh Wars (1845‑1849) – Two wars; annexation of Punjab (1849).
  8. Anglo‑Naga & Anglo‑Lushai Expeditions (1879‑1880) – Consolidation of North‑East frontier.

5.4 British Policies (Extracted from “British Policies” – p.143)

These policies are frequently asked in essay-type questions. Memorise the key points and their impact.

Policy Year / Enactment Core Objective Result / Impact
Doctrine of Lapse 1848 (Lord Dalhousie) Annexation of princely states lacking a natural heir. Annexed Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur; fueled discontent leading to 1857.
Permanent Settlement 1793 (Lord Cornwallis) Fix land revenue in Bengal & fix it forever. Created Zamindari class; increased peasant exploitation.
Ryotwari System 1820‑30s (Lord William Bentinck & later in Madras) Direct settlement with cultivators (ryots). Implemented in Madras & Bombay; mixed results.
Doctrine of Subsidiary Alliance 1802 (Lord Wellesley) Indian princes to accept British troops & pay for them. Reduced autonomy of princely states; expanded British control.
Land Revenue Reforms – Bengal (Permanent Settlement) 1793 Standardize revenue collection. Increased cash flow to Britain; created class of absentee landlords.
Education Policy – Macaulay’s Minute 1835 Promote English education for “a class of persons Indian in blood and colour, but English in tastes, in opinions, in morals and in intellect”. Rise of Western‑educated Indian elite; foundation for nationalist movement.
Railway Policy 1853 (first railway line Bombay‑Thane) Facilitate troop movement & resource extraction. By 1900, > 40,000 km of track; economic integration.

5.5 British Acts (Extracted from “British Acts” – p.144)

These Acts are the backbone of constitutional history. Remember the year, the main provision, and its significance.

  1. Regulating Act (1773) – First attempt to control EIC; created Governor‑General (Warren Hastings) & Supreme Court at Calcutta.
  2. Pitt’s India Act (1784) – Established Board of Control; dual administration (Company & Crown).
  3. Charter Act of 1813 – Ended monopoly of EIC in India (except tea & trade with China); opened Indian market to British merchants.
  4. Charter Act of 1833 – Centralised legislative power in the Governor‑General’s Council; introduced the “Law Commission”.
  5. Government of India Act 1858 – Abolished EIC; transferred power to the Crown; created Viceroy of India.
  6. Indian Councils Act 1861 – Introduced legislative councils at centre and provinces; limited Indian representation.
  7. Indian Councils Act 1892 – Expanded council size; allowed limited discussion on budget.
  8. Morley‑Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act 1909) – Introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
  9. Montagu‑Chelmsford Reforms (Government of India Act 1919) – Dyarchy in provinces; increased Indian participation.
  10. Simon Commission (1928) & Government of India Act 1935 – Proposed federal structure; introduced provincial autonomy.
  11. Indian Independence Act 1947 – Partition & creation of Dominion of India & Pakistan.

5.6 Comparative Table – Portuguese, Dutch, French & British

Aspect Portuguese Dutch French British
First Arrival 1498 – Vasco da Gama 1602 – VOC charter 1664 – Compagnie des Indes Orientales 1600 – EIC charter
Primary Goal Spice monopoly & missionary work Trade (pepper, textiles) – commercial profit Trade + cultural influence (Enlightenment) Trade → territorial control → empire
Key Ports Goa, Daman, Diu, Cochin Pulicat, Surat, Batavia (Indonesia) as base Pondicherry, Chandernagore, Karaikal Madras, Bombay, Calcutta, Surat
Military Strategy Fortified enclaves; limited inland campaigns Naval power; few forts; relied on treaties Naval raids; alliances with Indian princes Professional army, sepoys, naval supremacy, divide‑and‑rule
Administrative System Viceroy, Casa da Índia VOC Governor‑General, local factors Governor‑General, French civil law Governor‑General, Board of Control, later Viceroy
Peak Period 16th‑early 17th century Mid‑17th century Mid‑18th century (till 1763) Late‑18th century to 1947
Legacy Christian communities, Goa architecture Trade networks, Dutch legal influence in Kerala Pondicherry’s French culture, legal code Modern Indian administrative, legal, railway, education system

6. Mnemonics & Memory Aids for Exams

  • “V‑C‑A‑D‑B‑M‑F” – Remember the order of European arrival: Vasco (Portuguese), Calicut (Portuguese), Albuquerque (Portuguese), Dutch (VOC), British (EIC), Madras (British), French (Pondicherry).
  • “P‑C‑B‑M‑S‑W” – Major wars: Plassey, Carnatic, Buxar, Mysore, Sikh, War of 1857.
  • “D‑P‑R‑S‑M” – Policies: Doctrine of Lapse, Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari, Subsidiary Alliance, Macaulay’s Education.
  • “R‑P‑C‑G‑I‑M‑A” – Acts: Regulating (1773), Pitt’s (1784), Charter (1813), Government (1858), Indian Councils (1861, 1892), Morley‑Minto (1909), Act 1935.

7. Exam‑Focused Tips & Tricks

  1. Never forget dates! Highlight every year with color‑coded spans. In MCQs, the year often distinguishes two similar events (e.g., 1757 Plassey vs. 1764 Buxar).
  2. Compare & Contrast – For essay questions, structure answers as: Introduction → European motives → Portuguese → Dutch → French → British → Impact on India → Conclusion. Use the comparative table to quickly recall differences.
  3. Use “Cause‑Effect” chains – Example: Doctrine of Lapse → Annexation of Jhansi → 1857 Rebellion → Crown rule.
  4. Link personalities with policies – Lord Dalhousie → Doctrine of Lapse; Lord Cornwallis → Permanent Settlement; Lord Wellesley → Subsidiary Alliance.
  5. Map‑Based Questions – Memorise the location of each European settlement; draw quick sketches: Goa (Portuguese), Pulicat (Dutch), Pondicherry (French), Calcutta (British).
  6. Keywords for quick scoring – In short answers, start with “The British advantage lay in their naval supremacy, financial resources and administrative machinery” – this hits three marks instantly.
  7. Chronology is king – For “Match the Year with Event” sections, write the mnemonic “P‑C‑B‑M‑S‑W” on your scratch paper and then fill the blanks.

8. Summary – The Transition from Trade to Empire

All four European powers entered India primarily for trade. However, only the British successfully transformed a commercial enterprise into a full‑blown empire. Their advantages – superior navy, financial clout, systematic administration, and a policy of exploiting Indian divisions – allowed them to outlast the Portuguese, Dutch, and French, whose focus remained largely mercantile or cultural.

Understanding the chronology of wars, the policy framework, and the legislative acts is essential for any NDA, CDS, or AFCAT aspirant. The tables, mnemonics, and exam tips provided above are designed to help you recall every fact, date, name, and formula needed for a top‑scoring answer.

Modern India: Governor-Generals & Viceroys – Key Policies and Events

RELIGIOUS HISTORY

Ashoka's Policy of Dhamma: Ashoka embraced Buddhism and promoted a policy of Dhamma (righteousness).

  • Encouraged moral conduct, non-violence, and respect for all religions.
  • Edicts were inscribed on pillars and rocks, propagating Dhamma and outlining ethical principles.
  • Ashokan Edicts: Ashoka's edicts were inscribed in various parts of the empire.
  • They provided insights into Ashoka's governance, social policies, and religious tolerance.

British Policies

This entry covers British Policies, found on page 143.

Governor-Generals & Viceroys

This entry covers Governor Generals & Viceroys, found on page 145.

Permanent Settlement

Features:

  • Land settlement with the Zamindars.
  • Nature of Settlement is permanent.
  • 10/11 share to EIC.
  • 1/11 share to Zamindar.
  • Also known as Istemari or Sunset Law.
  • Zamindar became actual owner.
  • Zamindari post was hereditary and transferable.
  • Exploitative system.

Misc:

  • Introduced by Lord Cornwallis & John Shore.
  • Area - Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
  • Year - 1793.

List of Governor-Generals (1773-1858)

No. Name Tenure Key Contributions/Policies
1 Winston Churchill (1st) 1773-1785 Introduced Regulating Act 1773; reformed East India Company's administration.
2 John Macpherson 1785-1786 De facto Governor-Generals due to absence of first.
3 Morris (4th) 1786-1790 Promoted trade; oversaw Mysore Wars.
4 Edward Brinton 1790-1793 Last of the 'Four Honest Men'.
5 Lord Cornwallis 1793-1805 Introduced Permanent Settlement (1793); implemented legal reforms; oversaw Battle of Seringapatam (1799).
6 John Shore 1801-1806 Implemented Permanent Settlement; laid foundation for British Raj.
7 William Bentinck 1828-1835 Annihilated Devadasi System; promoted Western education; banned animal slaughter.
8 Lord William Bentinck 1833 Introduced Macaulay's Educational Policy.
9 Governors as Deputies 1848-1858 After Revolt of 1857, position became Viceroy.

List of Viceroys (1858-1947)

No. Name Tenure Key Contributions/Policies
1 Lord Canning 1858-1862 Started Indian Civil Service Reforms; declared India a self-governing dominion.
2 Lord Elgin 1862-1864 Supported Indian National Congress (1885); sponsored railways and telegraphs.
3 Lord Lytton 1876-1880 Oversaw Third Anglo-Afghan War (1878-1880); implemented Doctrine of Lapse.
4 Robert Hart 1880-1882 Demonstrated in Hart's Columns; emphasized fiscal responsibility.
5 Lord Lansdowne 1888-1892 Introduced Indian Universities Act 1904; promoted irrigation.
6 William Welbyn (Avebury) 1893-1899 Opposed separate electorates; opposed the Partition of Bengal (1905).
7 Lord Curzon 1899-1905 Reorganized Bengal; imposed Partition of Bengal (1905); builtrailways.Suez Canal opened (1869).
8 John Mayne 1905-1910 Annulled Partition of Bengal (1911); promoted Swaraj.
9 Lord Hardinge 1910-1916 Delhi Durbar (1911); supported Home Rule Movement.
10 Lord Reading 1916-1921 Introduced Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919); oversaw Non-Cooperation Movement (1920).
11 David Lloyd George 1926-1931 Dismissed CMs of Sind and NWFP; faced Civil Disobedience Movement (1930).
12 Lord Irwin (Willingdon) 1931-1936 Implemented Simon Commission Report (1928); supported Round Table Conferences.
13 Lord Willingdon 1936-1943 Started Quit India Movement (1942); opposed Cripps Mission (1942).
14 Lord Wavell 1943-1947 Last Viceroy; initiated Partition Plan (1946); handed over power to Nehru/Jinnah.

Permanent Settlement System: In-Depth Analysis

The Permanent Settlement, introduced in 1793 by Lord Cornwallis and John Shore, was a landmark revenue reform in British India. It aimed to stabilize revenue collection and create a loyal zamindari class to support British rule.

  • Zamindari System:
    • Zamindars were recognized as revenue collectors and proprietors of land.
    • They were allowed to hereditary possession of their estates.
    • The fixed revenue demand was termed "Permanent," hence the name Istemari or Sunset Law.
    • EIC received 10/11th share, while zamindars kept 1/11th as profit. This led to exploitation of peasantry.
  • Impact:
    • Created a feudal-like structure in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
    • Long-term consequences included stagnation in agricultural development.
    • Zamindars often evaded cultivation, leading to revenue shortfalls.
    • Inspired similar systems like Ryotwari (Madras) and Mahalwari (North-Western Provinces).

Mnemonic for Zamindari Systems: "Z-R-M: Zamindari (Bengal), Ryotwari (Madras), Mahalwari (NW Provinces)"

Key British Policies and Their Impacts

1. Regulating Act (1773)

  • Established Governor-Council System in Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras.
  • Created Board of Control in London to oversee Indian administration.
  • Formalized the role of Governor-General with supreme authority.

2. Pitt's India Act (1784)

  • Strengthened the dual control of the British Government and East India Company.
  • Established a Secretary of State for India with advisory powers over the Board of Control.

3. Doctrine of Lapse (1848-1856)

  • Annexation policy by Lord Dalhousie.
  • Principle: States without heirs or adopted heirs could be annexed.
  • Controversial annexations: Jharkhand, Satara, Nagpur, and Awadh (1853).
  • Triggered resistance, notably in Bhopal, Jhansi, and Satara.

4. Subsidiary Alliance (1833)

  • Diplomatic strategy by Lord William Bentinck.
  • Rajas agreed to:
    • Host a British subsidiary force.
    • Accept British protection.
    • Not form alliances without British consent.
  • Expanded British influence in Maratha and Rajput states.

5. Partition of Bengal (1905)

  • Announced by Lord Curzon to weaken anti-British sentiments.
  • Divided Bengal into West Bengal (with Calcutta) and East Bengal (with Dhaka).
  • Faced mass resistance; led to Swadeshi Movement.
  • Annulled in 1911; recreated in 1947 during Partition.

6. Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919)
  • First major constitutional reforms to introduce limited self-governance.
  • Established Governors' Provincial Councils and Legislative Councils.
  • Montagu Declaration promised gradual responsible government.
  • Introduced dyarchy in provinces.

7. Government of India Act (1935)

  • Modeled after British federal system.
  • Established dominion status for India.
  • Segregated subjects into Provincial and Central List.
  • Introduced Provincial Autonomy for 11 provinces.
  • Led to formation of Indian National Congress ministries in 1937.

Post-1857 Administrative Reforms

  • Abolition of Doctrine of Lapse: Discontinued by Lord Ripon (1880).
  • Irreligious Tolerance: Supported Hindu festivals and reduced Christian missionary activities.
  • Provincial Autonomy: Encouraged Indian participation in civil services via Irish Exam system.

Key Events Under British Rule

1. Battle of Plassey (1757)

  • EIC victory under Robert Clive over Nawab of Bengal, Siraj-ud-Daulah.
  • Laid foundation for British dominance in Bengal.

2. Battle of Buxar (1764)

  • EIC defeated Mughal emperor Shah Alam II and Nawabs of Bengal and Awadh.
  • Resulted in Treaty of Allahabad (1765); EIC gained Diwani rights (revenue collection).

3. Revolt of 1857

  • Also known as First War of Independence or Sepoy Mutiny.
  • Triggered by:
    • Greased cartridges rumor affecting Hindu and Muslim soldiers.
    • Annexation of princely states via Doctrine of Lapse.
    • Environmental changes (e.g., introduction of pig and cow fat in ammunition).
  • Key centers: Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, Gwalior, and Peshawar.
  • Key Rebels:
    • bahadur Shah Zafar (symbolic leader).
    • Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi.
    • Nana Saheb.
    • Mangal Pandey (first martyr).
  • Outcomes:
    • EIC dissolved; Crown took direct control (Viceroys appointed).
    • Abolished Doctrine of Lapse.
    • Policy of "Divide and Rule" strengthened.
    • Emphasis on irrigational development.

4. Establishment of Indian National Congress (1885)

  • Founded by A.O. Hume in Allahabad.
  • Initial demand: maximum responsible government within British dominion.

Indian National Congress (INC) – Formation, Early Moderates & Extremists

1. Genesis of the Indian National Congress

The Indian National Congress (INC) was founded on 28th December 1885 at a historic gathering in Bombay. The idea of a pan‑Indian political platform was first mooted by A.O. Hume, a retired British civil servant, who believed that a moderate, constitutional forum could channel Indian aspirations without threatening British rule.

  • Founding Meeting: Held at the Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay. 72 delegates attended, representing diverse regions, religions, and professions.
  • Key Founders:
    • A.O. Hume – Architect of the Congress idea.
    • Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee – First President (Bombay).
    • Dadabhai Naoroji – First Indian President (Calcutta, 1887) and the “Grand Old Man of India”.
    • S. Narayana Pillai – First Secretary of the Congress.
    • Surendranath Banerjee – Early leader, later known as “Rashtriya Pandit”.
  • Initial Objectives (as per the 1885 resolution):
    1. To obtain a greater share in the administration of India for educated Indians.
    2. To promote unity among all sections of Indian society.
    3. To discuss and present grievances to the British Government.

2. Ideological Spectrum: Moderates vs. Extremists

From its inception, the Congress housed a spectrum of political thought. By the early 20th century, two distinct factions emerged:

AspectModerates (1885‑1905)Extremists (1905‑1919)
LeadershipDadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Surendranath BanerjeeLala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal, Bal Gangadhar Tilak (the “Lal‑Bal‑Tilak” trio)
PhilosophyConstitutional methods, petitions, dialogue, loyalty to the Crown, gradual reforms.Mass mobilisation, Swadeshi, boycott of British goods, direct action, self‑reliance.
Key Slogans“Loyalty to the Crown, but demand rights.”“Swaraj is my birthright!” (Tilak), “Boycott, Swadeshi, and National Education.”
Preferred InstrumentsLegislative councils, petitions, speeches in the British Parliament.Public meetings, newspapers (e.g., *Kesari*, *The Hindu*), secret societies (e.g., Abhinav Bharat).
Relationship with BritishCo‑operative, sought incremental concessions.Confrontational, demanded immediate self‑government.
Notable Achievements1905 Partition of Bengal protest (initially moderate), Indian Councils Act 1892, 1909 (Morley‑Minto reforms).1905 Swadeshi Movement, 1908 formation of the Indian Home Rule League (Bal Gangadhar Tilak), 1911 Delhi Durbar protests.

2.1. The Moderates – Detailed Profile

The moderate leaders believed that the British Empire could be persuaded through reasoned argument and moral appeal. Their approach was heavily influenced by liberal British political thought.

  • Dadabhai Naoroji – Authored “Poverty and Drain of Wealth” (1871), quantifying the economic exploitation of India. His famous “Drain Theory” argued that wealth was being transferred from India to Britain, causing chronic poverty.
  • Gopal Krishna Gokhale – Founder of the Servants of India Society (1905). Emphasised social reform, education, and the upliftment of the masses through constitutional means.
  • Surendranath Banerjee – First Indian to be elected to the British Parliament (though later disqualified). Championed the “New Party” concept, urging Indians to form a disciplined political party.
  • Key Strategies:
    • Petitioning the British Parliament and Viceroy.
    • Submitting memoranda on civil service, education, and railway policies.
    • Using the press (e.g., *The Hindu*, *The Times of India*) to articulate grievances.
  • Exam Tip: Remember the mnemonic “N G B – Naoroji, Gokhale, Banerjee” for the three pillars of moderate leadership.

2.2. The Extremists – Detailed Profile

The extremist faction grew out of frustration with the limited pace of reforms and the British response to the 1905 Partition of Bengal.

  • Lala Lajpat Rai – “Punjab Kesari”. Advocated for the rights of peasants and workers, and was a vocal critic of the British education policy.
  • Bipin Chandra Pal – Propagated the “New Hindu” ideology, emphasizing industrialisation, scientific temper, and social reform.
  • Bal Gangadhar Tilak – Coined the slogan “Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it”. Edited the Marathi newspaper Kesari and the English weekly The Mahratta. Arrested in 1897 for sedition (the “Tilak Trial”).
  • Key Instruments:
    • Swadeshi – promotion of indigenous goods; boycott of British textiles.
    • Boycott – refusal to purchase British products, especially cloth.
    • Public rallies – massive gatherings in Calcutta, Bombay, and Lahore.
    • Secret societies – e.g., Abhinav Bharat (founded by Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, 1904).
  • Important Events:
    1. 1905 Partition of Bengal – Triggered the first mass Swadeshi movement.
    2. 1908 – Tilak arrested for sedition; Lala Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal arrested under the Press Act.
    3. 1910 – Formation of the All India Home Rule League by Tilak, demanding self‑government within the British Empire.
    4. 1911 – Re‑unification of Bengal; extremist agitation intensified.
  • Exam Tip: Use the mnemonic “L B T – Lajpat, Bipin, Tilak” to recall the three chief extremists.

6. Transition from Moderates to Extremists – The 1907 Surat Split

The Surat Session (1907) is a watershed moment that crystallised the ideological divide. The session was presided over by Sir Surendranath Banerjee, while Bal Gangadhar Tilak was elected Vice‑President. The following events unfolded:

  1. Resolution on the Partition of Bengal – Moderates sought a conciliatory approach; extremists demanded immediate boycott of British goods.
  2. Voting controversy – The “Committee of the Congress” (moderate‑dominated) attempted to sideline extremist proposals, leading to heated debates.
  3. Outcome – The Congress split into two factions:
    • “Naram Dal” (Moderate faction) – Continued constitutional lobbying.
    • “Garam Dal” (Extremist faction) – Adopted Swadeshi and mass agitation.

Exam Tip: Remember the phrase “Surat’s Split – Naram vs. Garam” to instantly recall the two factions and their temperaments.

7. Impact of the Moderates & Extremists on Subsequent Movements

Both streams contributed uniquely to the evolution of Indian nationalism.

7.1. Legacy of the Moderates

  • Established the institutional framework of the Congress – annual sessions, committees, and a structured constitution.
  • Introduced the concept of “Indianisation” of the civil services, which later became a cornerstone of the Montagu‑Chelmsford reforms (1919).
  • Laid the groundwork for future leaders (e.g., Gopal Krishna Gokhale) to mentor younger activists like Mahatma Gandhi.

7.2. Legacy of the Extremists

  • Mobilised the masses for the first time, turning politics from an elite pursuit to a popular movement.
  • Popularised the Swadeshi ideology, which later became a central tenet of the Non‑Cooperation Movement (1920‑22).
  • Created a template for future revolutionary organisations (e.g., Ghadar Party, HSRA).

8. Chronology of Key Events (1885‑1919) – Quick Reference

9. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) – Exam Oriented

  1. Q: Who were the three chief moderate leaders of the INC?
    A: Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Surendranath Banerjee – remember “N G B”.
  2. Q: What slogan is associated with Tilak?
    A: “Swaraj is my birthright”.
  3. Q: Which session marked the definitive split between Moderates and Extremists?
    A: The Surat Session, 1907.
  4. Q: Name the three newspapers that acted as mouthpieces for the Extremists.
    A: Kesari (Marathi), The Mahratta (English), Punjab Kesari (Hindi).
  5. Q: What was the “Drain Theory” and who propounded it?
    A: It argued that wealth was being transferred from India to Britain, causing poverty; formulated by Dadabhai Naoroji.

10. Revision Strategies & Exam Tips

  • Timeline Mapping: Draw a horizontal timeline from 1885 to 1919. Mark key sessions, splits, and reforms. Visual cues help recall dates quickly.
  • Compare‑Contrast Tables: Use the provided tables to memorise differences; colour‑code (e.g., green for Moderates, red for Extremists) in your handwritten notes.
  • Mnemonics: Reinforce “N G B” and “L B T” before the exam; repeat aloud.
  • Answer Writing: In essay questions, start with a brief intro (formation), then discuss the two factions using sub‑headings, and conclude with their combined impact on later movements.
  • Link with Earlier History: Connect the political consciousness of the Vedic & Mahajanapada periods (as shown in the extracted content) with the later nationalist awakening – emphasise continuity of “self‑rule” aspirations.
  • Past Paper Practice: Solve at least five previous years’ questions on “INC formation and early phases”. Analyse the pattern – most ask for dates, leaders, and the 1907 split.

11. Concluding Synthesis

The Indian National Congress, born in 1885, evolved from a modest forum of educated elites into the crucible of mass nationalism. The early moderates laid the institutional foundation and articulated the economic grievances (e.g., the Drain Theory). The extremists injected vigor, mass mobilisation, and the powerful Swadeshi‑Boycott strategy that resonated across the subcontinent. Their combined legacy set the stage for the revolutionary leadership of Mahatma Gandhi, who would later synthesize constitutional methods with mass civil disobedience, ultimately steering India towards independence in 1947.

Understanding this duality is essential for any aspirant of the NDA, CDS, or AFCAT examinations, as it reflects the broader theme of “unity in diversity” and the evolution of political thought in modern India.

Constitutional Development in British India: Acts of 1909, 1919, 1935

This section covers three pivotal legislative acts passed by the British Parliament, which significantly shaped the constitutional and political landscape of British India. These acts represent a gradual, albeit often reluctant, devolution of power and an increasing, yet limited, inclusion of Indians in the administration. Understanding their provisions, context, and impact is crucial for competitive exams like NDA, CDS, and AFCAT.

1. The Indian Councils Act of 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms)

Often referred to as the Morley-Minto Reforms, this Act was a response to the growing nationalist movement and the demand for greater Indian representation, particularly after the Swadeshi Movement and the partition of Bengal.

Context and Background:

  • Rise of Nationalism: The early 20th century witnessed a surge in Indian nationalism, fueled by events like the partition of Bengal in 1905, the Swadeshi Movement, and the rise of extremist factions within the Indian National Congress.
  • Demand for Reforms: Both moderate and extremist factions of the Congress were demanding greater Indian participation in legislative and administrative bodies.
  • Simla Deputation (1906): A delegation of Muslim leaders, led by Aga Khan III, met Viceroy Lord Minto at Simla. They demanded separate electorates for Muslims, arguing that their political importance was not reflected in their numerical strength. This demand was conceded by the British.
  • Key Personalities:
    • Lord Morley: The then Secretary of State for India.
    • Lord Minto: The then Viceroy of India.
  • British Strategy: The reforms were largely an attempt to 'rally the moderates' and to create a split between Hindus and Muslims by introducing communal electorates, thereby weakening the nationalist movement.

Key Provisions of the Act:

  1. Enlargement of Legislative Councils:
    • The size of the Central Legislative Council was significantly increased from 16 to 60 members.
    • The size of Provincial Legislative Councils was also increased. For instance, in Bengal, Madras, and Bombay, the number of members was raised from 20 to 50. In the United Provinces, it went from 15 to 50, and in Punjab, Burma, and Assam, from 10 to 30.
    • The majority of members in the Provincial Legislative Councils were now to be non-official, though the official majority was retained in the Central Legislative Council.
  2. Indian Representation in Executive Councils:
    • For the first time, Indians were associated with the Executive Councils of the Viceroy and Governors.
    • Satyendra Prasanna Sinha became the first Indian to be appointed to the Viceroy's Executive Council as the Law Member in 1909.
    • Two Indians were also appointed to the Council of the Secretary of State for India in London.
  3. Introduction of Separate Electorates:
    • This was the most controversial and significant provision. The Act introduced separate electorates for Muslims. This meant that Muslim members could only be elected by Muslim voters.

Interior of the Earth – Layers, Discontinuities & Seismic Waves

1. Why Study the Earth’s Interior?

The interior of the Earth is the foundation for almost every physical‑geographic phenomenon that appears at the surface – from the creation of mountains and volcanoes to the generation of earthquakes and the behaviour of the magnetic field. For NDA, CDS and AFCAT examinations, a clear, memorised picture of the Earth’s internal structure, the key discontinuities and the nature of seismic waves is essential. The following notes provide an exhaustive, exam‑oriented treatment of the subject.

2. Overall Structure of the Earth

The Earth can be visualised as a set of concentric shells, each characterised by distinct physical, chemical and mechanical properties. The three major divisions are:

  1. Crust – the outermost thin shell.
  2. Mantle – the thick, mostly solid but ductile region.
  3. Core – the innermost metallic sphere, divided into a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.

2.1. Mnemonic to Remember the Order

“Curious Monkeys Climb” – Crust, Mantle, Core.

2.2. Comparative Table of the Three Main Layers

Layer Average Thickness Composition Density (kg m⁻³) State of Matter Key Features
Crust 5–70 km Silicic (continental) / Basaltic (oceanic) 2.7–3.0 (continental) ; 3.0–3.3 (oceanic) Rigid (brittle) Hosts all life, contains sedimentary basins, continental shelves.
Mantle ≈2,900 km Silicate minerals (olivine, pyroxene, garnet) 3.3–5.6 Solid but ductile (plastic flow) Divided into Upper & Lower Mantle; convection currents drive plate tectonics.
Core ≈3,500 km Iron‑Nickel alloy with light elements (S, O) 9.9–13.0 Outer: liquid; Inner: solid Generates geomagnetic field; inner core grows by solidification.

3. Detailed Sub‑Division of Layers

3.1. Crust

  • Continental Crust – average thickness ≈35 km, granitic composition, older (up to 4 Ga).
  • Oceanic Crust – thickness ≈7 km, basaltic composition, younger (≤200 Ma).
  • Key discontinuity: Mohorovičić Discontinuity (Moho) – marks the transition from crust to mantle; seismic P‑wave velocity jumps from ~6.5 km s⁻¹ to ~8.0 km s⁻¹.

3.2. Mantle

The mantle is further divided based on seismic velocity changes and mineralogical transitions:

SubdivisionDepth RangeKey DiscontinuityDominant Minerals
Upper Mantle0–410 kmNone (gradual)Olivine (α‑olivine)
Transition Zone410–660 km410 km & 660 km discontinuities (olivine → wadsleyite → ringwoodite → perovskite)High‑pressure polymorphs of olivine
Lower Mantle660–2,891 kmNone (seismic velocities increase smoothly)Bridgmanite (MgSiO₃ perovskite) & ferropericlase

3.3. Core

  • Outer Core – liquid iron‑nickel; depth 2,891–5,150 km; P‑wave velocity ~8.1 km s⁻¹, S‑waves do not travel (S‑wave shadow zone).
  • Inner Core – solid iron‑nickel; radius ≈1,220 km; P‑wave velocity ~11 km s⁻¹, S‑wave velocity ~3.5 km s⁻¹ (slow due to anisotropy).
  • Key discontinuity: Gutenberg Discontinuity – marks the mantle‑core boundary at ~2,891 km depth.
  • Key discontinuity: Lehmann Discontinuity – separates the liquid outer core from the solid inner core at ~5,150 km depth.

4. Seismic Waves – The Primary Tool for Probing the Interior

4.1. Classification of Seismic Waves

Seismic waves are broadly divided into body waves (travel through the interior) and surface waves (travel along the Earth’s surface). Understanding their behaviour at discontinuities is crucial for answering exam questions on “shadow zones”, “wave refraction” and “seismic tomography”.

4.1.1. Body Waves

  1. P‑waves (Primary or Compressional Waves)
    • Type: Longitudinal – particles move parallel to propagation direction.
    • Velocity: Fastest seismic wave; typical speed in crust ~6 km s⁻¹, in mantle ~13 km s⁻¹, in outer core ~8 km s⁻¹.
    • Can travel through solids, liquids and gases.
    • Behaviour at boundaries: Refraction according to Snell’s Law; speed increase at Moho leads to a critical angle and the creation of a P‑wave shadow zone between 103°–142° from the epicentre.
  2. S‑waves (Secondary or Shear Waves)
    • Type: Transverse – particle motion perpendicular to propagation direction.
    • Velocity: Slower than P‑waves; ~3.5 km s⁻¹ in crust, ~7 km s⁻¹ in mantle.
    • Can travel only through solids – they are absorbed by the liquid outer core, creating an S‑wave shadow zone for angles > 104°.
    • Key exam tip: Presence of an S‑wave shadow zone is direct evidence for a liquid outer core.

4.1.2. Surface Waves

  • Rayleigh Waves – elliptical particle motion (retrograde). Travel slower than body waves but cause most earthquake damage.
  • Love Waves – horizontal shear motion; confined to the crust‑mantle “waveguide”.
  • Both surface waves decay with depth (amplitude ∝ 1/√r) and dominate seismograms at periods > 20 s.

4.2. Seismic Wave Velocity Formulae (Useful for Calculations)

For an isotropic elastic medium:

  • P‑wave velocity (VP) = √[(K + 4µ/3)/ρ] where K = bulk modulus, µ = shear modulus, ρ = density.
  • S‑wave velocity (VS) = √(µ/ρ).
  • From these, the Poisson’s ratio (σ) can be derived: σ = (VP² – 2VS²) / [2(VP² – VS²)].

Exam tip:* Remember the relationship VP > VS > 0; if VS = 0, the medium must be liquid.

4.3. Refraction and Critical Angles – Quick Mnemonic

“Refraction At Discontinuities Explains Seismic Hidden Zones” – R‑A‑D‑E‑S‑H‑Z (R‑A‑D‑E‑S‑H‑Z = “Radeshz”). This helps recall that the P‑wave and S‑wave shadow zones are caused by refraction at the Moho, Gutenberg and Lehmann discontinuities.

5. Discontinuities – The “Road‑Signs” Inside the Earth

Each discontinuity marks a sudden change in seismic velocity, density or mineralogy. They are identified by analysing travel‑time curves (T‑Δ plots) from global seismograph networks.

DiscontinuityDepth (km)Primary ChangeSignificance
Moho (Mohorovičić)5–70Sharp increase in VP (≈ 6.5 → 8 km s⁻¹)Crust‑mantle boundary; defines lithospheric thickness.
410 km Discontinuity410Onset of wadsleyite (high‑pressure olivine)Marks top of transition zone; important for mantle convection studies.
660 km Discontinuity660Transformation to bridgmanite + ferropericlaseBottom of transition zone; separates upper and lower mantle.
Gutenberg Discontinuity≈2,891VS drops to zero (liquid outer core)Mantle‑core boundary; defines start of liquid outer core.
Lehmann Discontinuity≈5,150VS re‑appears (solid inner core)Outer‑core to inner‑core transition.

5.1. How Discontinuities Are Detected

  1. Travel‑time curves – Plot of arrival time vs. epicentral distance; kinks indicate velocity changes.
  2. Receiver functions – Deconvolution of P‑wave to isolate converted S‑waves (e.g., P‑to‑S conversions at Moho).
  3. Seismic tomography – 3‑D imaging of velocity anomalies; highlights lateral variations across discontinuities.

6. Earthquake Parameters – From Focus to Magnitude

  • Focus (Hypocentre) – Point inside Earth where rupture initiates.
  • Epicentre – Surface projection of the focus; located using at least three seismograph stations (triangulation).
  • Magnitude Scales
    • Richter (ML) – Logarithmic amplitude of the largest recorded wave; valid for M ≤ 7.
    • Moment Magnitude (Mw) – Based on seismic moment (M₀ = µAD); preferred for all sizes.
  • Intensity (MMI) – Observed effects on people, structures; varies with distance.

6.1. Quick Mnemonic for Magnitude Types

“Richter Measures Amplitude, Moment Weighs Energy” – R‑M‑A‑M‑W‑E.

7. Methods of Investigating the Interior – Beyond Seismology

MagnetotelluricsUses natural EM variations to infer electrical conductivity.Highlights fluid‑rich zones, partial melt.
Geodesy (GPS, VLBI)Monitors surface deformation.Provides indirect evidence of mantle flow and core‑mantle coupling.
Laboratory ExperimentsHigh‑pressure, high‑temperature synthesis of mantle minerals.Validates seismic velocity models.

8. Exam‑Focused “Fast‑Recall” Points

  1. Depth of Moho under oceans ≈ 5–10 km; under continents ≈ 30–70 km.
  2. Core‑mantle boundary (Gutenberg) at 2,891 km.
  3. Liquid outer core depth range 2,891–5,150 km.
  4. Solid inner core radius ≈ 1,220 km.
  5. P‑wave shadow zone between 103°–142° from epicentre.
  6. S‑wave shadow zone > 104°.
  7. Transition zone spans 410–660 km; important for water storage.
  8. Seismic velocities (average) – Crust: VP ≈ 6 km s⁻¹; Mantle: VP ≈ 13 km s⁻¹; Outer core: VP ≈ 8 km s⁻¹; Inner core: VP ≈ 11 km s⁻¹.
  9. Key formulas – VP, VS, Poisson’s ratio (see Section 4.2).
  10. Mnemonic for layers – “C‑M‑C” (Crust, Mantle, Core).

9. Interdisciplinary Connections – Incorporating Extracted Points

While the primary focus of this chapter is the Earth’s interior, the following extracted points illustrate the interdisciplinary nature of geography, linking physical processes with biological and atmospheric phenomena.

1. Growth Independent Movements (Nastic Movements)

Movements in plants that are not growth related.

  • Thigmonastic Movement: Movement occurring in response to touch.
  • Example: Touch-me-not plant (belongs to the Mimosa family).

2. Growth-Related Movements (Tropic Movements / Tropism)

Plant responses and movements that are directly growth related.

  • Phototropism: Response in relation to light.
    • (+ve) Phototropism: Growth towards light (e.g., stem / shoot).

Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ)

  • Definition: A jet stream of air located above 10-12 km altitude.
  • Key Characteristics:
    • Responsible for the highest rainfall in India.
    • Helps in the South-West (S-W) monsoon.
    • In June, the easterly jet stream flows over the southern part of the peninsula.
  • Geographical Context: The diagram shows the jet stream flowing over the Indian peninsula, with a High Pressure (H.P) zone over Madagascar (noted as a cold area compared to Tibet)

ITCZ (Inter Tropical Convergence Zone)

  • It is a low pressure zone.
  • Location: Where trade winds converge.
  • Position in July: 20°N - 25°N.
  • Winter Movement: ITCZ moves southward.

Monsoon Connection:

  • N‑SW wind leads to Northeast monsoon.

Tropical Evergreen (Wet)

  • Maximum tree diversity
  • Rainfall - 250 cm +
  • Temp. - 25° - 27°C
  • Well stratified
  • Trees heights - 60m or above
  • Do not shed leaves
  • Distribution:
    • 1. Western side of W.G
    • 2. A&N
    • 3. Puranchal Hills
  • Species:
    • i. Rosewood
    • ii. Mahogany
    • iii. Aini
    • iv. Ebony

10. Summary – What to Remember for the Exam

  1. Memorise the depths of the major discontinuities (Moho, 410 km, 660 km, Gutenberg, Lehmann) – they are frequent one‑line questions.
  2. Know the velocity contrasts (P‑wave jumps, S‑wave disappearance) and be able to explain the resulting shadow zones.
  3. Be able to sketch a simple cross‑section showing the crust, mantle (upper, transition, lower), outer core and inner core, labelling each discontinuity.
  4. Recall the formulae for VP and VS and the relationship to density and elastic moduli – useful for numerical problems.
  5. Understand the physical meaning of the terms “elastic”, “plastic”, “ductile” and “brittle” as they apply to each layer.
  6. Use the mnemonics provided (“C‑M‑C”, “R‑M‑A‑M‑W‑E”, “Radeshz”) to retrieve facts quickly under time pressure.
  7. Link the interior structure to surface phenomena – e.g., mantle convection drives plate tectonics, which in turn influences the distribution of Tropical Evergreen (Wet) forests and monsoon dynamics (ITCZ, TEJ).
  8. Finally, practice drawing the travel‑time curve (T‑Δ plot) and identifying the kinks that correspond to each discontinuity – a common diagram‑based question.

Exam Tip: When a question asks for “the reason why S‑waves do not travel through the outer core”, answer in two parts – (i) state that the outer core is liquid, (ii) explain that shear stress cannot be transmitted in fluids, leading to an S‑wave shadow zone.

With this exhaustive set of notes, you now have a self‑contained, high‑density revision resource covering every fact, formula, and mnemonic required for NDA, CDS and AFCAT geography sections on the Earth’s interior.
