Semiconductors & Basic Electronics – Diodes, Transistors, Logic Gates

1. Quick Overview

Electronics for NDA/CDS/AFCAT revolves around the ability to identify, analyse and apply the behaviour of semiconductor devices. The three pillars are:

  1. Semiconductor fundamentals – intrinsic & extrinsic materials, energy bands, carrier concentration.
  2. Two‑terminal devices – diodes (PN, Zener, LED, Schottky, Photodiode, Varactor).
  3. Three‑terminal devices – transistors (BJTs, FETs, MOSFETs) and their use in logic gates (AND, OR, NAND, NOR, XOR, XNOR, universal gates).

Exam tip: Memorise the characteristic voltage values (VBE ≈ 0.7 V for silicon, VF ≈ 2 V for red LED) – they appear in MCQs and numerical problems.

2. Semiconductor Fundamentals

2.1 Energy Band Theory

  • Valence band (VB) – fully occupied at 0 K.
  • Conduction band (CB) – empty at 0 K; electrons here are free to conduct.
  • Band gap (Eg) – energy difference between VB and CB. For silicon, Eg = 1.12 eV; for germanium, Eg = 0.66 eV.
  • Temperature dependence: Eg(T) ≈ Eg(0) – αT²/(T+β) (Varshni’s equation).

2.2 Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Semiconductors

Feature Intrinsic Semiconductor Extrinsic Semiconductor
Purity Pure crystal (Si, Ge) Intentionally doped with impurities
Major carriers Equal electrons & holes (n = p) Either electrons (n‑type) or holes (p‑type) dominate
Conductivity (σ) σ = q (nμn + pμp) – very low at room temp. σ ↑ dramatically with doping concentration (ND or NA)
Typical dopants – n‑type: Phosphorus (P), Arsenic (As); p‑type: Boron (B), Aluminium (Al)

2.3 Doping & Carrier Concentration

When a pentavalent atom (group V) replaces a Si atom, it contributes an extra electron → donor level just below CB. Conversely, a trivalent atom (group III) creates an acceptor level just above VB.

Mnemonic: “Five gives a free electron, three takes one away”.

Carrier concentration formulas (non‑degenerate case):

  • n ≈ NC exp[−(EC−EF)/kT]
  • p ≈ NV exp[−(EF−EV)/kT]

Where NC and NV are effective density of states in CB and VB respectively.

3. Diodes – The One‑Way Valve

3.1 PN Junction Formation

A p‑type region placed next to an n‑type region creates a depletion zone where mobile carriers recombine, leaving behind fixed ionised donors (positive) and acceptors (negative). This region establishes an internal electric field (built‑in potential Vbi).

Key formula: Vbi = (kT/q) ln(NAND/ni²). At 300 K, (kT/q) ≈ 26 mV.

3.2 Ideal Diode Equation

For forward bias (V > 0):

I = IS (e^{qV/kT} – 1)
  • IS – saturation current (≈ 10⁻¹² A for silicon diodes).
  • At V ≈ 0.7 V, e^{qV/kT} ≈ 10⁶ → I ≈ IS·10⁶ ≈ 1 mA (practical turn‑on point).

Exam tip: For quick calculations, use the “0.7 V rule” for silicon and “0.3 V rule for germanium.

3.3 Types of Diodes & Their Characteristics

Diode Type Key Feature Typical Forward Voltage (VF) Special Application
Silicon PN Diode Standard rectifier 0.6–0.7 V Power supplies, clipping circuits
Germanium Diode Low forward drop 0.2–0.3 V High‑frequency detectors, RF mixers
Zener Diode Breakdown in reverse bias (Zener or avalanche) Varies 2–200 V (depends on ZR) Voltage regulation, reference
LED (Light Emitting Diode) Electroluminescence; colour depends on band‑gap Red: 1.8–2.2 V; Blue/White: 3.0–3.6 V Indicators, displays, optical communication
Schottky Diode Metal‑semiconductor junction → low VF, fast recovery 0.2–0.4 V High‑speed switching, RF mixers
Photodiode Generates current when illuminated (photoconductive mode) Zero bias (photovoltaic) or reverse bias (photoconductive) Light meters, optical communication receivers
Varactor (Varicap) Diode Capacitance varies with reverse bias voltage Capacitance range: few pF to 100 pF Voltage‑controlled oscillators, tunable filters

3.4 Reverse‑Bias Characteristics & Breakdown

  • Leakage current (IR) – typically 10⁻⁹ A for silicon, higher for germanium.
  • Zener breakdown (VZR < 5 V) – quantum tunnelling.
  • Avalanche breakdown (VAR > 5 V) – carrier multiplication.

Mnemonic for breakdown type: “Zener = Z‑low, Avalanche = A‑high”.

3.5 Diode Applications in Defence Exams

  • Rectifier circuits – half‑wave, full‑wave, bridge.
  • Clipping & clamping – protect sensitive instrumentation.
  • Voltage regulation – Zener diode as reference for sensor circuits.
  • Optoelectronic devices – LEDs in signalling, photodiodes in laser range‑finders.

4. Transistors – The Amplifier & Switch

4.1 Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT)

Three‑layer device: Emitter (E), Base (B), Collector (C). Two polarities:

  • NPN – E and C are n‑type, B is p‑type.
  • PNP – E and C are p‑type, B is n‑type.

Mnemonic: “NPN = N‑Positive‑N (current flows from emitter to collector)”.

4.1.1 BJT Configurations

Configuration Input/Output Current Gain Common‑Term Typical Use
Common‑Emitter (CE) VBE (input), VCE (output) β (≈ 50–200) Common Emitter Voltage amplification, switching
Common‑Base (CB) VEB (input), VCB (output) α ≈ 0.98–0.998 Common Base High‑frequency amplifiers
Common‑Collector (CC) – Emitter Follower VBE (input), VCE (output) ≈ β (unity voltage gain) Common Collector Impedance matching, buffer

4.1.2 BJT Characteristic Equations

  • Active region (forward‑biased BE, reverse‑biased BC): IC = β IB = IS (e^{VBE/VT} – 1).
  • Saturation (both junctions forward): VCE(sat) ≈ 0.2 V (silicon).
  • Cut‑off: IC ≈ 0 (BE reverse‑biased).

Exam tip: In numerical problems, assume VBE = 0.7 V and VCE(sat) = 0.2 V unless otherwise specified.

4.2.1 JFET (Junction FET)

Physical Chemistry – Matter: States, Properties, Changes & Classification

1. Overview

Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass. In physical chemistry we study its classification, the states of aggregation, the properties that define each state, and the changes it can undergo. Mastery of these concepts is essential for NDA, CDS, AFCAT and other competitive exams because they form the basis of many MCQs, numerical problems and conceptual questions.

2. Classification of Matter

2.1 Pure Substances vs. Mixtures

Category Definition Examples Key Features for Exams
Pure Substance Has a fixed chemical composition throughout the sample. Distilled water (H₂O), Oxygen (O₂), Sodium chloride (NaCl) Single set of physical & chemical properties; obeys ideal gas law when gaseous.
Mixture Combination of two or more substances that retain their individual identities. Air (N₂ + O₂ + Ar + CO₂), Soil, Brass (Cu + Zn) Properties are *averaged*; may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.

2.2 Elements vs. Compounds (Pure Substances)

  • Elements: Consist of only one type of atom. Symbolized by a single capital letter (or two letters, second lowercase). Example: Fe, O.
  • Compounds: Two or more different elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio. Example: H₂O, CO₂.

2.3 Homogeneous vs. Heterogeneous Mixtures

Type Definition Examples Exam Tip
Homogeneous (Solutions) Uniform composition throughout; particles < 0.1 µm. Sugar solution, Air, Brass Use mole fraction or molarity for calculations.
Heterogeneous Composition varies from point to point; visible phases. Oil‑water mixture, Soil, Concrete Identify phases before applying any formula.

3. States of Matter

Classical textbooks list four states, but modern physical chemistry recognises several more, each with distinct properties.

3.1 Classical States

  1. Solid
  2. Liquid
  3. Gas
  4. Plasma – ionised gas, conducts electricity.

3.2 Modern/Exotic States

  • Bose‑Einstein Condensate (BEC) – observed at < 0.2 K for alkali atoms.
  • Supercritical Fluid – above critical temperature (374 °C for H₂O) and pressure.
  • Liquid Crystals – exhibit properties between liquids and solids; used in LCDs.
  • Amorphous Solids – glass, polymers; lack long‑range order.

3.3 Comparative Table of Classical States

Property Solid Liquid Gas Plasma
Shape Definite Indefinite (takes container’s shape) Indefinite Indefinite
Volume Definite Definite Indefinite Indefinite
Particle Arrangement Close‑packed lattice (ordered) Short‑range order, random Widely spaced, random Highly energetic ions & electrons
Intermolecular Forces (IMFs) Strong (ionic, covalent, metallic, network) Moderate (hydrogen bonding, dipole‑dipole, London) Weak (mainly London dispersion) Electrostatic forces dominate
Compressibility Very low Low High Very high (but limited by ionisation)
Typical Energy (kJ mol⁻¹) ≈ 300–800 (lattice) ≈ 40–80 (cohesive) ≈ 0–5 (kinetic) ≥ 1000 (ionisation)

3.4 Mnemonic for Order of Strength of IMFs

“I H D L” – Ionic > Hydrogen bonding > Dipole‑dipole > London dispersion.

4. Phase Changes (Changes of State)

4.1 Types of Phase Transitions

  • Melting (Fusion) – Solid → Liquid
  • Freezing (Solidification) – Liquid → Solid
  • Vaporisation – Liquid → Gas (includes boiling and evaporation)
  • Condensation – Gas → Liquid
  • Sublimation – Solid → Gas (direct)
  • Deposition (Desublimation) – Gas → Solid (direct)
  • Ionisation – Gas → Plasma (energy input)
  • Recombination – Plasma → Gas (energy release)

4.2 Energy Involved – Latent Heats

Transition Symbol Typical Value (kJ kg⁻¹) Equation
Fusion (Melting) ΔH_fus ≈ 334 (water) q = m·ΔH_fus
Vaporisation ΔH_vap ≈ 2260 (water) q = m·ΔH_vap
Sublimation ΔH_sub ≈ 2834 (dry ice) q = m·ΔH_sub
Ionisation (to plasma) ΔH_ion ≈ 1312 kJ mol⁻¹ (Cl₂) q = n·ΔH_ion

4.3 Clausius–Clapeyron Equation (For Vaporisation & Sublimation)

For a phase change between two phases (1 ↔ 2):

ln(P₂/P₁) = – (ΔH_trans / R)·(1/T₂ – 1/T₁)

Where ΔH_trans is the latent heat of the transition, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. This relation is frequently asked in numerical problems involving vapour pressure at two temperatures.

4.4 Critical Point & Triple Point

  • Triple Point – Unique T‑P condition where solid, liquid and gas coexist in equilibrium.
    • For water: 0.01 °C and 0.006 atm.
  • Critical Point – Beyond this, liquid and gas become indistinguishable (supercritical fluid).
    • For water: 374 °C and 22.1 atm.

4.5 Exam Tip – Quick Identification of Phase Change Type

Use the mnemonic “MFSVSDI” (Melting, Freezing, Sublimation, Vaporisation, Solidification, Deposition, Ionisation). The first letter tells you whether the transition is endothermic (M, S, V, I) or exothermic (F, D).

5. Quantitative Aspects of Gaseous States

5.1 Ideal Gas Law

PV = nRT

  • P – pressure (Pa or atm)
  • V – volume (m³ or L)
  • n – moles
  • R – universal gas constant (0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ or 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
  • T – absolute temperature (K)

5.2 Real Gases – Van der Waals Equation

(P + a n²/V²)(V – nb) = nRT

  • a – measures attraction between molecules (units: Pa·m⁶ mol⁻²).
  • b – excluded volume per mole (units: m³ mol⁻¹).
  • For CO₂: a = 0.364 Pa·m⁶ mol⁻², b = 4.27 × 10⁻⁵ m³ mol⁻¹.

5.3 Compressibility Factor (Z)

Z = PV / nRT

Interpretation:

  • Z = 1 → Ideal behaviour.
  • Z < 1 → Attractive forces dominate (common at low T, moderate P).
  • Z > 1 → Repulsive forces dominate (high P).

5.4 Molar Volume at STP

At 0 °C and 1 atm, one mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.414 L. This value is used frequently in stoichiometric gas calculations.

ai-gen-chemistry-states-of-matter-kineti:
Physical Chemistry – States of Matter

1. Introduction

The behaviour of gases, liquids and solids is explained by the Kinetic Molecular Theory (KMT). For defence‑service examinations (NDA, CDS, AFCAT) a thorough command of the theory, the classical gas laws and the van der Waals equation is essential because they form the basis of many multiple‑choice and numerical problems.

2. Kinetic Molecular Theory (KMT)

2.1 Postulates of KMT

  1. All matter consists of a huge number of tiny particles (atoms or molecules) in constant motion.
  2. These particles are point masses; the volume of the particles themselves is negligible compared with the volume of the container (ideal gas assumption).
  3. Particles move in straight lines until they collide with each other or with the walls of the container.
  4. Collisions are perfectly elastic; no kinetic energy is lost.
  5. The average kinetic energy of the particles is directly proportional to the absolute temperature:
    Ek = (3/2) kBT
  6. There are no attractive or repulsive forces between particles (again, ideal‑gas assumption).

2.2 Types of Molecular Motion

  • Translational motion – movement of the centre of mass in three mutually perpendicular directions.
  • Rotational motion – rotation about axes; diatomic and polyatomic gases have rotational degrees of freedom.
  • Vibrational motion – periodic motion of atoms within a molecule; becomes significant at high temperatures.

2.3 Speed Distribution – Maxwell‑Boltzmann

The probability that a molecule has speed between v and v + dv is given by:

f(v) = 4π ( m / 2πkBT )3/2 v2 e‑mv²/2kBT

Key characteristic speeds:

SpeedExpressionPhysical Meaning
Most‑probable speed (vmp) √(2RT/M) Speed at which the distribution curve peaks.
Mean speed (v̄) √(8RT/πM) Arithmetic average of all molecular speeds.
Root‑mean‑square speed (vrms) √(3RT/M) Square root of the average of the squares of speeds; directly related to kinetic energy.

2.4 Derivation of PV = nRT from KMT

Consider N molecules of mass m in a cubic container of side L. The pressure exerted on one wall is:

P = (1/3) (N m vrms²) / V

Substituting vrms² = 3kBT/m gives:

PV = NkBT = nRT

where n = N/ NA (moles) and R = NAkB = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

3. Classical Gas Laws

3.1 Boyle’s Law (Pressure–Volume)

Postulate: At constant temperature and amount of gas, pressure is inversely proportional to volume.

P₁V₁ = P₂V₂

Mnemonic: “Boyle – Big Volume → Low pressure”.

3.2 Charles’s Law (Temperature–Volume)

At constant pressure, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂

Historical note: Discovered by 1797 (Jacques Charles).

3.3 Gay‑Lussac’s Law (Pressure–Temperature)

At constant volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂

3.4 Avogadro’s Law (Volume–Moles)

Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

V₁/n₁ = V₂/n₂

Mnemonic: “Avogadro – All Volumes equal when moles equal”.

3.5 Combined Gas Law

Combines Boyle, Charles and Gay‑Lussac:

(P₁V₁)/T₁ = (P₂V₂)/T₂

3.6 Ideal Gas Equation

Incorporates Avogadro’s law:

PV = nRT

Key constants:

  • R = 0.08206 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (useful for pressure in atm and volume in L).
  • R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (SI units).

3.7 Molar Volume at STP

At 273 K and 1 atm, one mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.414 L. This value is frequently used in quick calculations for NDA/CSIR exams.

3.8 Density of a Gas

From PV = nRT, substituting n = m/M (mass/ molar mass):

ρ = PM / RT

Useful for determining molecular weight from experimental data.

3.9 Dalton’s Law of Partial Pressures

In a mixture of non‑reacting gases, the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures:

Ptotal = Σ Pi

3.10 Graham’s Law of Effusion

Rate of effusion ∝ 1/√M (M = molar mass).

Rate₁/Rate₂ = √(M₂/M₁)

3.11 Henry’s Law (Solubility of Gases)

At a constant temperature, the amount of gas dissolved in a liquid is directly proportional to its partial pressure above the liquid.

C = kHP

4. Real Gases – Deviations from Ideal Behaviour

4.1 Why Real Gases Deviate

  • Finite molecular volume – at high pressures molecules occupy a significant fraction of the container.
  • Inter‑molecular forces – attractive forces lower the pressure; repulsive forces become dominant at very short distances.

4.2 Compressibility Factor (Z)

Defined as:

Z = PV / nRT

For an ideal gas, Z = 1. Real gases show Z ≠ 1; the deviation is plotted in Z‑charts (exam‑friendly).

5. van der Waals Equation

5.1 Historical Background

Johannes Diderik van der Waals introduced his equation in 1873 to incorporate molecular size and attraction. He received the Nobel Prize in 1910.

5.2 Equation Form

(P + a n²/V²)(V – nb) = nRT

where:

  • a – measures the magnitude of attractive forces (units: L² atm mol⁻²).
  • b – effective volume occupied by one mole of particles (units: L mol⁻¹).

5.3 Physical Meaning of a and b

ConstantOriginEffect on P‑V Curve
a Attractive forces between molecules (London dispersion, dipole‑dipole). Reduces pressure; curve lies below ideal‑gas line at moderate pressures.
b Finite volume of molecules; excluded volume. Increases pressure; curve rises sharply at high pressures.

5.4 Critical Constants from van der Waals

At the critical point (where liquid and vapour become indistinguishable), the following relations hold:

Vc = 3nb  Pc = a / (27 b²)  Tc = 8a / (27 Rb)

These formulas are frequently asked in objective questions; remember the “27” and “8” factors.

5.5 Reduced Variables and Corresponding States Principle

Define reduced quantities:

  • pr = P / Pc
  • vr = V / Vc
  • tr = T / Tc

For gases with similar reduced variables, the compressibility factor Z is nearly the same – a powerful shortcut for quick estimation.

5.6 Solving van der Waals Problems – Stepwise Method (Exam Tip)

  1. Identify the given data (P, V, T, n). Convert all units to SI or consistent units (L, atm, K, mol).
  2. Write the van der Waals equation in the form (P + a n²/V²)(V – nb) = nRT.
  3. If solving for V, rearrange to a cubic in V and use either:
    • Iterative substitution (quick for multiple‑choice).
    • Graphical method – plot left‑hand side vs V and locate intersection.
  4. For critical‑constant questions, memorize the three formulas above; plug in the given a and b values.
  5. Check the sign of the correction terms: +a n²/V² (adds pressure) and ‑nb (reduces volume).

6. Comparative Summary – Ideal vs Real Gases

AspectIdeal GasReal Gas (van der Waals)
Assumption about particle volume Negligible Finite; accounted by b
Inter‑molecular forces None Attractive forces accounted by a
Equation of state PV = nRT (P + a n²/V²)(V – nb) = nRT

Thermochemistry – Enthalpy, Hess’s Law & Bond Energies

1. Enthalpy (ΔH) – The Heat Content of a System

Enthalpy is a state function that represents the total heat content of a system at constant pressure. It is defined as:

H = U + pV

where U is internal energy, p pressure and V volume.

The change in enthalpy for a process carried out at constant pressure is:

ΔH = H_products – H_reactants = q_p

ΔH is expressed in kJ mol⁻¹. Positive ΔH indicates an endothermic reaction (heat absorbed), while negative ΔH indicates an exothermic reaction (heat released).

1.1 Standard Enthalpy Changes (ΔH°)

  • All reactants and products are in their standard states (1 atm or 1 bar, pure substance, most stable allotrope).
  • Temperature is usually 298 K (25 °C).
  • Notation: ΔH°_reaction, ΔH°_f (formation), ΔH°_c (combustion), ΔH°_s (sublimation), ΔH°_vap (vaporisation), ΔH°_sol (solution), ΔH°_neut (neutralisation).

1.2 Common Standard Enthalpy Values (Quick Reference)

Process Symbol ΔH° (kJ mol⁻¹)
Formation of H₂O(l) from elements ΔH°_f (H₂O,l) -285.8
Formation of CO₂(g) from elements ΔH°_f (CO₂,g) -393.5
Combustion of CH₄(g) ΔH°_c (CH₄) -890.4
Vaporisation of water ΔH°_vap (H₂O,l) 44.0
Sublimation of I₂(s) ΔH°_sub (I₂) 62.4
Neutralisation (strong acid + strong base) ΔH°_neut -57.1

1.3 Sign Conventions – Quick Mnemonic

“E” for Exothermic = Energy out (negative ΔH); “E” for Endothermic = Energy in (positive ΔH).”

Remember: ΔH = –q (released) for exothermic processes.

1.4 Exam Tip

  • Always check the pressure condition. If the question mentions “at constant volume”, use ΔU and relate it to ΔH via ΔH = ΔU + Δ(pV).
  • Convert all enthalpy values to the same units before using them in calculations (usually kJ).

2. Calorimetry – Measuring Heat Changes

Calorimetry is the experimental technique to determine q (heat) transferred during a reaction or physical change.

2.1 Fundamental Equation

q = m·c·ΔT

  • m – mass of the sample (g)
  • c – specific heat capacity (J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)
  • ΔT – temperature change (final – initial) in K (or °C, same magnitude)

2.2 Heat Capacity of Calorimeter (C_cal)

When the calorimeter itself absorbs heat, its heat capacity must be added:

q_total = (m·c + C_cal)·ΔT

2.3 Example Problem (Typical NDA Question)

Problem: 2.00 g of H₂ gas is burnt in excess O₂ at 298 K inside a coffee‑cup calorimeter. The temperature rises from 25 °C to 30 °C. The calorimeter’s heat capacity is 2.5 kJ K⁻¹. Calculate ΔH° for the combustion of H₂ (per mole).

  1. Convert mass of H₂ to moles: n = 2.00 g / 2.016 g mol⁻¹ = 0.992 mol.
  2. ΔT = 30 °C – 25 °C = 5 K.
  3. Heat absorbed by calorimeter: q_cal = C_cal·ΔT = 2.5 kJ K⁻¹ × 5 K = 12.5 kJ.
  4. Assuming negligible heat capacity of gases, q_rxn = –q_cal = –12.5 kJ (exothermic).
  5. ΔH° per mole = q_rxn / n = –12.5 kJ / 0.992 mol ≈ –12.6 kJ mol⁻¹.

Exam Tip: Always watch the sign of q. In a calorimeter, the system (reaction) loses heat, so q_rxn = –q_cal.

3. Hess’s Law – Enthalpy is a State Function

Hess’s Law states that the total enthalpy change for a reaction is independent of the pathway taken; it depends only on the initial and final states.

3.1 Formal Statement

ΔH°_overall = ΣΔH°_steps (products) – ΣΔH°_steps (reactants)

3.2 Common Uses

  • Calculate ΔH° for reactions where direct measurement is difficult.
  • Derive enthalpies of formation, combustion, or sublimation from known data.
  • Construct thermochemical cycles (e.g., Born‑Haber cycle).

3.3 Mnemonic for Remembering Hess’s Law

“HESS – Heat is a State Function, So the Sum is Same!”

3.4 Worked Example – Enthalpy of Formation of CO(g)

Given:

  • ΔH°_f (CO₂,g) = -393.5 kJ mol⁻¹
  • ΔH°_f (C(s, graphite)) = 0 kJ mol⁻¹ (reference)
  • ΔH°_f (CO(g)) = ?
  • ΔH°_sub (C(s) → C(g)) = 716.7 kJ mol⁻¹
  • ΔH°_f (O₂(g)) = 0 kJ mol⁻¹

Reaction to be formed:

C(s) + ½ O₂(g) → CO(g)

Construct a Hess cycle:

  1. C(s) → C(g)  ΔH = +716.7 kJ (sublimation)
  2. C(g) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g)  ΔH = –393.5 kJ (formation of CO₂)
  3. CO₂(g) → CO(g) + ½ O₂(g)  ΔH = ? (reverse of CO formation)

Rearrange to isolate ΔH°_f (CO):

ΔH°_f (CO) = ΔH°_sub (C) + ΔH°_f (CO₂) – ΔH°_diss (CO₂ → CO + ½ O₂)

But ΔH°_diss is the negative of the enthalpy of formation of CO, so solving gives:

ΔH°_f (CO) = 716.7 kJ – 393.5 kJ = +323.2 kJ mol⁻¹

Thus, formation of CO from its elements is endothermic.

3.5 Exam Tip

  • Write all given reactions in their standard direction. If you reverse a reaction, change the sign of ΔH°.
  • Multiply coefficients only after adjusting the sign; the ΔH° scales linearly with the stoichiometric coefficient.
  • Use a table to keep track of each step – this reduces arithmetic errors.

4. Bond Enthalpy (Bond Dissociation Energy)

Bond enthalpy is the energy required to break one mole of a specific type of bond in the gas phase, producing isolated atoms.

4.1 Definition & Units

D(A–B) = ΔH required for: A–B(g) → A(g) + B(g)

Units: kJ mol⁻¹.

4.2 Average vs. Specific Bond Enthalpies

  • Average bond enthalpy – obtained from a series of compounds; useful for quick estimates.
  • Specific bond enthalpy – measured for a particular molecule; more accurate.

4.3 Typical Bond Enthalpy Values (Average)

Bond Average D (kJ mol⁻¹)
C–C (single)347
C=C (double)614
C≡C (triple)839
C–H413
C–O358
C=O799
O–H463
N–H391
N≡N945
Cl–Cl242

4.4 Using Bond Enthalpies to Estimate ΔH°_reaction

General formula:

ΔH°_rxn ≈ Σ D(bonds broken) – Σ D(bonds formed)

All bonds must be considered in the gas phase.

4.5 Example – Enthalpy of Formation of CH₄(g)

Given average bond enthalpies:

  • C–H = 413 kJ mol⁻¹
  • C–C = 347 kJ mol⁻¹
  • H–H = 436 kJ mol⁻¹

Reaction (formation from elements):

C(s) + 2 H₂(g) → CH₄(g)

Step‑wise bond analysis:

  1. Break 2 H–H bonds: 2 × 436 = 872 kJ
  2. Form 4 C–H bonds: 4 × 413 = 1652 kJ

Physical Chemistry – Chemical Equilibrium

1. What is Chemical Equilibrium?

Chemical equilibrium is the state of a reversible reaction in which the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction. At this point, the concentrations (or partial pressures) of all reactants and products remain constant with time, although the reactions continue to occur at the molecular level.

The concept is governed by the Law of Mass Action (Guldberg & Waage, 1864), which states that the rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the concentrations of the reactants, each raised to a power equal to its stoichiometric coefficient.

2. The Equilibrium Constant

2.1 Definition of Kc

For a general gas‑phase reaction:

aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD

The equilibrium constant in terms of concentration (Kc) is:

Kc = \(\frac{[C]^c [D]^d}{[A]^a [B]^b}\)

[X] denotes the molar concentration (mol L‑1) of species X at equilibrium. The exponents are the stoichiometric coefficients, not experimental orders.

2.2 Definition of Kp

When dealing with gases, it is often convenient to use partial pressures (in atm or bar). The equilibrium constant in terms of pressure (Kp) is:

Kp = \(\frac{(P_C)^c (P_D)^d}{(P_A)^a (P_B)^b}\)

P_X is the equilibrium partial pressure of gas X.

2.3 Relationship Between Kp and Kc

The two constants are linked by the ideal‑gas equation. For a reaction where the total moles of gas change by Δn = (c + d) – (a + b):

Kp = Kc (RT)^{Δn}

R = 0.08206 L atm mol‑1K‑1 (or 8.314 J mol‑1K‑1), T = temperature in Kelvin (use K), and Δn is dimensionless.

Kp ↔ Kc Conversion Table
Δn (Δmoles gas) Expression Units of Kc (if any) Units of Kp (if any)
0 Kp = Kc dimensionless dimensionless
+1 Kp = Kc (RT) mol‑1L atm·L·mol‑1
‑1 Kp = Kc / (RT) L·mol‑1 atm‑1·L‑1·mol
±2, ±3 … Kp = Kc (RT)^{Δn} Varies with Δn Varies with Δn

2.4 Units of Equilibrium Constants

In modern practice, equilibrium constants are treated as dimensionless by dividing each concentration or pressure by a standard state (1 M for solutions, 1 atm for gases). However, many textbooks still list units; remember the rule:

  • If Δn = 0 → K is dimensionless.
  • If Δn ≠ 0 → K carries units of (concentration)Δn or (pressure)Δn. In exam answers, write the units only when explicitly asked.

3. Le Chatelier’s Principle

Le Chatelier’s principle predicts the direction in which a system at equilibrium will shift when subjected to an external change. The system counteracts the disturbance to re‑establish equilibrium.

3.1 Factors Affecting Equilibrium

  1. Concentration / Partial Pressure
    • Adding a reactant or product shifts the equilibrium toward the opposite side.
    • Removing a species shifts the equilibrium toward the side from which it is removed.
    • For gases, changing total pressure (by changing volume) affects equilibria with Δn ≠ 0.
  2. Temperature
    • Endothermic forward reaction (ΔH > 0): Raising T favours products (shift right).
    • Exothermic forward reaction (ΔH < 0): Raising T favours reactants (shift left).
    • Quantitatively, use the van’t Hoff equation:
      ln(K₂/K₁) = –ΔH°/R (1/T₂ – 1/T₁)
  3. Catalyst
    • Accelerates both forward and reverse rates equally.
    • Does not change the position of equilibrium.
  4. Inert Gas (at constant volume)
    • Adding an inert gas at constant volume does not change partial pressures; equilibrium unchanged.
    • At constant pressure, adding an inert gas increases total volume, effectively lowering partial pressures – shift depends on Δn.
  5. Solvent Effects (for heterogeneous equilibria)
    • Changing the solvent can alter activity coefficients, especially for weak electrolytes.

3.2 Mnemonic for Quick Recall

“C‑T‑P‑I‑S” – Conc., Temp, Pressure, Inert gas, Solvent.

Use this to remember the five main Le Chatelier perturbations.

4. Quantitative Treatment of Equilibrium

4.1 ICE (Initial‑Change‑Equilibrium) Tables

The ICE table is the backbone of most equilibrium calculations. Steps:

  1. Write the balanced equation.
  2. Express Kc or Kp with concentrations/pressures.
  3. Set up an ICE table with Initial (given), Change (±x), and Equilibrium (initial ± change) rows.
  4. Substitute equilibrium expressions into the K expression and solve for x.
  5. Calculate required quantities (e.g., % dissociation, equilibrium concentrations).

Tip: For reactions with large K (≫1) assume reactants are almost completely consumed; for very small K (≪1) assume products are negligible. This simplifies algebra.

4.2 Example 1 – Gas‑Phase Equilibrium

Problem: At 500 K, the equilibrium mixture of N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) has a total pressure of 10 atm. The equilibrium constant Kp = 0.05. Find the mole fraction of NH₃.

Solution Sketch:

  1. Let the initial moles of N₂ = a, H₂ = 3a (stoichiometric). Assume no NH₃ initially.
  2. Let x be the extent (in moles) of reaction that proceeds forward.
  3. Equilibrium moles: N₂ = a – x, H₂ = 3a – 3x, NH₃ = 2x.
  4. Total moles = a – x + 3a – 3x + 2x = 4a – 2x.
  5. Partial pressures = (mole fraction) × P_total.
  6. Write Kp = (P_NH₃)² / (P_N₂)(P_H₂)³ = 0.05.
  7. Substitute P_i = (n_i / n_total) × 10 atm and solve for x/a.
  8. Result: mole fraction of NH₃ = 2x / (4a – 2x) ≈ 0.12 (12 %).

Exam Tip: When total pressure is given, always convert to partial pressures using mole fractions; avoid mixing concentrations and pressures in the same K expression.

4.3 Example 2 – Solution Equilibrium (Acid Dissociation)

Problem: The acid dissociation constant Ka for HCN at 25 °C is 4.9 × 10⁻¹⁰. Calculate the pH of a 0.010 M HCN solution.

Solution Sketch:

  1. Write dissociation: HCN ⇌ H⁺ + CN⁻.
  2. ICE table: Initial [HCN] = 0.010 M, [H⁺] = 0, [CN⁻] = 0.
  3. Change: –x, +x, +x.
  4. Equilibrium: [HCN] = 0.010 – x, [H⁺] = x, [CN⁻] = x.
  5. Ka = x² / (0.010 – x) ≈ 4.9 × 10⁻¹⁰.
  6. Since Ka is very small, assume x ≪ 0.010 → denominator ≈ 0.010.
  7. x = √(Ka × 0.010) = √(4.9 × 10⁻¹²) ≈ 7.0 × 10⁻⁶ M.
  8. pH = –log₁₀(x) ≈ 5.15.

Mnemonic: “Ka tiny → assume x ≪ C₀” – useful for weak acids/bases with Ka < 10⁻⁴.

5. Special Types of Equilibria

5.1 Heterogeneous Equilibria

When phases differ (solid, liquid, gas), the concentration of pure solids and liquids is omitted from the equilibrium expression.

CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) → Kp = P_CO₂

Key Point: Only gaseous or aqueous species appear in Kc/Kp.

5.2 Solubility Product (Ksp)

For a sparingly soluble salt AB(s) ⇌ A⁺(aq) + B⁻(aq), the equilibrium constant is called the solubility product:

Ksp = [A⁺][B⁻]

Application: Predict precipitation, common‑ion effect, and calculate molar solubility (s). For AB₂, Ksp = 4s³ (since [A⁺] = s, [B⁻] = 2s).

5.3 Acid‑Base Equilibria (Ka, Kb, Kw)

  • Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ (at 25 °C). Temperature dependent: Kw increases with temperature.
  • Relationship: pKa + pKb = 14 (at 25 °C).
  • For polyprotic acids, each dissociation has its own Ka (Ka₁, Ka₂, …). The stepwise constants decrease dramatically (Ka₁ ≫ Ka₂ ≫ Ka₃).

5.4 Redox Equilibria (E° and K)

The Nernst equation links the standard cell potential (E°) to the equilibrium constant:

ΔG° = –nFE° = –RT ln K  ⇒ K = e^{nFE°/RT}

Where n = number of electrons transferred, F = 96 485 C mol⁻¹. This is crucial for electrochemical equilibrium questions.

6. Temperature Dependence – van’t Hoff Equation

The van’t Hoff equation quantifies how K changes with temperature:

ln K₂ – ln K₁ = –ΔH°/R (1/T₂ – 1/T₁)

Physical Chemistry – Solutions: Types, Concentration, & Colligative Properties

1. Introduction to Solutions

Definition of Solution

  • A solution is a homogeneous mixture.
  • It can be formed by mixing solid, liquid, and gases (e.g., CO2 gas).

Properties of Solutions

  • Particles do not scatter a beam of light (Tyndall effect is absent) because the size of particles is very small.
  • The path of light is not visible.
  • Components cannot be separated physically.
  • Particles cannot be seen by naked eyes.

Examples

  • Alloys are homogeneous mixtures.
  • Tincture of Iodine: A solution of Iodine (solid) in Alcohol

2. Classification of Solutions

2.1 Based on Physical State of Components

Solvent Solute Typical Example
Gas Gas Air (N2, O2, CO2)
Liquid Gas Carbonated water (CO2 in H2O)
Liquid Liquid Alcoholic solution (ethanol in water)
Liquid Solid Salt solution (NaCl in water)
Solid Solid Alloy (Cu‑Zn – brass)

2.2 Based on Concentration

  • Dilute Solution – Solute concentration is low; properties follow ideal behaviour.
  • Concentrated Solution – High solute concentration; deviations from ideality become noticeable.
  • Unsaturated, Saturated & Supersaturated – Relates to the solubility limit at a given temperature.

2.3 Based on Nature of Solute & Solvent

  • Electrolytic Solutions – Solutes dissociate into ions (e.g., NaCl, HCl).
  • Nonelectrolytic Solutions – No ion formation (e.g., sugar, ethanol).
  • Binary, Ternary, Multicomponent Solutions – Number of distinct solutes.

3. Concentration Terms – Definitions, Formulas & Units

Understanding the various ways to express concentration is crucial for solving numerical problems in NDA, CDS, AFCAT and other defence exams. The table below summarises the most frequently asked concentration expressions.

Term Formula Units Typical Use
Molarity (M) M = \(\dfrac{n_{\text{solute}}}{V_{\text{solution (L)}}}\) mol L−1 Standard laboratory calculations, titrations.
Molality (m) m = \(\dfrac{n_{\text{solute}}}{m_{\text{solvent (kg)}}}\) mol kg−1 Colligative property calculations (temperature‑dependent).
Normality (N) N = \(\dfrac{eq_{\text{solute}}}{V_{\text{solution (L)}}}\) eq L−1 Acid‑base and redox titrations.
Mass Percent (w/w %) \(\% w/w = \dfrac{m_{\text{solute}}}{m_{\text{solution}}}\times 100\) % Industrial formulations, food chemistry.
Volume Percent (v/v %) \(\% v/v = \dfrac{V_{\text{solute}}}{V_{\text{solution}}}\times 100\) % Mixtures of liquids (e.g., alcoholic beverages).
Mass/Volume Percent (w/v %) \(\% w/v = \dfrac{m_{\text{solute}}}{V_{\text{solution (mL)}}}\times 100\) % (g mL−1) Pharmaceutical solutions.
Mole Fraction (X) XA = \(\dfrac{n_A}{\sum n_i}\) dimensionless Thermodynamic calculations, Raoult’s law.
Parts per Million (ppm) ppm = \(\dfrac{m_{\text{solute}}}{m_{\text{solution}}}\times10^6\) mg kg−1 Environmental analysis, trace contaminants.
Parts per Billion (ppb) ppb = \(\dfrac{m_{\text{solute}}}{m_{\text{solution}}}\times10^9\) µg kg−1 Ultra‑trace analysis.

3.1 Mnemonic for Concentration Units

“Many Old New Wizards Visit Wonderful Magical Places”

  • M – Molarity
  • O – Osmolarity (used in physiology, similar to molarity)
  • N – Normality
  • W – w/w %
  • V – v/v %
  • W – w/v %
  • M – Mole fraction
  • P – ppm / ppb

3.2 Quick Conversion Tips (Exam Focus)

  • 1 M solution = 1 mol L−1. Multiply by molecular weight to get g L−1.
  • Molality is independent of temperature – useful when the problem involves temperature change (colligative properties).
  • Normality = M × n (where n = number of equivalents per mole). Remember for acids: HCl (n=1), H2SO4 (n=2).
  • For dilute aqueous solutions, mole fraction of solute ≈ M / (55.5 mol kg−1), because 1 kg of water ≈ 55.5 mol.

4. Colligative Properties – Theory, Equations & Applications

Colligative properties depend **only on the number of solute particles** and not on their nature. The four classical colligative properties are:

  1. Vapor Pressure Lowering (Raoult’s Law)
  2. Boiling Point Elevation
  3. Freezing Point Depression
  4. Osmotic Pressure

4.1 Vapor Pressure Lowering – Raoult’s Law

For an ideal solution:

\(P_{\text{solution}} = X_{\text{solvent}} \times P^{\circ}_{\text{solvent}}\)

  • P°solvent – Vapor pressure of pure solvent.
  • Xsolvent – Mole fraction of solvent.
  • Vapor pressure lowering, ΔP = P°solvent – Psolution = Xsolute P°solvent

Key Point for Exams: For dilute solutions, Xsolute ≈ \(\dfrac{n_{\text{solute}}}{n_{\text{solvent}}}\) and ΔP can be expressed using molality:

ΔP = Kp m

where Kp = P°solvent · Msolvent / 1000 (Msolvent = molar mass of solvent in g mol−1).

4.2 Boiling Point Elevation

When a non‑volatile solute is added, the boiling point rises.

ΔTb = Kb · m · i

  • Kb – Boiling point elevation constant (also called ebullioscopic constant).
  • m – Molality of the solution.
  • i – Van’t Hoff factor (number of particles the solute yields in solution).

Typical values for water:

  • Kb = 0.512 °C kg mol−1
  • Kf (freezing point depression constant) = 1.86 °C kg mol−1

4.3 Freezing Point Depression

Analogous to boiling point elevation:

ΔTf = Kf · m · i

Freezing point of pure water is 0 °C. Adding solute lowers it; the magnitude of depression is directly proportional to the total number of solute particles.

4.4 Osmotic Pressure (π)

Osmosis is the movement of solvent through a semipermeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to higher concentration. For dilute solutions:

π = i · M · R · T

  • M – Molarity (mol L−1).
  • R – Universal gas constant = 0.0821 L atm K−1 mol−1.
  • T – Temperature in Kelvin.
  • π is expressed in atm, but can be converted to mm Hg (1 atm = 760 mm Hg).

Medical Relevance (Exam Tip): Normal osmotic pressure of blood plasma ≈ 7.5 atm (≈ 5700 mm Hg). Any deviation indicates pathological conditions.

4.5 Van’t Hoff Factor (i) – Quick Mnemonic

“**I**ons **C**reate **P**articles” → i = number of particles formed.

  • NaCl → i = 2 (Na⁺ + Cl⁻)
  • CaCl₂ → i = 3 (Ca²⁺ + 2Cl⁻)
  • Glucose (non‑electrolyte) → i = 1

4.6 Real vs Ideal Solutions – Deviations

Deviation Type Cause Effect on Colligative Property
Positive Deviation Weaker intermolecular forces between unlike molecules (e.g., ethanol‑water) Higher vapor pressure than predicted; lower boiling point elevation.
Negative Deviation Stronger intermolecular forces (e.g., H₂O‑H₂SO₄) Lower vapor pressure; higher boiling point elevation.

4.7 Sample Numerical Problem (Step‑by‑Step)

Problem: Calculate the boiling point of a 0.200 m aqueous solution of NaCl. (Kb for water = 0.512 °C kg mol−1).

Solution:

  1. Identify i for NaCl: i = 2.
  2. Use ΔTb = Kb · m · i
  3. ΔTb = 0.512 × 0.200 × 2 = 0.2048 °C.
  4. Normal boiling point of water = 100 °C. Therefore, boiling point of solution = 100 + 0.2048 ≈ 100.20 °C.

Exam Tip: Always keep track of units (molality in mol kg−1, Kb in °C kg mol−1) and apply the van’t Hoff factor correctly.

5. Detailed Derivation of Colligative Formulas

5.1 Derivation of Vapor Pressure Lowering

Consider a binary ideal solution of solvent (A) and non‑volatile solute (B). The chemical potential of A in the solution (μA) equals that of the pure solvent at a reduced vapor pressure (PA).

μA(solution) = μA⁰ + RT ln XA

μA(vapour) = μA⁰ + RT ln (PA/P°A)

Equating the two gives: ln (PA/P°A) = ln XA → PA = XA P°A.

5.2 Derivation of Boiling Point Elevation

At the boiling point, the liquid and vapour phases are in equilibrium. Adding a solute lowers the solvent’s vapour pressure, requiring a higher temperature to reach the same vapour pressure as the pure solvent.

Using the Clausius‑Clapeyron equation for small temperature changes:

ΔTb = \(\dfrac{R T_b^2}{\Delta H_{vap}}\) · Xsolute

Substituting Xsolute = \(\dfrac{m M_{solvent}}{1000}\) leads to the familiar form ΔTb = Kb · m · i.

5.3 Derivation of Freezing Point Depression

Analogous to boiling point elevation, but using the enthalpy of fusion (ΔHfus) and the melting temperature (Tf).

ΔTf = \(\dfrac{R T_f^2}{\Delta H_{fus}}\) · Xsolute → ΔTf = Kf · m · i.

5.4 Derivation of Osmotic Pressure

Consider a semipermeable membrane separating pure solvent from a solution. At equilibrium, the chemical potential of the solvent on both sides is equal:

μsolvent⁰ (pure) = μsolvent (solution) + V̅ · π

Using μ = μ⁰ + RT ln a (activity) and assuming dilute solution (a ≈ Xsolvent ≈ 1 – Xsolute), we obtain:

π = i · M · R · T

6. Applications of Colligative Properties in Defence & Everyday Life

  • Antifreeze in Aircraft Engines – Uses ethylene glycol (i = 1) to lower the freezing point of coolant water, preventing ice formation at high altitudes.
  • De‑icing of Runways – Salt (NaCl) solution lowers the freezing point of water, melting ice quickly.
  • Osmotic Pressure in Biological Systems – Understanding blood plasma osmolarity is vital for field medics.
  • Boiling Point Elevation in High‑Altitude Cooking – At lower atmospheric pressure, water boils at lower temperature; adding solutes can raise the boiling point to achieve proper cooking.
  • Industrial Separation – Fractional distillation relies on vapor pressure differences; knowledge of Raoult’s law helps in designing efficient columns.

Exam Tip – Quick Recall Table for Water

Property Value for Water
Boiling point (pure)100 °C
Freezing point (pure)0 °C
Kb0.512 °C kg mol−1
Kf1.86 °C kg mol−1
Vapor pressure at 25 °C23.8 mm Hg

7. Common Mistakes & How to Avoid Them (Exam Strategies)

  1. Confusing Molarity and Molality – Remember: Molarity uses **volume of solution**, Molality uses **mass of solvent**. Molality is temperature‑independent.
  2. Ignoring the Van’t Hoff factor – Always multiply by i for electrolytes. Forgetting i leads to under‑estimation of ΔT or π.
  3. Using wrong units for Kb and Kf – They are expressed per **kg of solvent**, not per litre.
  4. Mixing up ΔTb and ΔTf – Boiling point **rises**, freezing point **drops**. Sign convention matters.
  5. Applying Raoult’s law to non‑ideal solutions without checking deviation – For strong solute‑solvent interactions, expect negative deviation.
  6. Forgetting to convert temperature to Kelvin in osmotic pressure calculations – Use T (K) = °C + 273.15.

Mnemonic for the Four Colligative Properties

“**V**ery **B**old **F**ighters **O**perate” → Vapor pressure lowering, Boiling point elevation, Freezing point depression, Osmotic pressure.

8. Summary – One‑Page Quick Revision

  • Solution – homogeneous mixture of two or more substances; no Tyndall effect.
  • Concentration Terms – M, m, N, % (w/w, v/v, w/v), mole fraction, ppm/ppb.
  • Colligative Properties – depend only on number of particles:
    • ΔP = Xsolute P° (Raoult’s law)
    • ΔTb = Kb · m · i
    • ΔTf = Kf · m · i
    • π = i · M · R · T
  • Key Constants for Water – Kb = 0.512 °C kg mol−1, Kf = 1.86 °C kg mol−1.
  • Van’t Hoff factor (i) – count of particles formed; essential for electrolytes.
  • Exam Tips – keep units consistent, use molality for temperature‑dependent problems, remember i, and check for ideal vs non‑ideal behaviour.

9. Integrated Mind‑Map Extract (Metals & Non‑Metals)

Metals

The central node of the mind map is Metals, with the following branches/properties:

  • Basic oxides – Metals form basic oxides.
  • Lustre – Metals in their pure state have a shining surface.
  • Malleability – Metals can be beaten into thin sheets.
    • Most malleable metals:
      • Gold
      • Silver
  • Sonorous – Metals that produce a sound on striking a hard surface.
    • School bells are malle.
  • Ductility – Metals can be drawn into thin wires.
    • 1 gm of go

10. Chemical Properties Extract

Chemical Properties

  • Metal in air: metal + oxygen → metal oxide.
    • Example: 2Cu + O2 → 2CuO – Copper(II) oxide (black).
  • Anodising: Al (Aluminium).

12. Final Exam Checklist

  1. Identify the type of solution required (ideal vs real, dilute vs concentrated).
  2. Choose the correct concentration expression (M, m, N, % etc.).
  3. Calculate the van’t Hoff factor for electrolytes.
  4. Apply the appropriate colligative formula, remembering the sign (elevation vs depression).
  5. Convert temperature to Kelvin for osmotic pressure.
  6. Check units: Kb and Kf are per kg of solvent; R is 0.0821 L atm K−1 mol−1.
  7. Validate answer with reasonable physical sense (e.g., boiling point cannot exceed 150 °C for a typical aqueous solution).

Master these concepts, memorize the constants, and practice a variety of numerical problems – you will be fully prepared for any NDA, CDS, or AFCAT question on solutions.
ai-gen-chemistry-important-compounds-oxi:
Inorganic Chemistry – Important Compounds (Oxides & Salts) & Their Uses

1. Introduction

Inorganic chemistry for NDA/CDS/AFCAT focuses heavily on the identification, preparation, properties and industrial/biological uses of oxides and salts. These compounds appear in multiple‑choice questions (MCQs), match‑the‑column, and assertion‑reason type questions. The following notes are a one‑stop revision guide covering every fact, formula, date and exception you may encounter.

2. Oxides – Classification & General Features

Oxides are binary compounds of oxygen with another element. Their behaviour in water determines the classification.

Type of Oxide General Reaction with Water Typical Examples Key Uses
Acidic Oxides Oxide + H₂O → Acid (e.g., CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃)
  • CO₂ (Carbon dioxide)
  • SO₂ (Sulphur dioxide)
  • SO₃ (Sulphur trioxide)
  • NO₂ (Nitrogen dioxide)
  • P₄O₁₀ (Phosphorus pentoxide)
  • Carbonated drinks (CO₂)
  • Acid rain (SO₂, SO₃)
  • Fertiliser production (H₂SO₄ from SO₃)
  • Explosives (NO₂)
  • Dehydrating agent (P₄O₁₀)
Basic Oxides (Metal Oxides) Oxide + H₂O → Base (e.g., CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂)
  • CaO (Calcium oxide)
  • MgO (Magnesium oxide)
  • Na₂O (Sodium oxide)
  • K₂O (Potassium oxide)
  • BaO (Barium oxide)
  • Construction (lime – CaO)
  • Refractory material (MgO)
  • Glass & ceramics (Na₂O, K₂O)
  • Fire‑proofing (BaO)
Amphoteric Oxides React with both acids and bases
  • Al₂O₃ (Aluminium oxide)
  • ZnO (Zinc oxide)
  • SnO (Tin(II) oxide)
  • PbO (Lead(II) oxide)
  • Ceramics & pigments (Al₂O₃)
  • Antacid (ZnO)
  • Solar cells (SnO)
  • Lead‑acid batteries (PbO)
Neutral Oxides Do not react with water; often covalent
  • CO (Carbon monoxide)
  • N₂O (Nitrous oxide)
  • NO (Nitric oxide)
  • SiO₂ (Silicon dioxide)
  • TiO₂ (Titanium dioxide)
  • Fuel gas (CO)
  • Analgesic & anesthetic (N₂O)
  • Atmospheric chemistry (NO)
  • Glass making (SiO₂)
  • White pigment (TiO₂)

2.1 Mnemonic for Acidic Oxides – “CASH‑P”

Carbon dioxide, And Sulphur oxides, Hydrogen‑related (NO₂), Phosphorus pentoxide.

Remember: “CASH‑P” is always acidic – keep it in your pocket for quick recall.

2.2 Mnemonic for Basic Oxides – “BASIC‑M”

Barium oxide, Alkaline earth oxides (CaO, MgO), Sodium oxide, Iodine? (ignore), Calcium oxide, Magnesium oxide.

3. Detailed Review of Important Oxides

3.1 Carbon Dioxide (CO₂)

  • Formula: CO₂
  • Discovery: Recognised as a distinct gas by 1772 (Joseph Priestley).
  • Physical State: Colourless, odourless gas; sublimates at –78.5 °C.
  • Acidic Nature: Reacts with water → carbonic acid (H₂CO₃).
  • Key Uses:
    • Carbonated beverages – 2–5 % CO₂ by volume.
    • Fire extinguishers – non‑flammable, smothers fire.
    • Supercritical fluid extraction – high‑pressure (≈ 73 bar) and temperature (≈ 31 °C) region.
    • Plant growth – photosynthesis (CO₂ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂).
  • Environmental Note: Primary greenhouse gas; contributes to global warming. Exam tip: Remember the link CO₂ ↔ acid rain via formation of H₂SO₄ and HNO₃.

3.2 Sulphur Dioxide (SO₂) & Sulphur Trioxide (SO₃)

Both are pivotal in the industrial production of sulphuric acid – the “king of chemicals”.

  • SO₂
    • Formula: SO₂
    • Preparation: Burning sulphur in air (S + O₂ → SO₂) – discovered 1777 (Carl Wilhelm Scheele).
    • Properties: Pungent, toxic, soluble → forms H₂SO₃ (weak acid).
    • Uses: Preservative for dried fruits, bleaching agent, and as a reducing agent in the contact process.
  • SO₃
    • Formula: SO₃
    • Preparation: Oxidation of SO₂ using V₂O₅ catalyst (Contact Process) – industrialized 1880.
    • Properties: Viscous liquid; reacts violently with water → H₂SO₄ (conc.).
    • Uses: Direct manufacture of concentrated sulphuric acid; also in making oleum (H₂S₂O₇).

3.3 Nitrogen Oxides – NO, NO₂, N₂O

  • NO (Nitric oxide)
    • Formula: NO
    • Preparation: Reduction of nitric acid with copper (Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂ + 2H₂O).
    • Properties: Colourless, paramagnetic, dimerises to N₂O₂ at low temperature.
    • Uses: Biological signalling molecule (vasodilation), precursor to NO₂.
  • NO₂ (Nitrogen dioxide)
    • Formula: NO₂
    • Preparation: Oxidation of NO in air (2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂).
    • Properties: Brown gas, strong oxidiser, forms HNO₃ on dissolution.
    • Uses: Manufacture of nitric acid (Ostwald process), explosives (TNT synthesis).
  • N₂O (Nitrous oxide)
    • Formula: N₂O
    • Discovery: 1772 (Joseph Priestley).
    • Properties: Colourless, slightly sweet odour, non‑flammable.
    • Uses: Dental analgesic (“laughing gas”), rocket oxidiser (in hybrid rockets).

3.4 Phosphorus Pentoxide (P₄O₁₀)

  • Formula: P₄O₁₀ (also written as P₂O₅)
  • Preparation: Heating elemental phosphorus in excess oxygen (P₄ + 5O₂ → P₄O₁₀) – discovered 1669 (Robert Boyle).
  • Properties: White crystalline solid; powerful dehydrating agent; reacts violently with water → phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄).
  • Uses: Laboratory drying agent, production of phosphoric acid, catalyst support.
  • Exam Tip: Remember “P₄O₁₀ = 5 × H₂O removed from H₃PO₄” – useful for stoichiometry questions.

3.5 Silicon Dioxide (SiO₂) – The Backbone of Glass

  • Formula: SiO₂
  • Occurrence: Quartz, sand, diatomaceous earth.
  • Properties: High melting point (≈ 1710 °C), chemically inert, amorphous (glass) and crystalline (quartz) forms.
  • Uses:
    • Glass manufacturing – soda‑lime glass (Na₂O·CaO·SiO₂).
    • Semiconductor industry – high‑purity SiO₂ as dielectric layer.
    • Construction – concrete aggregate.
  • Historical Note: First glass made by Romans around 1st century AD.

3.6 Titanium Dioxide (TiO₂) – White Pigment

  • Formula: TiO₂
  • Polymorphs: Rutile (most stable), Anatase, Brookite.
  • Uses: Paints, sunscreens (UV blocker), food colour (E171), photocatalysis (self‑cleaning surfaces).
  • Exam Fact: TiO₂ is a semiconductor with a band gap of ≈ 3.0 eV – useful in photocatalytic water splitting.

4. Salts – Classification, Important Examples & Uses

4.1 Classification Overview

Category General Formula Typical Examples Key Applications
Normal (Ionic) Salts MX (e.g., NaCl) NaCl, KCl, CaCl₂, MgSO₄ Food seasoning, de‑icing, electrolyte balance
Acidic Salts MXₙ (where X is a poly‑acidic anion) NaHSO₄, Na₂CO₃, K₂CO₃ Acid‑base titrations, glass making, baking soda
Basic (Alkaline) Salts Metal hydroxides or basic carbonates CaCO₃, Mg(OH)₂, Zn(OH)₂ Antacids, flame retardants, water softening

Carbon Compounds – Allotropy, Hydrocarbons & Functional Groups

1. Introduction to Carbon Chemistry

Carbon (C) is the backbone of organic chemistry. Its unique ability to catenate (form C‑C bonds) and hybridise in sp³, sp², and sp configurations gives rise to an immense variety of compounds. In defence‑related competitive exams (NDA, CDS, AFCAT) questions often test:

  • Allotropic forms of carbon and their industrial relevance.
  • Classification, nomenclature and reactions of hydrocarbons.
  • Recognition and reactivity of major functional groups.
  • Key numerical data – boiling points, densities, bond energies, etc.

2. Allotropy of Carbon

Allotropy refers to the existence of an element in two or more different structural forms. Carbon exhibits several important allotropes, each with distinct physical & chemical properties.

2.1 Major Allotropes

Allotrope Structure Hybridisation Key Properties Major Uses (Defence/Industrial)
Diamond 3‑D tetrahedral network sp³
  • Hardest natural material (Mohs 10)
  • High thermal conductivity, electrical insulator
  • Transparent, high refractive index
  • Cutting tools for armour plating
  • Heat‑sink in high‑power electronics
  • Optical windows in high‑pressure chambers
Graphite Layered sheets of hexagonal rings sp²
  • Soft, lubricating, conducts electricity parallel to layers
  • High melting point ≈ 3650 °C
  • Good thermal conductor perpendicular to layers
  • Electro‑type batteries, fuel‑cell electrodes
  • Lubricants for missile guidance mechanisms
  • Carbon‑fiber composites for aircraft & UAV frames
Fullerenes (C₆₀, C₇₀…) Closed‑cage spheroidal molecules sp² (curved)
  • Electron‑acceptor, semiconductor behaviour
  • Soluble in organic solvents
  • Drug delivery carriers for battlefield medics
  • Photovoltaic cells – high‑efficiency solar panels
Graphene Single atomic layer of sp² carbon sp²
  • Exceptional tensile strength (≈ 130 GPa)
  • Electrical conductivity ≈ 10⁶ S m⁻¹
  • Transparent (≈ 97% light transmission)
  • Flexible sensors for UAV health monitoring
  • EMI shielding in communication equipment
Carbon Nanotubes (CNTs) Rolled graphene sheets – single‑walled (SWCNT) or multi‑walled (MWCNT) sp²
  • Young’s modulus ≈ 1 TPa
  • Thermal conductivity up to 3000 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹
  • Reinforcement in composite armour
  • Field‑emission displays for night‑vision devices
Amorphous Carbon Disordered network of sp²/sp³ bonds Mixed
  • Hard, black, electrically conductive (depends on preparation)
  • Protective coatings on gun barrels
  • Electro‑static discharge (ESD) protection

2.2 Historical Milestones (Allotropy)

  • Diamond – First recorded in ~3000 BC (ancient India). Scientific study began after 1797 when H. Cavendish proved it is pure carbon.
  • Graphite – Recognised as a distinct form of carbon by Lavoisier in 1789.
  • Fullerenes – Discovered accidentally in 1985 by Kroto, Smalley & Curl (Nobel 1996).
  • Graphene – Isolated by Geim & Novoselov in 2004 (Nobel 2010).

2.3 Exam Tips – Allotropy

  • Remember the hybridisation: sp³ → diamond, sp² → graphite, graphene, fullerenes, CNTs.
  • Mnemonic for uses: Diamond – Drill (cutting), Graphite – Gun‑barrel coating, Fullerene – Field‑medicine, Graphene – GPS (sensor).
  • Key numbers to memorise: 3650 °C (graphite sublimation), 3.5 g cm⁻³ (diamond density), 2.2 g cm⁻³ (graphite density).

3. Hydrocarbons – Classification & Core Concepts

3.1 General Definition

Hydrocarbons are compounds composed solely of carbon and hydrogen. They are the primary source of fuel and raw material for many synthetic chemicals used in defence logistics.

3.2 Classification

Class General Formula Hybridisation Key Features Representative Examples
Alkanes (Saturated) CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ sp³
  • Only σ‑bonds
  • Low reactivity (except combustion)
  • Non‑polar
 Methane, Ethane, Propane, n‑Octane (C₈H₁₈)
Alkenes (Unsaturated) CₙH₂ₙ sp²
  • One or more C=C double bonds
  • Geometric (cis‑trans) isomerism
  • More reactive than alkanes
 Ethene (C₂H₄), Propene, But-2-ene
Alkynes (Unsaturated) CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ sp
  • One or more C≡C triple bonds
  • Acidic hydrogen (pKa ≈ 25)
  • Linear geometry around triple bond
 Acetylene (C₂H₂), Propyne, But-1-yne
Aromatic Hydrocarbons CₙHₙ (n = 4m+2) sp² (delocalised π)
  • Planar, conjugated ring systems
  • Stability due to aromaticity (Hückel’s rule)
  • Undergo substitution, not addition
 Benzene (C₆H₆), Toluene, Naphthalene

3.3 Isomerism in Hydrocarbons

Isomerism is a high‑frequency topic in NDA/CDS papers. Remember the two broad categories:

  • Structural (constitutional) isomers – differ in connectivity.
  • Stereoisomers – same connectivity, different spatial arrangement (cis‑trans, optical).

Mnemonic for stereochemistry: Cis‑Trans Can Trick Reactors – Cis and Trans are only for Cyclic or Trigonal alkenes with restricted rotation.

ai-gen-chemistry-organic-reactions-combu:
Organic Reactions – Combustion, Addition, Substitution & Polymerisation

1. Overview

Organic chemistry deals with carbon‑based compounds and their transformations. The four major reaction families examined in NDA/CDS/AFCAT are:

  • Combustion – Oxidative breakdown giving CO₂ & H₂O.
  • Addition – Two reactants combine across a multiple bond.
  • Substitution – An atom/group is replaced by another.
  • Polymerisation – Small monomers link to form macromolecules.

All these reactions obey the principles of thermodynamics, kinetics and orbital symmetry. Mastery of the mechanisms, reagents, conditions and typical products is essential for scoring full marks.

2. Combustion Reactions

2.1 Definition & General Equation

Combustion is a rapid oxidation reaction in which an organic molecule reacts with molecular oxygen (O₂) to give carbon dioxide, water and heat.

  CₓHᵧ + (x + y/4) O₂ → x CO₂ + (y/2) H₂O  +  ΔH

ΔH is negative (exothermic). The reaction is the basis of fuels, internal‑combustion engines and calorimetric determinations.

2.2 Types of Combustion

TypeOxygen AvailabilityProductsKey Features
Complete Combustion Excess O₂ CO₂ + H₂O Maximum heat release; clean flame; ΔH°c (kJ mol⁻¹) for CH₄ = -890
Incomplete Combustion Limited O₂ CO, C (soot), H₂O Lower heat, toxic gases, yellow flame
Partial Oxidation Controlled O₂ (industrial) Alcohols, aldehydes, acids (e.g., oxidation of ethylene to ethylene oxide) Used for specialty chemicals

2.3 Enthalpy of Combustion (ΔHc)

ΔHc values are tabulated for standard fuels. Memorise the following high‑yield numbers (useful for numerical questions):

  • CH₄ (methane) – -890 kJ mol⁻¹
  • C₂H₆ (ethane) – -1560 kJ mol⁻¹
  • C₃H₈ (propane) – -2220 kJ mol⁻¹
  • C₈H₁₈ (octane) – -5470 kJ mol⁻¹

Mnemonic: “My Energetic Pets Omit” → Methane, Ethane, Propane, Octane (remember the order of increasing carbon chain).

2.4 Combustion in the Laboratory

Typical set‑up: a Bunsen burner or a combustion spoon. Key safety points:

  • Carry out in a well‑ventilated hood.
  • Use a flame‑proof mat to avoid fire spread.
  • Never use open flame with halogenated organics – they may produce toxic HCl/ HBr.

3. Addition Reactions

3.1 General Concept

In addition reactions two (or more) reagents add across a carbon–carbon multiple bond (C=C or C≡C). The π‑bond is broken and a σ‑bond is formed with each reagent.

Key categories:

  • Hydrogenation (H₂ addition)
  • Halogenation (X₂ addition)
  • Hydrohalogenation (HX addition)
  • Hydration (H₂O addition)
  • Polymerisation (repeated addition)

3.2 Hydrogenation

Conversion of alkenes/alkynes to alkanes using H₂ in the presence of a metal catalyst.

  RCH=CH₂ + H₂  →[Ni, Pd, Pt]  RCH₂‑CH₃

Conditions:

  • Catalyst: Ni (Raney), Pd/C, Pt.
  • Pressure: 1–5 atm (industrial) or atmospheric (lab).
  • Temperature: 25–150 °C.

Exam tip: Remember that hydrogenation is *syn* addition – both H atoms add to the same face of the double bond.

3.3 Halogenation (X₂ addition)

Alkenes react with halogens (Cl₂, Br₂) to give vicinal dihalides.

  RCH=CH₂ + X₂ → RCHX‑CH₂X

Mechanism involves a cyclic halonium ion intermediate.

  • Cl₂: colourless → yellow‑brown solution.
  • Br₂: deep orange; decolourises rapidly – a classic test for unsaturation.

Mnemonic: “Br‑Br‑Br‑Br – Breaks the double bond”.

3.4 Hydrohalogenation (HX addition)

Alkenes add HX (HCl, HBr, HI) following Markovnikov’s rule:

The hydrogen atom attaches to the carbon bearing the greater number of hydrogen atoms; the halide attaches to the more substituted carbon.

Exception – anti‑Markovnikov addition with HBr in presence of peroxides (radical mechanism).

  RCH=CH₂ + HBr  →[peroxides]  RCH₂‑CH₂Br   (anti‑Markovnikov)

Key data for exam:

  • HCl, HI – always Markovnikov.
  • HBr – radical pathway only with 0.01 M peroxides.

3.5 Hydration (H₂O addition)

Alkenes convert to alcohols. Two main methods:

  1. Acid‑catalysed hydration (Markovnikov):
            RCH=CH₂ + H₂O  →[H₂SO₄]  RCH(OH)‑CH₃
  2. Oxymercuration–demercuration (anti‑Markovnikov, no rearrangement):
            RCH=CH₂ + Hg(OAc)₂, H₂O → RCH(OH)‑CH₃  (after NaBH₄ work‑up)

Remember the **“Mercury doesn’t rearrange”** rule for quick answer.

3.6 Polymerisation as an Addition Process

When a monomer with a C=C bond adds repeatedly, a long chain (polymer) forms. See Section 4 for detailed mechanisms.

3.7 Comparison of Common Addition Reactions

ReactionReagentsProduct TypeRegiochemistryKey Conditions
Hydrogenation H₂ + metal catalyst Alkane Syn (both H on same side) Pressure 1–5 atm, 25–150 °C
Halogenation X₂ (Cl₂/Br₂) Dihalide Anti‑addition (trans) Room temp, inert solvent
Hydrohalogenation HX (HCl/HBr/HI) Alkyl halide Markovnikov (except HBr/peroxides) Acidic medium; peroxides for anti‑Markovnikov
Hydration H₂O + acid or Hg(OAc)₂ Alcohol Markovnikov (acid) / anti‑Markovnikov (oxymercuration) 70 °C (acid) or 0 °C (oxymercuration)

4. Substitution Reactions

4.1 Classification

Substitution replaces a functional group (X) with another (Y). The three major families are:

  • Free‑radical substitution – typical for alkanes.
  • Nucleophilic substitution (SN1 & SN2) – for alkyl halides, sulfonates.
  • Electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS) – for benzene derivatives.

4.2 Free‑Radical Substitution (Alkanes)

General scheme:

  RH + X₂  →[Δ or hν]  R· + X·
  R· + X₂ → R‑X + X·   (Propagation)

Key points:

  • Initiation requires heat or UV (e.g., chlorination of methane).
  • Radical stability order: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl.
  • Product distribution follows radical stability, but steric hindrance may modify yields.

Mnemonic: “Cl‑CH₃ → CH₃Cl – Chlorine Hammers Carbon”.

4.3 Nucleophilic Substitution

4.3.1 SN2 (Bimolecular)

One‑step concerted mechanism; backside attack; inversion of configuration (Walden inversion).

  R‑LG + Nu⁻ → R‑Nu + LG⁻

Favourable when:

  • Substrate is primary or methyl.
  • Leaving group (LG) is good: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻.
  • Solvent is polar aprotic (e.g., DMSO, DMF).

4.3.2 SN1 (Unimolecular)

Two‑step: formation of a carbocation followed by nucleophilic attack.

  R‑LG → R⁺ + LG⁻   (rate‑determining)
  R⁺ + Nu⁻ → R‑Nu

Favoured when:

  • Substrate is tertiary or allylic/benzylic.
  • Solvent is polar protic (e.g., H₂O, alcohols) which stabilises carbocation.
  • Good leaving group present.

Result: racemisation (if chiral centre).

4.4 Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS)

Key steps: formation of a σ‑complex (arenium ion) followed by deprotonation.

  Ar‑H + E⁺ → σ‑complex → Ar‑E + H⁺

Common electrophiles & reagents:

  • Nitration: HNO₃/H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺
  • Sulfonation: H₂SO₄ (conc.) → SO₃H⁺
  • Halogenation: X₂/FeX₃ or Br₂/FeBr₃ → X⁺
  • Friedel‑Crafts Alkylation: R‑Cl/AlCl₃ → R⁺
  • Friedel‑Crafts Acylation: R‑COCl/AlCl₃ → R‑CO⁺

Directing Effects (order of activation):

GroupTypeDirecting
–OH, –OR, –NH₂, –NR₂Activating, o/pOrtho/para
–CH₃, –C₂H₅Activating, o/pOrtho/para

Fuels – Types, Calorific Value, Fossil Fuels & Alternative Fuels

1. Introduction

Fuel is any material that can be oxidised to release energy in the form of heat or work. In defence examinations (NDA, CDS, AFCAT) the term “fuel” is frequently linked with energy density, availability, environmental impact and logistics. Understanding the chemistry behind different fuels, their calorific values and the shift towards alternative fuels is essential for answering both objective and descriptive questions.

2. Classification of Fuels

Fuels are broadly classified on the basis of physical state, origin, and usage. The three‑dimensional matrix is shown below:

Basis of Classification Categories Examples (Indian Context)
Physical State Solid, Liquid, Gaseous Coal (solid), Petrol (liquid), Natural Gas (gaseous)
Origin Fossil, Renewable, Synthetic Coal, Biodiesel, Fischer‑Tropsch diesel
Usage Primary, Secondary, Tertiary Crude oil (primary), Kerosene for lamps (secondary), LPG for cooking (tertiary)

2.1 Physical‑State Classification

  • Solid Fuels – High carbon content, low volatility. Include coal, coke, charcoal, solid waste, biomass pellets.
  • Liquid Fuels – Medium carbon‑hydrogen ratio, easy handling. Include petrol, diesel, kerosene, aviation turbine fuel (ATF), biodiesel.
  • Gaseous Fuels – Highest H/C ratio, cleanest combustion. Include natural gas (CH₄), LPG (propane‑butane), hydrogen, biogas (CH₄‑CO₂ mix).

2.2 Origin‑Based Classification

  • Fossil Fuels – Formed from ancient organic matter over millions of years. Coal, petroleum, natural gas.
  • Renewable (Bio) Fuels – Derived from recent biomass. Ethanol, biodiesel, biogas, wood‑based charcoal.
  • Synthetic Fuels – Produced by chemical conversion of coal, natural gas or biomass (e.g., Fischer‑Tropsch liquids, methanol).

2.3 Usage‑Based Classification

  • Primary Fuels – Extracted directly from the earth without any processing. Crude oil, raw coal, natural gas in its raw state.
  • Secondary Fuels – Obtained after simple refining or distillation. Petrol, diesel, kerosene, LPG.
  • Tertiary Fuels – Result from further chemical modification. Biodiesel (trans‑esterification), ethanol (fermentation), synthetic gasoline.

3. Calorific Value – The Energy Metric

The calorific value (CV) of a fuel is the amount of heat released on complete combustion of a unit mass (or volume). Two standard definitions are used in Indian examinations:

  • Higher Heating Value (HHV) / Gross Calorific Value (GCV) – Includes the latent heat of vaporisation of water formed during combustion.
  • Lower Heating Value (LHV) / Net Calorific Value (NCV) – Excludes the latent heat of water vapour; more relevant for engines where exhaust water remains gaseous.

3.1 Formulae

For a generic hydrocarbon CₓHᵧ:

HHV ≈ 33.9x + 142.3y  (kJ/kg)   // Approximation using Dulong’s formula
LHV = HHV – 2.44 × W   (kJ/kg)   // W = mass % of water formed

Where 33.9 and 142.3 are the combustion heat contributions of carbon and hydrogen respectively (in kJ/g). The factor 2.44 kJ/g accounts for the latent heat of vaporisation of water.

3.2 Measurement Technique – Bomb Calorimeter

  1. Sample (≈1 g) is placed in a sealed steel “bomb”.
  2. Oxygen is pressurised to 30 atm and the bomb is immersed in a water bath.
  3. Ignition triggers combustion; the temperature rise (ΔT) of the water is recorded.
  4. Calorific value = (C × ΔT) / m, where C = calorimetric constant (J °C⁻¹) and m = mass of sample.

3.3 Typical Calorific Values (HHV) – Quick Reference

Fuel State HHV (MJ/kg) LHV (MJ/kg) Key Uses (Defence)
Anthracite Coal Solid 32.5 30.0 Ship boilers, tank‑engine furnaces
Bituminous Coal Solid 28.0 25.5 Railway locomotives (historical), power plants
Petrol (Octane 92) Liquid 44.4 42.0 Ground‑vehicle engines, UAV propulsion
Diesel (EN‑590) Liquid 45.5 43.0 Armoured vehicle engines, generators
Natural Gas (CH₄) Gaseous 55.5 50.0 Gas‑turbine generators, naval propulsion (dual‑fuel)
LPG (Propane‑Butane mix) Gaseous (liquefied) 46.0 44.0 Field kitchens, portable heaters
Ethanol (Anhydrous) Liquid 29.7 27.5 Flex‑fuel vehicle blends (E‑85)
Biodiesel (B100) Liquid 38.0 36.0 Auxiliary power units, naval auxiliary vessels
Hydrogen (Compressed) Gaseous 141.8 120.0 Fuel‑cell powered drones, future combat vehicles

4. Fossil Fuels – The Traditional Energy Backbone

4.1 Coal – Types, Formation & Indian Reserves

Coal is a carbon‑rich sedimentary rock formed from plant debris under high pressure and temperature over 150–300 million years. Indian coal reserves are classified into four main ranks (in decreasing order of carbon content):

Rank Carbon % (wt) Volatile Matter % Calorific Value (HHV) MJ/kg Typical Use
Anthracite 86–98 5–15 32–33 High‑temperature furnaces, naval boilers
Bituminous 70–86 15–35 28–30 Power stations, cement kilns
Lignite (Brown Coal) 45–60 30–45 15–20 Captive power plants, district heating
Peat 30–45 50–70 8–12 Rural fuel, experimental bio‑fuel blends

Mnemonic for Coal Ranks: “ABLP – A Big Little Pea” (Anthracite, Bituminous, Lignite, Peat).

Key Indian Coalfields (Historical Milestones)

  • Jharia (Jharkhand) – Discovered 1895; major coking coal source.
  • Raniganj (West Bengal) – First commercial coal mining in India, started 1774 (British East India Company).
  • Singrauli (M.P.) – “Energy Capital of India”, development accelerated after 1975.
  • Talcher (Odisha) – Largest coal reserves in the country, exploited heavily post 1990.

4.2 Petroleum – From Crude to End Products

Petroleum is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons (C₅–C₆₀) formed from marine plankton and algae over 50–200 million years. The key steps in its utilisation are:

  1. Exploration & Extraction – Seismic surveys, drilling, primary & secondary recovery.
  2. Primary Refining (Distillation) – Fractional distillation separates crude into naphtha, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, lubricating oil.
  3. Secondary Processing – Cracking (thermal, catalytic), reforming, alkylation, isomerisation to improve octane/cetane numbers.
  4. Tertiary Treatment – Desulphurisation, hydrofining, blending to meet environmental norms.

Important Petroleum Parameters

  • API Gravity – American Petroleum Institute measure of density.
    Formula: API = (141.5 / SG) –

Cell Biology – Complete Revision Notes

1. Discovery of the Cell

The concept of the cell evolved over centuries through a series of landmark observations and experiments.

  • Robert Hooke (1665) – First used the term “cell” after observing cork under a compound microscope. 1665
  • Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (1674‑1683) – Discovered living “animalcules” (bacteria, protozoa, spermatozoa) and described their motility. 1674‑1683
  • Matthias Schleiden (1838) – Proposed that all plants are composed of cells. 1838
  • Theodor Schwann (1839) – Extended the idea to animals, stating that all living things are made of cells. 1839
  • Rudolf Virchow (1855) – Added the third tenet: “All cells arise from pre‑existing cells” (Omnis cellula e cellula). 1855

Cell Theory (Three Fundamental Statements)

  1. All living organisms are composed of one or more cells.
  2. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living organisms.
  3. All cells arise from pre‑existing cells.

Exam Tip: Remember the years 1665, 1838, 1839, 1855 – they are frequently asked in “important dates” sections of NDA/CDS papers.

2. Types of Cells – Prokaryotic vs. Eukaryotic

Cells are broadly classified into two structural categories.

2.1. Prokaryotic Cells

  • Definition: Cells lacking a true nucleus and membrane‑bound organelles.
  • Domain: Bacteria and Archaea.
  • Size: Typically 0.5 – 5 µm in diameter.
  • Key Features:
    • DNA is a single circular chromosome located in the nucleoid region.
    • Presence of plasmids – extra‑chromosomal DNA.
    • Ribosomes are 70S (30S + 50S).
    • Cell wall composed of peptidoglycan (bacteria) or pseudo‑peptidoglycan (archaea).
    • May possess surface structures – capsules, fimbriae, pili, flagella.

2.2. Eukaryotic Cells

  • Definition: Cells with a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear envelope and numerous membrane‑bound organelles.
  • Domain: Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
  • Size: Typically 10 – 100 µm in diameter.
  • Key Features:
    • Linear DNA organized into multiple chromosomes within the nucleus.
    • Ribosomes are 80S (40S + 60S).
    • Presence of mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi, lysosomes, etc.
    • Plant cells have a rigid cell wall (cellulose) and chloroplasts; animal cells lack these.

2.3. Quick Comparison

Feature Prokaryotic Eukaryotic
Nucleus Absent – nucleoid region Present – double‑membrane nuclear envelope
DNA Form Circular, single chromosome Linear, multiple chromosomes
Organelles None (except ribosomes) Numerous membrane‑bound organelles
Ribosome Size 70S (30S+50S) 80S (40S+60S)
Cell Wall Composition Peptidoglycan (bacteria) / pseudo‑peptidoglycan (archaea) Cellulose (plants) / chitin (fungi) / absent (animals)
Typical Size 0.5‑5 µm 10‑100 µm
Examples Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, Methanogens Human skin fibroblast, Oak leaf cell, Yeast cell

Mnemonic for remembering the main differences: “N‑DNA‑R‑O‑S‑C” –
Nucleus (present/absent), DNA form (circular/linear), Ribosome size (70S/80S), Organelles (few/many), Size (µm), Cell wall (peptidoglycan/cellulose).

3. Organelles – Structure, Function & Key Points

3.1. Nucleus

  • Structure: Enclosed by a double membrane (nuclear envelope) perforated by nuclear pores.
  • Components:
    • Nucleolus – site of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) synthesis and ribosome assembly.
    • Chromatin – DNA + histone proteins; appears as euchromatin (active) and heterochromatin (inactive).
  • Function: Stores genetic material, controls gene expression, coordinates cell activities.
  • Exam Tip: Remember that the nucleolus is NOT a membrane‑bound organelle – a frequent MCQ trap.

3.2. Cytoplasm & Cytoskeleton

  • Cytoplasm: Gel‑like matrix (cytosol + organelles) where metabolic reactions occur.
  • Cytoskeleton: Network of protein filaments:
    • Microfilaments (Actin) – cell movement, muscle contraction.
    • Intermediate Filaments – mechanical support.
    • Microtubules (Tubulin) – chromosome separation, vesicle transport, cilia/flagella formation.
  • Key Point: Microtubules are the “highways” for organelle movement; drugs like colchicine disrupt them – a classic pharmacology link.

3.3. Cell Membrane (Plasma Membrane)

  • Model: Fluid‑mosaic model – phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins, cholesterol, glycolipids.
  • Functions:
    • Selective permeability – regulates entry/exit of substances.
    • Signal transduction – receptors (e.g., G‑protein coupled).
    • Cell‑cell recognition – glycoproteins & glycolipids.
  • Key Numbers: Typical thickness ≈ 5‑10 nm.
  • Mnemonic: “FLUID” – Fats, Lipids, Uniform proteins, Integral & Diffuse.

3.4. Cell Wall (Plants, Fungi, Some Prokaryotes)

  • Composition: Cellulose microfibrils + pectin (plants); chitin (fungi); peptidoglycan (bacteria).
  • Function: Provides rigidity, protection, and determines cell shape.
  • Key Fact: Plant cell wall thickness varies from 0.1‑0.5 µm in parenchyma to > 1 µm in sclerenchyma.

3.5. Ribosomes

  • Structure: Two subunits (small + large) composed of rRNA + proteins.
  • Types:
    • Free ribosomes – synthesize cytosolic proteins.
    • Bound ribosomes – attached to rough ER, synthesize secretory & membrane proteins.
  • Size: 70S in prokaryotes, 80S in eukaryotes.
  • Exam Tip: Remember that “70S = 30S + 50S” and “80S = 40S + 60S”.

3.6. Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)

  • Rough ER (RER): Studded with ribosomes; site of protein synthesis, initial folding, and N‑linked glycosylation.
  • Smooth ER (SER): Lacks ribosomes; involved in lipid synthesis, detoxification (Cytochrome P450), calcium storage.
  • Key Distinction: RER = “Ribosome‑rich”; SER = “Synthesis (lipids) & detox”.

3.7. Golgi Apparatus (Golgi Complex)

  • Structure: Stacked cisternae (usually 3‑12 stacks) with cis (receiving) and trans (shipping) faces.
  • Functions:
    • Modification of proteins (phosphorylation, sulfation).
    • Sorting & packaging into vesicles.
    • Formation of lysosomes (via mannose‑6‑phosphate tagging).
  • Mnemonic: “CIS‑TRANS = RECEIVE‑DISPATCH”.

3.8. Lysosome

  • Structure: Membrane‑bound vesicle containing hydrolytic enzymes (acid hydrolases).
  • pH: Acidic interior ≈ 4.5‑5.0.
  • Functions: Intracellular digestion, autophagy, recycling of macromolecules, apoptosis (via cathepsins).
  • Clinical Link: Deficiency of specific lysosomal enzymes leads to storage disorders (e.g., Tay‑Sachs, Gaucher’s disease).

3.9. Peroxisome

  • Key Enzymes: Catalase, urate oxidase, acyl‑CoA oxidase.
  • Functions:
    • Breakdown of fatty acids via β‑oxidation (short‑chain).
    • Detoxification of hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) → H₂O + O₂ (catalase reaction).
  • Exam Note: Peroxisomes are abundant in liver and kidney cells.

3.10. Mitochondrion – “Powerhouse of the Cell”

  • Structure: Double membrane; inner membrane folded into cristae; matrix contains DNA, ribosomes, enzymes.
  • DNA: Circular, ~16.5 kb, encodes 13 proteins, 2 rRNAs, 22 tRNAs.
  • Functions:
    • ATP production via oxidative phosphorylation (ETC & chemiosmosis).
    • Regulation of apoptosis (cytochrome c release).
    • Calcium homeostasis.
  • Key Numbers: Approx. 100‑1000
